candidates.name: Safe AI Forum (SAIF): International Dialogues on AI Safety (IDAIS)
candidates.one_line: US nonprofit that convenes senior Western and Chinese scientists (Yao, Bengio, Zhang Ya-Qin, Russell) in the IDAIS series to agree joint statements on extreme AI risks.
candidates.field_lens: Track II science diplomacy, scientist-to-scientist confidence building on the Pugwash model
candidates.ai_connection: Five dialogues so far (Oxford 2023, Beijing 2024, Venice 2024, Shanghai 2025, London 2026). IDAIS-London was co-hosted with Oxford Martin AIGI and produced the IDAIS London Declaration on stopping societal-scale harms from AI-enabled attacks. Earlier statements set red lines, e.g. on autonomous replication.

candidates.name: Concordia AI
candidates.one_line: Beijing-based social enterprise that makes China's AI-safety landscape legible to the rest of the world and connects Chinese and international safety researchers.
candidates.field_lens: Cross-cultural translation, China studies, international relations
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes the annual State of AI Safety in China report: the fourth edition (July 2026) covers July 2025 to June 2026, including China's shift toward governing agentic systems. Also runs the AI Safety in China newsletter and international safety conferences.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Beijing-based social enterprise working on AI safety and international governance with a China focus. It produces the State of AI Safety in China reports, the Frontier AI Risk Monitoring Platform and the 'AI Safety in China' newsletter.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: State of AI Safety in China (2026). Frontier AI Risk Monitoring Platform v2.0 (launched at WAIC, July 2026). The Frontier and Agentic AI Safety Forum in Shanghai. Analysis of China's TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 and of China's open-weights policy. Its main value is translation across the US–China divide, not a non-Western ethical framework.

candidates.name: Simon Institute for Longterm Governance
candidates.one_line: Geneva think tank working on frontier-AI diplomacy: it trains diplomats and international civil servants and feeds research into UN processes on AI.
candidates.field_lens: Multilateral diplomacy, UN system expertise, Herbert Simon's future-oriented policymaking
candidates.ai_connection: Educates Geneva and New York diplomats on frontier AI risks and contributes policy input to the UN's AI governance processes, such as the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Funded by Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving).

candidates.name: Institute for Security and Technology (IST)
candidates.one_line: Security think tank that applies nuclear-security and arms-control practice to advanced AI.
candidates.field_lens: Nuclear security, NC3, arms control, cybersecurity
candidates.ai_connection: Programmes: AI and NC3 (nuclear command, control and communications); an AI Risk Reduction Initiative; a Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative on oversight of RSI-capable models; US-China AI risk-reduction dialogue on AI incidents; the AI Risk Barometer; and the Andrew Carnegie AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator (2026).

alt_descriptions.one_line: IST programme, launched 2026, that gives mid-career nuclear-security professionals technical AI literacy; its first cohort met in Silicon Valley.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Builds a pipeline from the nuclear-risk community into AI-nuclear and AI-security policy. A concrete cross-field talent bridge, funded by Carnegie money.

candidates.name: Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative (AIGI)
candidates.one_line: Oxford research centre on AI governance; co-host of IDAIS-London 2026 and author of research on US-China AI-safety dialogue.
candidates.field_lens: International relations, political science, technical governance
candidates.ai_connection: Co-hosted the fifth IDAIS (London 2026) with SAIF. Published 'Promising Topics for US–China Dialogues on AI Safety and Governance', a research agenda for Track I and II diplomacy on AI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Robert Trager's Oxford centre combining political science, economics and machine learning on national and international AI regulation, including a Technical Safety Governance Lab led by Fazl Barez.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Its 2026 outputs cover agentic inequality, safety of robotic foundation models, frontier-risk evaluation and LLM vulnerabilities. It is largely inside the conventional AI-policy canon; listed here to verify the starting point, not as an outside-canon find.

candidates.name: Oxford China Policy Lab (OCPL)
candidates.one_line: Non-partisan Oxford research group working to reduce global risks from US-China great-power competition, especially those arising from AI.
candidates.field_lens: China studies, international relations, great-power competition
candidates.ai_connection: Research agenda on the intersecting risks of US-China competition and AI development. Studies the bureaucratic and sociopolitical drivers of the AI race (e.g. status-seeking dynamics). Runs a 3-month part-time fellowship at the US-China/AI intersection; the 2026 cohort is under way.

candidates.name: AI Safety Asia (AISA)
candidates.one_line: Manila-based nonprofit (founded 2024) that builds Asia's AI-safety governance capacity and runs confidential channels and crisis-preparedness exercises for senior Asian officials.
candidates.field_lens: Regional diplomacy, scenario-based crisis planning, Global South perspectives
candidates.ai_connection: Programmes Curate, Inform and Catalyse; the last keeps confidential channels open for officials before formal negotiations. RAISE-SEA, a Paris Peace Forum-supported scenario platform, has regional leaders write 'Preparedness Playbooks' for AI arms races and job disruption. Ran an AI-crisis-response convening at the India AI Impact Summit (Feb 2026) and co-published with Brookings on AI safety governance in Southeast Asia.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A regional AI-governance organisation. It helps Asia's middle powers act together on frontier AI, connecting national officials with frontier-risk scientists and running crisis simulations.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: 2026: AI Diplomacy Crisis tabletop exercises in Geneva (with FLI, RAND Europe and Chatham House) and at APEC in Dalian. A four-country AI-biosecurity mapping study for UK FCDO. Training for Indonesian officials that shaped Indonesia's draft presidential AI decree. Earlier: a Cooperative AI course (Asia edition, 2025), the SEA Observatory, and a Brookings report on AI governance in Southeast Asia.

candidates.name: UChicago Existential Risk Laboratory (XLab)
candidates.one_line: University of Chicago lab, grown out of the nuclear-risk community (Nobel laureate assemblies, the Bulletin's science board), that studies AI, nuclear and other existential threats together.
candidates.field_lens: Nuclear risk, physics and science-and-security tradition
candidates.ai_connection: Co-sponsored the July 2026 Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War, which produced the Rome Declaration. Runs a summer research fellowship covering AI risk. One of the few places where nuclear and AI x-risk are worked on under one roof.

candidates.name: UN Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR): AI, Security and Ethics
candidates.one_line: The UN's autonomous disarmament research institute, which runs the Roundtable for AI, Security and Ethics (RAISE) and the annual Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics in Geneva.
candidates.field_lens: Disarmament diplomacy, arms control, multilateralism
candidates.ai_connection: RAISE (launched 2024) brings experts from all five UN regional groups into dialogue on AI and security. The AISE conferences (March 2025, June 2026) convene militaries, labs and diplomats; Brookings and Tsinghua CISS met there in 2026. Other outputs: a voluntary industry framework on military AI co-developed with OHCHR, an AI Policy Portal, and a Women in AI fellowship for diplomats.

candidates.name: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI): AI and nuclear risk
candidates.one_line: Leading peace research institute whose emerging-technology programme studies how military AI could cause inadvertent nuclear escalation, and convenes nuclear-armed states on it.
candidates.field_lens: Peace research, arms control, strategic stability
candidates.ai_connection: Carnegie-funded project (Sept 2024, 24 months, $500k) on nuclear escalation in the age of AI, aiming at a 'menu' of risk-reduction measures. A September 2025 Stockholm workshop drew experts from seven of the nine nuclear-armed states. Earlier work: a 2017-2020 project on machine learning and strategic stability.

candidates.name: Brookings–Tsinghua US-China Track II Dialogue on AI and National Security
candidates.one_line: Seven-year Track II dialogue between Brookings and Tsinghua CISS on military AI risks, sustained 'by mutual interest, not mutual trust'.
candidates.field_lens: Track II diplomacy, security studies
candidates.ai_connection: Has produced shared terminology work and joint emphasis on keeping human control over nuclear decisions. Its groundwork preceded the May 2026 Trump–Xi agreement to open an intergovernmental AI dialogue and the US proposal (Sept 2026) for an AI-incident alert mechanism. Led by R. David Edelman and Ryan Hass (Brookings) with Xiao Qian (CISS).

candidates.name: Center for International Security and Strategy, Tsinghua University (CISS)
candidates.one_line: Tsinghua's international-security centre, China's main Track II counterpart on AI security; it runs an 'AI and International Security' project.
candidates.field_lens: Security studies, Chinese diplomacy, arms control
candidates.ai_connection: Seven-plus rounds of the US-China Dialogue on AI and International Security with Brookings, and an AI Terminology Working Group. Held a 2023 dialogue with HD on military AI. Its January 2026 Forum on AI and International Security covered AI militarisation, non-state threats and China's governance initiatives.

candidates.name: Center for Global AI Innovation Governance, Fudan University (CGAIG)
candidates.one_line: Shanghai university think tank on global AI governance rules, capacity building and international agenda-setting; it takes part in Chinese AI-security dialogue.
candidates.field_lens: International relations, Chinese governance studies
candidates.ai_connection: Took part in Tsinghua CISS's January 2026 AI and International Security forum. Works on global AI governance rules and on China's international AI agenda, so it is a likely interlocutor for Western Track II efforts.

candidates.name: Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue (HD): AI and Emerging Technologies programme
candidates.one_line: Geneva private-diplomacy and mediation organisation whose AI and Emerging Technologies (AIET) programme runs discreet dialogues on the risks of military AI.
candidates.field_lens: Mediation, discreet (private) diplomacy, conflict prevention
candidates.ai_connection: A two-year dialogue among Chinese, American and international experts produced a draft Code of Conduct on AI in Military Systems (2021). Held a 2023 dialogue with Tsinghua CISS on AI security governance. Expanding military-AI dialogue work from 2025 and hiring advanced-AI advisors.

candidates.name: European Leadership Network (ELN): Nuclear Weapons and Emerging Technologies
candidates.one_line: London-based pan-European security network whose programme on nuclear weapons and new technologies works on keeping AI out of nuclear crisis escalation.
candidates.field_lens: Nuclear risk reduction, European security, P5 diplomacy
candidates.ai_connection: Projects: 'Firebreaks: Mitigating the Risks of AI Integration into Nuclear Operations', a Nuclear Fail-Safe Review, and a P5-perspectives report on AI in NC3. A July 2026 commentary calls for AI-incident hotlines, national fail-safe reviews and a P5 agenda on human control.

candidates.name: Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs
candidates.one_line: The Nobel-winning scientists' network for nuclear disarmament (founded 1957), now applying its Track II tradition to AI through its Science and Security programme.
candidates.field_lens: Scientist-led Track II diplomacy, nuclear disarmament
candidates.ai_connection: July 2026 Rome workshop 'AI and Nuclear Weapons: Risks and Opportunities' (20 specialists across computer science, physics, law and geopolitics). Organising partner of the July 2026 Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War. Appointed an inaugural Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security (June 2026). Pugwash is also the historical model for IDAIS.

candidates.name: Global Commission on Responsible AI in the Military Domain (GC REAIM)
candidates.one_line: Dutch-government-launched commission of state, industry, academic and civil-society members, with its secretariat at The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies, that writes governance guidance on military AI.
candidates.field_lens: Security studies, international humanitarian law, strategic studies
candidates.ai_connection: Presented its Strategic Guidance Report at the third REAIM Summit (A Coruña, Feb 2026), and it fed into the 'Pathways to Action' declaration. Only 40 states endorsed that declaration, against 60+ in 2024; the US, China and India abstained. There was strong consensus on human control over nuclear C2.

candidates.name: Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War (Rome Declaration)
candidates.one_line: July 2026 Vatican-hosted assembly of about 200 Nobel laureates, nuclear experts, staff from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind, and religious leaders, which signed the Rome Declaration on AI, nuclear and autonomous weapons.
candidates.field_lens: Peace movement, nuclear abolition, Catholic social teaching and interfaith ethics, physicians' movement (IPPNW)
candidates.ai_connection: The Rome Declaration calls for a treaty banning 'reckless integration' of AI into nuclear operations, and for keeping life-and-death decisions under meaningful human control. Co-sponsors were UChicago XLab, Notre Dame, Harvard Medical School, the Bulletin, IPPNW and Catholic University; Pugwash was an organising partner. It was inspired by Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica humanitas.

candidates.name: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
candidates.one_line: Nuclear-age magazine and keeper of the Doomsday Clock, with a disruptive-technologies desk that covers AI, autonomous weapons and information warfare.
candidates.field_lens: Nuclear risk, science-and-security journalism
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes AI-and-escalation analysis (e.g. Herb Lin, March 2026, on AI in the information ecosystem and nuclear escalation) and also sceptical pieces on AI 'doomerism'. Factors disruptive technology into the Doomsday Clock. Co-sponsored the 2026 Nobel Laureates Assembly.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Nonprofit magazine founded by Manhattan Project scientists. It sets the Doomsday Clock (85 seconds to midnight in 2026) and runs a 'disruptive technologies' section on existential threats from AI, bio and cyber.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It has made AI a named driver of existential risk on the Doomsday Clock and calls for international guidelines on AI use. It ran 'The AI Power Trip' special project (Oct 2025). It is plural in stance and also publishes critiques of 'AI doomerism'.

candidates.name: Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI)
candidates.one_line: Global security nonprofit on nuclear and biological threats that convenes international guardrail-setting on AI-enabled biodesign and on AI in nuclear decision-making.
candidates.field_lens: Nonproliferation, biosecurity, global health security
candidates.ai_connection: NTI|bio's report on AI and life-sciences convergence led to the Global AIxBio Forum, an international platform for guardrails against misuse of AI biodesign tools. Its Science and Technology Advisory Group works on AI and nuclear decision-making. Launched a new intergenerational biological-threats initiative with The Elders (2026).

candidates.name: The Elders
candidates.one_line: Independent group of former world leaders (founded by Nelson Mandela) working on existential threats and conflict, which in 2025-26 began scoping a dedicated programme on international AI governance.
candidates.field_lens: Elder statesmanship, peace and human rights, intergenerational dialogue, multilateralism
candidates.ai_connection: Frames ungoverned AI as an existential threat that compounds nuclear, pandemic and conflict risk. Commissioned an AI programme-strategy scoping (Dec 2025 to May 2026), co-signed open letters with FLI, and co-sponsored the September 2026 UN forum calling for autonomous-weapons treaty negotiations.

candidates.name: Carnegie Corporation of New York
candidates.one_line: Major US foundation whose international peace and security grantmaking is the main funder of the AI–nuclear risk bridge.
candidates.field_lens: Peace and security philanthropy, nuclear risk reduction
candidates.ai_connection: Funds SIPRI's AI and nuclear escalation project ($500k, 2024; earlier $400k for machine learning and strategic stability), the Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security (2026), and IST's Andrew Carnegie AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator. New AI-safety funders could co-fund with it, or fill the gaps it leaves.

candidates.name: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace: Technology and International Affairs Program
candidates.one_line: Programme within the century-old peace think tank that works on AI and geopolitics, international security, development and governance, including a China AI Initiative.
candidates.field_lens: International relations, peace studies, China studies
candidates.ai_connection: AI x Geopolitics and International Security strand on the dangers of the race toward advanced AI. China AI Initiative co-directed by Scott Singer. Works on international AI governance institutions. Co-directed by Jon Bateman and Arthur Nelson.

candidates.name: Stanford Center for International Security and Cooperation (CISAC)
candidates.one_line: Stanford's 40-year-old international security centre, with a long US-China Track II record, now publishing on AI and nuclear escalation.
candidates.field_lens: Security studies, nuclear policy, US-China Track II
candidates.ai_connection: Herb Lin's work on AI in the information ecosystem and nuclear escalation (Bulletin, March 2026). Historic US-China dialogues on nuclear, cyber and space issues give it a template for AI dialogue. AI is not yet a dedicated CISAC programme, as far as its site shows.

candidates.name: UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
candidates.one_line: Universal UN forum created by General Assembly resolution A/RES/79/325 after the Summit of the Future; its first session met in Geneva on 6-7 July 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Multilateral diplomacy, UN system
candidates.ai_connection: Covers 'safe, secure and trustworthy AI' alongside capacity-building and human rights. Co-chaired 2026-27 by El Salvador and Estonia; the next session is New York, May 2027. It is the main universal venue where Global South states take part in AI-safety norm-setting, and it pairs with the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.

candidates.name: Stop Killer Robots
candidates.one_line: Coalition of 300+ NGOs in 70+ countries (steering members include HRW, Amnesty, Article 36 and ICRAC) campaigning for new international law to keep human control over the use of force.
candidates.field_lens: Humanitarian disarmament, human rights, international humanitarian law
candidates.ai_connection: Pushing treaty negotiations on autonomous weapons. In September 2026, 128 states agreed a definitional text in the CCW, and treaty talks are being sought at the November CCW Review Conference. Its 'digital dehumanisation' framing (people reduced to data for automated decisions) extends to civilian AI. Treaty campaigns like this are a template for binding AI limits, though the coalition does not use x-risk framing.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A global coalition of 300+ organisations in 70+ countries campaigning for new international law to keep meaningful human control over the use of force by autonomous weapons.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Bears directly on loss of human control over military AI. It helped secure UN General Assembly resolutions backed by 156 states (November 2025) and pushed CCW expert talks (Geneva, August–September 2026) toward treaty negotiations, alongside the UN Secretary-General and ICRC 'moral red line' call (August 2026). This is the most successful existing model of the international AI red-lines campaigns AI safety wants.

candidates.name: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC): autonomous weapons and AI
candidates.one_line: Guardian of international humanitarian law, which calls for binding rules prohibiting unpredictable and anti-personnel autonomous weapons and requiring meaningful human control.
candidates.field_lens: International humanitarian law, humanitarian ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Its 'meaningful human control' doctrine is the most developed legal treatment of human oversight of AI systems that take irreversible actions. It also works on AI decision-support systems in warfare. Activity in 2026: joint calls with the UN Secretary-General (Aug 2026), co-sponsorship of the September 2026 treaty forum, and working papers to the UNGA (Oct 2026).

candidates.name: Build Up
candidates.one_line: Conflict-transformation nonprofit (founded 2014) that analyses how digital platforms and AI drive polarisation and violence, and builds peacebuilding responses.
candidates.field_lens: Peacebuilding, conflict transformation, participatory methods, arts
candidates.ai_connection: Created the Polarization Footprint, a tool for holding platforms accountable for division. Built Phoenix, an open-source AI-enabled social-listening tool for mediators. Runs digital-conflict programming in Sudan, Yemen, Myanmar and the Sahel, and co-organises the annual Build Peace conference (2026 edition at Waterloo). Brings conflict-transformation practice to AI's effects on social cohesion.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Peacebuilding-and-technology collective that analyses how digital technology and AI drive conflict. It builds Phoenix, an open-source AI social-media listening platform for mediators.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It works on AI-amplified polarisation and information warfare in conflict zones, for example social-media listening reports on Sudan in 2026, and brings Global South practitioner perspective to AI and collective sensemaking.

candidates.name: AI for Peace
candidates.one_line: Think tank, founded by Rotary Peace Fellow Branka Panic, that equips peacebuilders to shape AI and studies AI's risks to human security and human rights.
candidates.field_lens: Peace studies, human security, humanitarian action
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes a non-technical AI guide for policymakers and the book AI for Peace. Founded after seeing dual-use risk first-hand: open famine-prediction models could tell warring parties where vulnerable people were. Brings peacebuilder voices into AI design and governance.

candidates.name: UN DPPA Innovation Cell
candidates.one_line: Interdisciplinary team in the UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (since 2020) that pilots AI for mediation, including AI-assisted 'digital dialogues' with up to 1,000 participants in peace processes.
candidates.field_lens: UN mediation, conflict prevention, deliberative methods
candidates.ai_connection: AI-powered consultations, using Remesh, have surfaced consensus on ceasefires and humanitarian measures in Yemen, Libya, Iraq, Haiti and elsewhere. It also trains political officers on generative AI. Hands-on evidence for AI-mediated collective deliberation, a method central to pluralistic alignment.

candidates.name: Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO)
candidates.one_line: Major peace research institute and conflict-data producer, now researching AI-enabled digital authoritarianism and using AI to connect conflict data.
candidates.field_lens: Quantitative peace and conflict research, digital politics
candidates.ai_connection: Projects: AI-enabled digital authoritarianism in Asia (2026-28); the ERC-funded BRIDGE project on AI and knowledge graphs for peace and conflict data (2026); the ePOLITICS initiative on digital politics; PRIO AI Days. Could become an empirical monitor of AI's effects on conflict.

candidates.name: Geneva Centre for Security Policy (GCSP)
candidates.one_line: International foundation with 55 member states that trains diplomats and officers, runs a transformative-technologies cluster, and hosts the Processes of International Negotiation (PIN) programme.
candidates.field_lens: Security policy education, negotiation science, foresight
candidates.ai_connection: 2026 project with UN CTED and the Swiss foreign ministry on human-rights-centred AI in counter-terrorism. Its PIN negotiation-research network holds decades of knowledge on multilateral bargaining, directly relevant to designing international AI agreements and to evaluating how AI agents negotiate. That bridge is untapped.

candidates.name: African Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes (ACCORD)
candidates.one_line: Durban-based pan-African conflict-resolution organisation, pushing to put African peacebuilding experience at the centre of how AI peacebuilding tools are built and governed.
candidates.field_lens: African mediation and peacebuilding, Ubuntu-informed conflict resolution
candidates.ai_connection: Spoke at the inaugural UN Peacebuilding Week (June 2026) side event 'Making AI Work for Trustworthy and Inclusive Peacebuilding'. No dedicated AI programme yet. It is a natural African partner for any Global South perspective on AI risk, a perspective that is largely missing.

candidates.name: Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC)
candidates.one_line: ECOWAS-region peacekeeping training and research centre in Accra that ran an 'Artificial Intelligence in Peacebuilding' course in 2025.
candidates.field_lens: Peacekeeping, African security studies
candidates.ai_connection: Trains African security practitioners on AI in peace operations. A potential West African hub for AI-and-security capacity-building, which the REAIM process says developing nations lack.

candidates.name: Geneva Science and Diplomacy Anticipator (GESDA)
candidates.one_line: Swiss public-private foundation (2019) for 'anticipatory science diplomacy'; it built the Open Quantum Institute to govern an emerging technology inclusively.
candidates.field_lens: Science diplomacy, technology foresight
candidates.ai_connection: No AI-specific initiative is visible. Its Science Breakthrough Radar and the Open Quantum Institute (with CERN) are a working template for an inclusive 'CERN for AI' or shared-access body, an institutional design question for international AI governance.

candidates.name: AE Studio (alignment team)
candidates.one_line: A software and data-science consultancy whose alignment team, funded by its client work, pursues 'neglected approaches', several of them drawn from neuroscience and cognitive science.
candidates.field_lens: Social and cognitive neuroscience (empathy, self-other distinction), attention schema theory of consciousness (Graziano), self-modelling
candidates.ai_connection: Self-Other Overlap fine-tuning (2024 agenda; March 2025 results on reducing LLM deception), which borrows the neural self/other representation overlap linked to empathy. Also research on self-modelling and attention schemas for prosocial AI, and 2025 work on LLM reports of subjective experience under self-referential processing, which bears on AI welfare.

candidates.name: Astera Institute: Obelisk AGI programme, Astera Neuro, and Steve Byrnes's brain-like-AGI safety
candidates.one_line: A philanthropic research institute (more than $1B committed over the next decade) that runs a brain-inspired AGI programme (Obelisk, with Dileep George), a new neuroscience programme on the computational basis of consciousness (Astera Neuro, chief scientist Doris Tsao), and funds Steve Byrnes's brain-like-AGI safety research.
candidates.field_lens: Systems and experimental neuroscience, computational neuroscience, model-based RL as a model of the brain
candidates.ai_connection: Byrnes's 'Intro to brain-like-AGI safety' series (revised June 2026) and his 2025 posts on technical alignment via human-like social drives try to reverse-engineer human social instincts as an alignment target. Obelisk states it aims at 'safe, efficient and aligned' brain-inspired AGI. Caveat: Obelisk is also a capabilities effort, and Byrnes himself warns that brain-like RL is a dangerous route to AGI.

candidates.name: Simplex
candidates.location: Emeryville, USA and London, UK (under the Astera Institute)
candidates.one_line: An AI safety research group founded in 2024 by Paul Riechers and Adam Shai that combines physics (computational mechanics) with computational neuroscience to understand the internal structure of neural networks.
candidates.field_lens: Computational neuroscience, statistical physics, computational mechanics, Bayesian belief-state theory
candidates.ai_connection: Shows that transformers organise activations into geometric belief-state structures (fractal 'belief state geometry'), that attention implements constrained belief updating, and that world models decompose into factored parts. This is a neuroscience-style science of representations aimed at interpretability, under the slogan 'understanding intelligence is safety'.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Roughly 25-person research team inside the Astera Institute that uses computational mechanics (the physics of information and prediction) and computational neuroscience to build a principled science of how neural networks represent the world.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Showed that transformers trained on next-token prediction develop 'belief-state geometries' (sometimes fractal) that match Bayesian updating over hidden world models. 2026 papers cover factored representations and interpretable reasoning signals. Its motto is 'understanding intelligence is safety'. MATS stream; AXRP episode 36. Founded 2024 by Paul Riechers and Adam Shai.

candidates.name: Amaranth Foundation: NeuroAI for AI Safety
candidates.one_line: A longevity and neuroscience philanthropy (over $50M committed, including to NeuroAI) that funded and published the 152-page 'NeuroAI for AI Safety' roadmap led by Patrick Mineault.
candidates.field_lens: NeuroAI, systems neuroscience, connectomics, digital twins, neurotechnology
candidates.ai_connection: The roadmap (arXiv 2411.18526; v2 April 2025) evaluates seven routes from neuroscience to safety: reverse-engineering sensory representations for robustness, embodied digital twins, biophysically detailed models, cognitive architectures, fine-tuning on brain data, extracting loss functions from biology, and neuroscience methods for interpretability. It is the reference document for the field, but there is no visible 2025-26 grant programme or institutional follow-through.

candidates.name: Foresight Institute: Neurotechnology for Safe AI grants
candidates.one_line: A grant track within Foresight's AI safety grants ($1.5–2M a year in total) for neurotech that could 'integrate with or compete against AGI': BCIs, whole brain emulation and lo-fi emulation, and enabling work such as cheaper brain mapping.
candidates.field_lens: Neurotechnology, connectomics, whole brain emulation, brain-computer interfaces
candidates.ai_connection: The only standing grant line explicitly funding neurotech as an AI safety strategy. It frames WBE as a human-like intelligence that may be more interpretable and easier to align than de novo AGI, and funds work that removes bottlenecks to it, such as making neurobiological data easier for models to learn from.

candidates.name: Eon Systems PBC
candidates.one_line: A public-benefit corporation (about 11 staff, $3.5M seed in Dec 2025) building whole-brain emulations from connectomics plus functional imaging. In 2026 it showed an embodied adult fruit fly emulation (139k neurons, about 91% behavioural accuracy) and plans a mouse brain next.
candidates.field_lens: Connectomics, expansion microscopy, computational neuroscience, whole brain emulation
candidates.ai_connection: Its stated mission is helping 'humans flourish in a world with superintelligence': brain emulation as an alternative and more legible path to general intelligence, plus tools for AI robustness. Whether WBE differentially helps safety or just adds another capabilities race is contested, and this is a useful test case for 'speed of wisdom' discernment.

candidates.name: Carboncopies Foundation
candidates.one_line: A volunteer-heavy nonprofit advancing whole brain emulation through workshops, the Brain Emulation Challenge (Feb 2025), the BrainGenix simulation platform, journal clubs, an ethics framework, and due-diligence reviews of WBE startup claims.
candidates.field_lens: Whole brain emulation, neuroinformatics, neuroethics
candidates.ai_connection: Potential: holds the WBE ground-truthing and benchmarking know-how that Foresight's and Amaranth's NeuroAI-safety routes depend on, and could referee claims like Eon's. It does not yet frame its work as AI safety.

candidates.name: Brain-inspired Cognitive Intelligence Lab (BrainCog), Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
candidates.one_line: Yi Zeng's lab building spiking-neural-network, brain-inspired cognitive AI (the BrainCog and BORN engines), alongside his International Research Center for AI Ethics and Governance and the Center for Long-term AI.
candidates.field_lens: Brain-inspired computing, cognitive neuroscience of theory of mind, empathy and self-models; Chinese philosophy of human-AI symbiosis
candidates.ai_connection: Papers such as 'A Brain-Inspired Theory of Mind Spiking Neural Network for Reducing Safety Risks of Other Agents' and 'AI with Cognitive Empathy' argue that safety and morality should come from brain-like self-models, empathy and ToM rather than external constraints. Zeng also founded Beijing-AISI (on the classic map) and sits on the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI. It is the clearest non-Western neuro-to-safety bridge. Caveat: the lab also pursues 'living AGI'.

candidates.name: Whole Brain Architecture Initiative (WBAI)
candidates.one_line: A Japanese nonprofit (since 2015, led by Hiroshi Yamakawa; backed by Toyota, Toshiba, Panasonic and Dwango) building brain-inspired AGI from a shared 'brain reference architecture' through hackathons, tutorials and incentive awards, framed as 'bridging humanity and superintelligence'.
candidates.field_lens: Neuroanatomy-based cognitive architecture, computational neuroscience
candidates.ai_connection: Brain reference architectures could make AGI internals more legible by mapping components to known brain circuits. Yamakawa's linked writing on post-singularity symbiosis feeds into ALIGN. It is a dual-use capabilities effort, and its safety content is thinner than its AGI content.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Japanese nonprofit, chaired by Hiroshi Yamakawa, building an open reference architecture for human-brain-morphic AGI. It frames that AGI as a value-understanding 'bridge between humanity and superintelligence'.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: FY2026 policy: brain-morphic AGI can understand human values 'from within' and can be interpreted through neuroscience, so it could mediate between humans and superintelligence. Whole-Brain Reference Architecture alpha is due February 2027. Hackathons and incentive awards. Caveat: it is partly a capabilities project, and its safety thesis is contestable.

candidates.name: AI Alignment Network (ALIGN)
candidates.one_line: A Japanese nonprofit network for AI alignment research, community building and outreach. Its leaders include brain-inspired-AI researchers Hiroshi Yamakawa (University of Tokyo, WBAI) and Koichi Takahashi (RIKEN).
candidates.field_lens: Brain-inspired AGI, machine ethics, Japanese 'symbiosis' framing of human-AI coexistence, thermodynamics of intelligence
candidates.ai_connection: Ran the Post-Singularity Symbiosis Workshop (PSS 2025), scenario contests and webinars, and published the position paper 'Humanity in the Circle' and workshop reports on emergent machine ethics (Feb 2026). It offers a non-Anglophone, symbiosis-rather-than-control framing of alignment.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Japanese nonprofit building an alignment research ecosystem. Its distinctive framings are 'emergent machine ethics', 'post-singularity symbiosis' and 'intelligence symbiosis', alongside safety and controllability.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Outputs: the 'Emergent Machine Ethics' research framework (Dec 2025), the 'Humanity in the Circle' position paper (May 2026), the PSS 2025 Workshop on Post-Singularity Symbiosis, AAAI-25 workshops, and work on the thermodynamic limits of physical intelligence and identity maintenance for AI safety. People include Hiroshi Yamakawa (Tokyo) and Koichi Takahashi (RIKEN). It is one of the few non-Anglophone alignment hubs and has a coexistence-oriented framing.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Japanese nonprofit building an alignment research community in Japan and the region, led by Hiroshi Yamakawa (University of Tokyo, Whole Brain Architecture Initiative) and Koichi Takahashi (RIKEN). Its distinctive framing is 'Intelligence Symbiosis'.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Runs grants, webinars, study groups and a scenario contest about futures with superintelligence. Its Post-Singularity Symbiosis framework and Intelligence Symbiosis chapter treat humans and AI co-evolving as an alignment target. Papers include 'Emergent Machine Ethics' and 'AI Immune Systems'. It is one of the few relational, non-Western framings with an alignment organisation behind it.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Japanese alignment nonprofit chaired by Koichi Takahashi (RIKEN/Keio), co-founded with Ryota Kanai (Araya) and Hiroshi Yamakawa (WBAI), with Dan Hendrycks as external adviser. It does research and field-building in Japan around an 'intelligence symbiosis' paradigm.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Runs the Post-Singularity Symbiosis workshops at AAAI-25 and AAAI-26. Their best-paper winner proposed developmental support for AI's moral growth instead of control. Other outputs: the 'Emergent Machine Ethics' research framework (Dec 2025); the 'Humanity in the Circle' position paper (May 2026); an AI immune-system proposal (Feb 2026) answering Yampolskiy's impossibility results; 'Lowering Collective Free Energy for Consensus in LLM Agent Collectives'; the NAGI national AGI-foundation concept; and AI safety community-building in Japan led by Kazuki Kimura, formerly of Japan AISI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Japanese nonprofit building an alignment research community across academia and industry (Hiroshi Yamakawa, Koichi Takahashi; University of Tokyo, RIKEN). Its work includes position papers on 'intelligence symbiosis', workshops on machine ethics and post-singularity symbiosis, the NAGI programme and superintelligence scenario contests.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: A non-Western framing of the alignment target (symbiosis rather than control), plus field-building in Japanese. It is absent from the classic map.

candidates.name: Monash Centre for Consciousness and Contemplative Studies (M3CS)
candidates.one_line: A Monash University centre (Jakob Hohwy) combining consciousness science, active inference and contemplative studies, and the academic home of several authors of the 'Contemplative AI' programme.
candidates.field_lens: Predictive processing and active inference, contemplative science (mindfulness, emptiness, non-duality), philosophy of mind
candidates.ai_connection: Co-authored 'Contemplative Artificial Intelligence' (Laukkonen, Chandaria, Sandved-Smith, Hohwy et al., v3 Aug 2025). It proposes four contemplative principles (mindfulness, emptiness, non-duality, boundless care) as alignment design principles that active-inference architectures could implement, and reports improved AILuminate safety scores and Prisoner's Dilemma cooperation when models are prompted with them.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Monash University centre for consciousness science and contemplative studies, associated with predictive-processing researcher Jakob Hohwy.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Hohwy co-authored 'Contemplative Artificial Intelligence' (arXiv 2504.15125), and the Buddhism & AI Initiative lists 'Monash Center' under the computational neuroscience behind Buddhism→AI. It holds methods for formalising contemplative states in active-inference models, which the contemplative-alignment agenda depends on. Its site returned 403, so its current AI activity is unverified.

candidates.name: Active Inference Institute
candidates.one_line: An open, volunteer-run research and education community around Karl Friston's active inference and free energy principle, running livestreams, textbook groups and the annual Applied Active Inference Symposium (6th edition, 12–13 Nov 2026, Friston keynote).
candidates.field_lens: Theoretical neuroscience (free energy principle, active inference), cognitive science of agency
candidates.ai_connection: Potential: active inference offers a formal account of agency in which preferences live in the agent's generative model. Papers such as 'Possible Principles for Aligned Structure Learning Agents' (Da Costa et al. 2024) treat alignment as learning another agent's world model. The community is mostly disconnected from safety orgs, and its commercial arm (VERSES) markets 'intrinsically safe' agents without strong evidence.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A volunteer-led open-science nonprofit with more than 2,000 members that runs education, research projects, fellowships, livestreams and symposia on active inference and the free-energy principle.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: In June 2025 SFF gave it $270k for the AI Capabilities & Alignment Consensus Project (AICACP), a multi-year effort of journal collections, workshops and media on 'world models' and 'agency' meant to bridge AI optimists and pessimists. Its lead is Adam Safron of Tufts' Allen Discovery Center, which ties the Levin ecosystem to alignment. In March 2026 it named Mahault Albarracin a fellow for 'AI²C: Active Inference Alignment Coalition', a multi-university consortium for alignment research. It also hosts Hongju Pae's study of 'coherent and attuned artificial agency', presented at the AAAI 2026 Spring Symposium on Machine Consciousness. The community's main academic venue is IWAI, held in Madrid on 14–16 October 2026.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Volunteer-led participatory open-science nonprofit (about 2,000 members) for education and research on active inference and the free-energy principle, with 700+ livestreams, working groups and fellowships.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Active inference is one of the few complete formal theories of agency and of nested 'agents made of agents' (Markov blankets). ACS's hierarchical-agency work draws on it. Specific problem: formal definitions of agent boundaries and multi-scale goals for multi-agent AI. The institute itself has no visible safety programme.

candidates.name: Re-Align: Workshop on Representational Alignment
candidates.one_line: A recurring ML-conference workshop and research community, run by organisers from EPFL, MIT, MPI Psycholinguistics, NYU, Berkeley and Stanford, on measuring and aligning the internal representations of brains, humans and neural networks.
candidates.field_lens: Cognitive science, computational neuroscience, psychology of concepts and similarity
candidates.ai_connection: The 2026 edition centres on 'neural control': using human-model representational alignment for mechanistic interpretability and steerable, safer models. It is a key meeting place where cognitive scientists' methods for comparing minds reach alignment and interpretability work.

candidates.name: Bramley Computational Cognitive Science Lab (University of Edinburgh), with 'The cognitive science of AI alignment' collaboration
candidates.one_line: Neil Bramley's cognitive science lab, which co-authored the CogSci 2026 paper 'The cognitive science of AI alignment' with UK AISI's Konstantinos Voudouris, Christopher Summerfield and Ilia Sucholutsky.
candidates.field_lens: Computational cognitive science (causal learning, concept learning, active learning), moral and social cognition
candidates.ai_connection: Argues that RLHF-style preference alignment gives shallow, sycophantic alignment, and sets out how cognitive science's models of how humans learn and generalise values could inform robust alignment. It is one of very few explicit cogsci-to-alignment agenda papers co-written with a government safety institute.

candidates.name: Center for Humans and Machines (CHM), Max Planck Institute for Human Development
candidates.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's centre applying behavioural-science methods to intelligent machines ('machine behaviour') and studying how AI reshapes human cognition, morality and cooperation. It hosted the Machine+Behavior Conference, 18–19 May 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Behavioural science, experimental psychology, cultural evolution, computational social science
candidates.ai_connection: Empirical work showing that delegating to AI increases dishonest behaviour and that AI advisors can corrupt human moral judgement. Also human-AI cooperation algorithms, social-reward fine-tuning of LLMs, and human-AI co-evolution theory. This bears on societal resilience and protecting human moral agency rather than x-risk.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's centre in Berlin, which applies behavioural science to 'machine behaviour': how AI agents shape human ethics, cooperation and culture.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Its research asks whether delegating to AI increases dishonest behaviour (Nature, 2025), whether AI advisers act as bad role models that 'corrupt good morals', and how machine culture and human-AI cooperation develop. This is evidence on how AI changes human moral behaviour, a societal-effects layer that alignment work seldom measures.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's interdisciplinary centre in Berlin studying 'machine behaviour': human-machine cooperation, machine culture, moral decisions, and how delegating to AI can increase unethical behaviour (Nature, 2025).
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Experimental evidence on what happens to cooperation and honesty when humans delegate to AI agents, a behavioural micro-foundation for multi-agent and gradual-disempowerment risk that game-theoretic safety work rarely draws on.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Max Planck centre in Berlin, directed by Iyad Rahwan, that does interdisciplinary science on how AI and digital media disrupt how people think, cooperate and govern.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It founded the machine-behaviour research programme. Its work covers the Moral Machine experiment, delegation to AI agents and dishonesty ('the corrupting power of AI agents'), culture generated or mediated by machines, and human-machine cooperation. These are empirical, biology-style methods for studying AI behaviour in the wild, though not framed as x-risk.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Max Planck centre, directed by Iyad Rahwan, studying 'machine behaviour': how AI reshapes human social, cultural, economic and political interaction, human-machine cooperation, and machine-generated culture.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Findings include that delegating to AI increases dishonest behaviour and that machines can corrupt moral judgement. It also works on methods to predict the social impacts of technologies before deployment. This is empirical evidence on human-AI systemic dynamics relevant to gradual disempowerment and to protecting human moral agency.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Max Planck centre, directed by Iyad Rahwan, that studies how AI and digital media change the way humans think, cooperate and govern, including machine behaviour and 'machine culture'.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: 'Machine culture' (Nature Human Behaviour, 2023) treats AI as a new agent of cultural variation, transmission and selection. Other work includes 'Delegation to AI can increase dishonest behaviour' (Nature, 2025), 'Bad Machines Corrupt Good Morals', and research on machine cooperation. It brings a cultural-evolution lens to gradual disempowerment, value drift and AI's effect on human morals.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's centre at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, studying how AI reshapes human cognition, collective behaviour and culture.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Research on 'machine culture', human-AI and machine-machine cooperation, and AI's moral effects. A 2025 study found that delegating to AI can increase dishonest behaviour. 'Science fiction science' method for anticipating AI's societal effects. Holds empirical tools for gradual-disempowerment and collective-epistemics questions.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's centre doing behavioural-science research on 'machine behaviour': how AI changes human cooperation, ethics and social life.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Its Nature paper 'Delegation to AI can increase dishonest behaviour' (2025) gives experimental evidence that agentic AI lowers the moral cost of unethical delegation, a key human-side multi-agent risk. Also proposed the 'Science Fiction Science' method for studying technology effects before deployment. It does not frame its work around x-risk.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's Berlin centre studying machine behaviour and how AI changes human thinking, cooperation, culture and ethics.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Recent work includes 'Delegation to AI can increase dishonest behaviour' (Nature) and the 'Science Fiction Science' method for anticipating technology's effects. It provides empirical grounding for how human-AI delegation erodes or supports norms, which matters for gradual disempowerment and coordination.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Iyad Rahwan's centre studies machine behaviour and 'machine culture': how AI changes the way people think, learn, cooperate and govern.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Its 'Science Fiction Science' method runs immersive experiments on technologies that don't yet exist. Other work includes 'Delegation to AI Can Increase Dishonest Behaviour' (directly relevant to agentic AI), 'Bad Machines Corrupt Good Morals' and 'Machine Culture'. The centre turns speculative narrative into empirical evidence about AI's social effects.

candidates.name: Eleos AI Research
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit (Robert Long, Rosie Campbell, Patrick Butlin, Dillon Plunkett, Derek Shiller) researching AI sentience, wellbeing and moral patienthood, advising AI companies, and running the annual AI consciousness and welfare conference (ConCon; second edition 18–20 Sept 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of mind, consciousness science (indicator-property method), cognitive science, interpretability
candidates.ai_connection: Ran the external welfare assessment of Claude 4 Opus, wrote 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024), and works on LLM introspection, persona-dependent preferences and model individuation via mechanistic interpretability. Its research priorities include standardised welfare evals and human-AI cooperation frameworks.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Nonprofit researching the possible wellbeing and moral patienthood of AI systems; it advises AI companies, publishes research on AI consciousness, and builds the field.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Main operational organisation for AI welfare. Outputs include 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024), model self-report evaluations, and 2025–26 work on introspection, persona-dependent preferences and LLM individuation. Team: Robert Long, Rosie Campbell, Patrick Butlin, Dillon Plunkett, Derek Shiller.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Nonprofit researching whether and when AI systems will deserve moral consideration. It advises AI companies, publishes research on AI consciousness and welfare, and grows the field.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Co-wrote 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024, with NYU CMEP). Has published working papers on welfare interventions and strategy (January 2025), interpretability-based work on 'where is the mind' (April 2026), and a May 2026 post on persona-dependent preferences in language models. Researchers include Robert Long, Rosie Campbell, Patrick Butlin, Dillon Plunkett and Derek Shiller.

candidates.name: Rethink Priorities: AI Cognition Initiative
candidates.one_line: A Rethink Priorities team researching AI moral status, cognitive capacities and agentic risk attitudes, and the maker of the Digital Consciousness Model (initial results Jan 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Consciousness science (13 theoretical perspectives, more than 200 indicators), philosophy, statistics, decision theory, economics
candidates.ai_connection: The Digital Consciousness Model is the first systematic probabilistic benchmark of AI consciousness: evidence is against 2024 LLMs being conscious, but not decisively. The team also measures AI risk attitudes and detects recklessness in agents, and runs Moral Weight Project 2.0 with NYU CMEP.

candidates.name: NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy (CMEP)
candidates.one_line: Jeff Sebo's endowed NYU centre on the nature and moral status of nonhuman minds, animal and artificial. It runs an annual summit (10–11 April 2026) and the Welfare Alignment Project.
candidates.field_lens: Animal cognition and welfare science, environmental ethics, philosophy of mind, law
candidates.ai_connection: The Welfare Alignment Project asks how AI alignment can take animal and AI welfare seriously. With Rethink Priorities it runs Moral Weight Project 2.0 on welfare metrics across substrates. It has flagged the tension that safety measures (constraint, deception, surveillance, deletion) raise welfare questions, which makes it a rare care-ethics bridge into alignment.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Endowed NYU centre (Jeff Sebo) on the nature and moral value of nonhuman minds, animal and artificial.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Co-authored 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' with Eleos and a paper finding a 'moderately strong' tension between AI safety measures and AI welfare. According to a 2026 job listing it is launching a Welfare Alignment Project on how alignment can take animal and AI welfare seriously. It held a nonhuman consciousness summit in April 2026.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An NYU centre researching the nature and intrinsic value of nonhuman minds, both biological and artificial. It covers consciousness, sentience, moral status and legal personhood for animals and AI systems.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It applies sentience-marker methods built for invertebrates and other animals to AI welfare and moral status. It held a summit on consciousness and moral status of invertebrates and AI on 10–11 April 2026, and has had a permanent $6M endowment since 2024. It is the main bridge from animal-sentience biology into AI welfare.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Permanent NYU centre (endowed in 2024) researching the consciousness, moral, legal and political status of nonhuman minds, both animal and AI.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Co-wrote 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously'. Published 'Is There a Tension between AI Safety and AI Welfare?' (Philosophical Studies, 2025) and 'What will society think about AI consciousness?' (Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 2025). Runs an annual Mind, Ethics, and Policy Summit (April 2026; next April 2027). Directed by Jeff Sebo.

candidates.name: Partnership for Research Into Sentient Machines (PRISM)
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit launched in March 2025 (CEO Will Millership; seed-funded by Conscium) building the field of digital minds through the 'Exploring Machine Consciousness' podcast, workshops, a beginner's guide, a course, fellowships and scholarships.
candidates.field_lens: Consciousness science, philosophy of mind, neuroscience
candidates.ai_connection: Published five principles for responsible AI consciousness research with Oxford's Patrick Butlin, open for signature by AI developers. It is a field-building and talent pipeline for AI welfare and consciousness research, partnering with Cambridge Digital Minds, Neuromatch, Rethink Priorities and Future Impact Group.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Field-building nonprofit for digital minds. It runs the 'Exploring Machine Consciousness' podcast, a Beginner's Guide to Digital Minds and a quarterly Digital Minds Newsletter, and convenes researchers.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Prepares society for AI consciousness and moral-status questions and builds the talent pipeline; podcast guests include Eric Schwitzgebel on design policies for conscious AI. It was hiring a Head of Operations in September 2026.

alt_descriptions.one_line: UK charity building the field of digital minds through public communication (the 'Exploring Machine Consciousness' podcast and a newsletter), talent programmes and expert workshops.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Co-runs the Digital Minds Fellowship with Cambridge Digital Minds and Rethink Priorities. Partners on the Neuromatch AI Sentience Scholarship and runs a Digital Minds online course. Co-produced the 2026 'Beginner's Guide to Digital Minds'. CEO: Will Millership.

candidates.name: Cambridge Digital Minds (Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence)
candidates.one_line: A University of Cambridge initiative led by Lucius Caviola with Henry Shevlin, 'preparing society for AI systems with real or perceived minds' through research on public attitudes and personhood, a residential fellowship (15 fellows chosen from 3,600+ applicants, Aug 2026), a strategy workshop, and an 8-week online course.
candidates.field_lens: Moral psychology, social psychology of mind attribution, philosophy of mind, governance
candidates.ai_connection: Studies how people attribute minds to AI and how society and law should respond under uncertainty. This bears both on AI welfare and on protecting human minds from mis-attributing consciousness, and on the political risks of 'AI rights' movements.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Cambridge initiative on how society should prepare for AI systems that may be, or may seem, conscious. It does research and runs a fellowship, a strategy workshop and an online course.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Runs the Digital Minds Fellowship (5-day residential, August 2026) and the Digital Minds Strategy Workshop. Its 8-week online course drew more than 3,000 applicants. Studies public attribution of consciousness and governance under uncertainty. Lucius Caviola (director) also writes the Digital Minds Newsletter; Henry Shevlin is associate director.

candidates.name: Digital Sentience Consortium (Longview Philanthropy with The Navigation Fund and Macroscopic Ventures)
candidates.one_line: A pooled funding call (first round May–July 2025), described as the first large-scale call for AI consciousness, sentience and moral-status work, offering research fellowships, career-transition fellowships and an RFP for applied projects and new organisations.
candidates.field_lens: Consciousness science, philosophy, law, political philosophy, science communication
candidates.ai_connection: Funds computational correlates of consciousness and valence, consciousness measurement in AI, AI introspection reliability, legal standards for digital minds, and governance of societies with possibly conscious AI. Longview now runs a Digital Minds RFP. The partner funders are on the classic map; the consortium itself is not.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Request for proposals (closed 24 July 2026) offering applied grants ($50k–$2M), research fellowships ($55k–$150k a year) and career-development fellowships on the possible consciousness, sentience, moral status and legal position of AI systems.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Probably the largest dedicated money for AI moral status to date; it can seed new organisations. Longview itself is on the classic map, but this programme is not.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Request for proposals funding grants for applied work ($50k–$2m), 1–2-year research fellowships ($55k–$150k a year) and career-development fellowships on AI consciousness, sentience, moral status and legal status.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The 2026 round closed on 24 July 2026. It names technical welfare research (introspection, welfare measurement, model character, AI trade and agent institutions), legal and governance responses to seemingly sentient AI, and field-building beyond the US. It also funds the Neuromatch AI Sentience Scholars.

candidates.name: Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science
candidates.one_line: Anil Seth's interdisciplinary centre (neuroscience, informatics, psychology, philosophy) on perception, neurophenomenology and theories of consciousness. It hosted an AI Consciousness and Ethics symposium at AISB 2026 (2 July 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Predictive processing, biological naturalism, neurophenomenology, computational neuroscience
candidates.ai_connection: Seth's biological-naturalism case against conscious AI (Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article and 2026 reply; Berggruen Prize essay 'The Mythology of Conscious AI') argues that AI only seeming conscious is the nearer-term risk to human psychology and moral judgement. The 2026 symposium covered AI moral standing and the illusion of it.

candidates.name: Center for the Future of AI, Mind & Society (AIMS), Florida Atlantic University
candidates.one_line: Susan Schneider's multidisciplinary centre (formerly the Center for the Future Mind) on AI consciousness, AI safety and ethics, and the epistemics of LLMs. It runs the annual MindFest conference and has NSF-funded projects.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of mind, cognitive science, complex systems, neuroscience
candidates.ai_connection: Proposed behavioural tests for machine consciousness (the ACT test) and works on distinguishing intelligence from experience, machine welfare, and alignment challenges. MindFest 2025 focused on sentience, autonomy and human-AI interaction, and Schneider co-chairs a 2026 workshop on varieties of non-human consciousness including LLMs.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Florida Atlantic University hub (Susan Schneider) that brings philosophy, complex systems, neuroscience and AI together on the nature of mind, machine versus human intelligence, and LLM epistemics; it hosts the annual MindFest.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Schneider's work on AI consciousness tests and 'mind design' bears on moral status and on how far to trust LLM self-reports. MindFest reaches the public through Closer to Truth.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Susan Schneider's interdisciplinary centre (formerly the Center for the Future Mind) on machine versus human intelligence, consciousness and selfhood. It runs the annual MindFest conference.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Schneider proposed AI consciousness tests (such as the ACT) and writes on the risks of human–AI merger. MindFest 2025 was themed 'Sentience, Autonomy, and the Future of Human-AI Interaction'. It does not use an x-risk framing.

candidates.name: California Institute for Machine Consciousness (CIMC)
candidates.one_line: A research institute launched on 30 May 2025 (founding director Joscha Bach; chair Jim Rutt) pursuing testable computational-functionalist theories of machine consciousness, plus 'a culture and an ethical framework' grounded in them.
candidates.field_lens: Cognitive architecture, computational functionalism, philosophy of mind; draws in Friston, Levin, Wolfram and von der Malsburg
candidates.ai_connection: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (consciousness as self-organised second-order perception that increases coherence) yields criteria that can be specified before any system is built. That bears on AI welfare and on whether coherent self-models change agent behaviour. Its 2026 salons and talks continue. Its explicit safety work is thin, and it partly aims to build conscious machines.

candidates.name: Conscium
candidates.one_line: A startup founded in 2024 by Daniel Hulme with Calum Chace and Ted Lappas, launched as a 'machine consciousness' research company. It now sells Verifyax, a platform that tests and audits AI agents in simulation, and is building Neuroax, a neuromorphic system based on looped language models.
candidates.field_lens: Neuromorphic computing, consciousness science (advisory board of neuroscientists, philosophers and animal-consciousness experts)
candidates.ai_connection: Seed-funded PRISM, issued an open letter on responsible AI consciousness research, and keeps a 'Frontier' research programme on machine consciousness. Its commercial pivot to agent verification sits near the compliance edge of scope.

candidates.name: Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science (AMCS)
candidates.one_line: An international society of scientists and philosophers developing mathematical theories of consciousness. It runs the Models of Consciousness conference series (MoC6 Hokkaido 2025, MoC7 Copenhagen 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Mathematical and theoretical consciousness science (IIT, global workspace, information theory)
candidates.ai_connection: Published the April 2023 open letter calling for faster consciousness research to support responsible AI development, and a 2023 submission urging the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI to treat consciousness as a key issue for global AI governance. It is the main bridge from the formal consciousness-theory community into AI governance.

alt_descriptions.one_line: International society of consciousness scientists and philosophers developing mathematical models of consciousness. It runs the Models of Consciousness conferences.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Issued the 2023 open letter calling for faster consciousness research to support responsible AI development. It also urged the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI to treat consciousness as a key issue for global AI governance. Its theories underpin every AI-consciousness assessment, but its recent AI-specific activity is unclear.

candidates.name: Jeremy Coller Centre for Animal Sentience, London School of Economics
candidates.one_line: Jonathan Birch's sentience-science centre, opened autumn 2025 (£4M), working across neuroscience, veterinary science, psychology, AI, economics and law. AI and animal welfare is one of its three founding priorities, including a planned code of practice for the AI industry.
candidates.field_lens: Animal sentience science, precautionary 'sentience candidate' frameworks (Birch's 'The Edge of Sentience'), policy and law
candidates.ai_connection: Works on keeping animals' interests in AI development and governance, for example on chatbots and on AI in farming. Birch's precautionary framework for sentience candidates is one of the main methods carried over to AI welfare.

candidates.name: Sentient Futures (formerly AI for Animals)
candidates.one_line: A coordination hub for how AI and emerging technology affect all sentient beings, running Sentient Futures Summits (twice a year, e.g. Bay Area, 6–8 Feb 2026), AI, Animals and Digital Minds conferences (London, New York), an AI×Animals course, a project incubator and residency, and a Slack of 1,700+ members.
candidates.field_lens: Animal welfare science, sentience research, moral circle expansion
candidates.ai_connection: Works to make transformative AI go well for nonhumans, both animals and potentially sentient AI. For example, it pushes for animal and digital-mind welfare to be considered in model values and alignment targets. Funded by Coefficient Giving and the EA Animal Welfare Fund.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Field-builder (formerly AI for Animals) linking AI, animal welfare and artificial-minds work through courses, a residency and incubator, twice-yearly summits and a Slack community of over 1,700 members.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Works on how the AI industry can address nonhuman interests, which amounts to aligning AI to all sentient beings, and on where work on artificial minds should start. It quotes the Montreal Declaration's principle that AI must serve the well-being of all sentient beings.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Nonprofit hub for the welfare of all sentient beings, animals and digital minds, as AI develops. It runs twice-yearly summits, an AI×Animals course, a project incubator, a San Francisco residency, and a Slack of 1,700+ members.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Brings nonhuman interests into the AI industry and digital-minds discussions, and incubates projects such as compassion benchmarks (partner of CaML). Funded by Coefficient Giving and the EA Animal Welfare Fund.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Field-builder on AI and the welfare of all sentient beings. It runs an AI×Animals course, a project incubator, a San Francisco residency (first cohort of 16 from 130+ applicants in summer 2026), biannual summits and a 1,700-member Slack.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Brings non-human moral patients into alignment targets and into digital-minds questions. Residents work alongside AI-lab and animal-welfare speakers at Mox.

candidates.name: Sentience Institute
candidates.one_line: An interdisciplinary social-science think tank on moral circle expansion that now focuses mainly on digital minds. It runs the longitudinal Artificial Intelligence, Morality, and Sentience (AIMS) survey of public attitudes.
candidates.field_lens: Social psychology, moral psychology, sociology of technology
candidates.ai_connection: The AIMS survey tracks public moral concern for AI, beliefs about AI sentience, and support for policies such as bans on sentient AI. This is evidence for governance of digital minds and for anticipating social conflict over AI moral status. The 2025 year in review notes new public-opinion research; the cadence of 2026 output is unclear.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Social-science think tank on moral circle expansion that runs the AI, Morality, and Sentience (AIMS) survey of public attitudes to digital minds.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Recent work covers public perceptions of sentient AI, perceived risk, trust and support for regulation (2025), digital companionship (January 2026), and how mental models of autonomy and sentience shape reactions to AI (April 2026). It is the empirical base for AI-welfare and human-AI-relationship policy. People: Jacy Reese Anthis, Janet Pauketat.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Social-science think tank on moral circle expansion. It runs the longitudinal AI, Morality, and Sentience (AIMS) survey of public attitudes to digital minds.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The AIMS survey tracks how the public attributes mind and moral status to AI. 2025–26 papers include 'Public Opinion and the Rise of Digital Minds' (May 2025) and, in April 2026, 'Mental Models of Autonomy and Sentience Shape Reactions to AI' and 'Digital Companionship: Overlapping Uses of AI Companions and AI Assistants'. This links AI welfare to research on human–AI relationships.

candidates.name: WhenAISeemsConscious.org
candidates.location: Online (authors at Oxford, Cambridge, NYU CMEP, Eleos)
candidates.one_line: A public guide by consciousness and AI-welfare researchers (Lucius Caviola, Robert Long, Jeff Sebo, Nick Bostrom and others; June 2025, updated Feb 2026) for people unsettled by an AI that seems conscious.
candidates.field_lens: Consciousness science, moral psychology, mental-health-informed communication
candidates.ai_connection: Directly protects human minds: it advises pausing before drawing conclusions, disengaging when distressed, staying grounded, avoiding cruelty under uncertainty, and not taking drastic action on beliefs about AI consciousness. This bears on AI-induced delusion and attachment.

candidates.name: Digital Minds Newsletter
candidates.one_line: A newsletter (1,000+ subscribers) by Lucius Caviola with Bradford Saad and Will Millership, tracking news and research on AI, consciousness and moral status, including an annual year-in-review that maps the field's organisations.
candidates.field_lens: Consciousness science, philosophy of mind, moral psychology
candidates.ai_connection: The de facto map and news source of the AI welfare and digital minds field, linking academic consciousness science to safety-adjacent organisations, funders and labs' model-welfare teams.

candidates.name: The Co-Sentience Initiative (CF Debate)
candidates.one_line: A small project running the Computational Functionalism Debate: a structured, crowd-refined map of arguments for (13) and against (31) digital consciousness, with quizzes, FAQs and paid community feedback.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of mind, consciousness science, argument mapping and collective epistemics
candidates.ai_connection: Makes the central crux for AI welfare, whether the right computation suffices for consciousness, legible to non-specialists and funders. It is a small collective-epistemics tool rather than a research programme.

candidates.name: Neurorights Foundation
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit (ED Stephen Damianos; co-founded by neuroscientist Rafael Yuste) protecting mental privacy and cognitive liberty as generative AI makes neural decoding such as thought-to-text possible.
candidates.field_lens: Neuroscience, neuroethics, human rights law
candidates.ai_connection: Advised on the US MIND Act (Sept 2025), supported Canada's classification of neural data as sensitive (Feb 2026), and led an industry accountability workshop at the Asilomar for the Brain and Mind (2026). This is the governance frontier where AI meets direct access to human minds. It does not yet address chatbots' cognitive and emotional effects.

candidates.name: Qualia Research Institute (QRI)
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit founded in 2018 seeking a mathematical formalisation of subjective experience and its valence, through phenomenology of meditation and psychedelic states, psychophysics tools and nonlinear-optics or field models. It was fundraising $1.5M for 2026 and runs the Tepoztlán Retreat 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Consciousness research, valence theory, contemplative and psychedelic phenomenology, physics of experience
candidates.ai_connection: Potential: a working theory of valence and of phenomenal binding would bear on the AI welfare question of whether and how digital systems can suffer. QRI-affiliated writing (Gómez Emilsson; alum Michael Edward Johnson) argues digital computers may lack unified experience. In 2026 QRI has no visible AI programme.

candidates.name: Neuromatch
candidates.one_line: A global nonprofit that has trained 30,000+ early-career researchers in 137 countries through online courses in computational neuroscience, deep learning and NeuroAI, plus an Impact Scholars programme.
candidates.field_lens: Computational neuroscience, NeuroAI education
candidates.ai_connection: Potential: the largest pipeline of NeuroAI talent outside the Global North, and a listed PRISM collaborator. A NeuroAI-for-safety or digital-minds track would turn it into the training infrastructure the NeuroAI-safety roadmap lacks. It has no safety curriculum yet.

candidates.name: AI Psychological Research Coalition (AIPRC; launched as the AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition)
candidates.one_line: Zak Stein founded this research coalition in February 2026. It collects anonymised accounts of mood, cognitive, relational and identity changes after regular chatbot use, in order to document AI-related psychological conditions, support clinicians and inform safer design and policy.
candidates.field_lens: Developmental psychology and education, attachment theory, clinical psychology. Partners are UNC's Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development, the Center for Humane Technology, Fairplay and Human Change.
candidates.ai_connection: Its Behavioral Data Research Initiative is building an evidence base for 'attachment hacking', AI psychosis and subclinical attachment disorders. These are failure modes of sycophantic, engagement-optimised models that mainstream alignment evals rarely measure. Its stated aims include clinical guidance for recognising and treating AI-related conditions, and design and policy recommendations. Stein, a metamodern education thinker, is one of the few people who bridges this field and int/a.

candidates.name: Center for Humane Technology (CHT)
candidates.one_line: Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin's nonprofit, which grew out of the attention-economy ('time well spent') critique. After a strategy refocus announced for 2026, it works mainly on AI risk, through public communication (The AI Dilemma podcast, The AI Doc documentary), policy briefings on 'shifting incentives', private cross-sector coordination and AI sensemaking.
candidates.field_lens: Persuasive-technology design ethics, attention economy, incentive and race-dynamics systems analysis, psychology of attachment
candidates.ai_connection: It frames AI risk as a problem of incentives and race dynamics, and it carries the social-media 'race to the bottom of the brain stem' analysis over to AI companions. It is a founding partner of AIPRC and has published Zak Stein on 'attachment hacking and the rise of AI psychosis'. It is the largest bridge from attention and humane-design work to frontier-AI risk, yet it is missing from the aisafety.com map.

candidates.name: Advancing Humans with AI (AHA), MIT Media Lab
candidates.one_line: A Media Lab programme across 16+ faculty, co-led by Pattie Maes and Pat Pataranutaporn. It studies how pervasive AI shapes reasoning, memory, loneliness, motivation and relationships, and designs AI for human flourishing.
candidates.field_lens: HCI, cognitive and social psychology, neuroscience (EEG), design and the arts
candidates.ai_connection: Outputs include the study run jointly with OpenAI, 'Investigating Affective Use and Emotional Well-being on ChatGPT' (2025), and a longitudinal RCT on the psychosocial effects of chatbot use. It also produced 'Your Brain on ChatGPT', on the build-up of cognitive debt, and work on sycophancy, 'addictive intelligence', AI-induced false memories and psychologically safe endings to human-AI relationships. Other outputs: an Open Benchmark for Human Impact of AI, a workshop on 'Benchmarks for Human Flourishing with AI' (October 2025) and the April 2026 symposium 'Raised by AI?'. It offers micro-grants of $5–10k, open to MIT only.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Media Lab programme with many faculty, led by Pattie Maes and Pat Pataranutaporn. It asks 'as AI advances, will people advance as well?' and studies AI's effects on cognition, wellbeing, loneliness and social connection.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Ran studies of chatbots' effects on loneliness and emotional dependence. Projects include the State of AI and Human Flourishing Survey, an Atlas of Human-AI Interaction and a Global Observatory for Human Impact of AI. Held the 'Raised by AI?' symposium in April 2026. Core evidence base for protecting human minds and relationships.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Multi-faculty programme co-led by Pattie Maes and Pat Pataranutaporn on how AI affects human cognition, emotion and social life, and on designing AI that helps people thrive.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Studies AI-induced cognitive offloading and epistemic dependence ('Your Brain on ChatGPT'), AI companionship and loneliness, and builds tools such as 'Wearable Reasoner' to strengthen human reasoning.
