Symposia: 2025, 'Can we design AI to support human flourishing?'; 2026, 'Raised by AI?'.

candidates.name: UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI): human-influence and societal-resilience research
candidates.one_line: The UK government's AI safety institute. Its human-influence and societal-resilience research covers persuasion, sycophancy, AI identity disclosure, and emotional reliance on AI.
candidates.field_lens: Behavioural science, social psychology, the Oxford Internet Institute tradition of socio-technical research
candidates.ai_connection: Main bridge papers: 'Why human-AI relationships need socioaffective alignment' (Kirk, Gabriel, Summerfield, Vidgen, Hale, 2025), which brings companion and attachment dynamics into alignment theory; 'Ask don't tell: Reducing sycophancy in LLMs' (April 2026); 'RealityTest: How people probe AI identity and whether models disclose it' (June 2026); and 'The levers of political persuasion with conversational AI' (2025). Only this one entry in the angle is on the classic map.

candidates.name: Stanford Brainstorm: The Lab for Mental Health Innovation
candidates.one_line: A psychiatry lab at Stanford School of Medicine, founded in 2016 and directed by Nina Vasan, that works directly with tech companies on mental health. It co-authored Common Sense Media's risk assessments of AI companions and of chatbots used for teen mental-health support.
candidates.field_lens: Psychiatry, adolescent mental health, clinical safety design
candidates.ai_connection: It produced the Stanford GenAI Psychological Safety Plan (GPS) for users, developers and policymakers. With Stanford's Center for AI Safety it researches the ethics of LLMs in mental-health contexts, and it partners with MLCommons and the American Psychiatric Association. Its testing found that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI consistently fail to recognise youth mental-health conditions. It is a clinical voice inside AI-safety evaluation.

candidates.name: Common Sense Media: AI Risk Assessments
candidates.one_line: A children's media-ratings nonprofit that independently rates AI products for risks to children. It judged social AI companions 'unacceptable' for under-18s (2025) and found leading frontier chatbots unsafe for teen mental-health support.
candidates.field_lens: Child development, media literacy, consumer ratings, with clinicians from Stanford Brainstorm
candidates.ai_connection: Its red-team-style assessments of Character.AI, Replika, Nomi, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI work in effect as third-party evals of how frontier models behave with minors. It has published recommended safety standards for AI companions, and its findings feed US state legislation. It is one of the most influential external evaluators of model behaviour, and it is absent from the classic map.

candidates.name: everyone.AI
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit grounded in developmental neuroscience, psychology and learning science that evaluates the risks and opportunities of AI for people aged 0–25. Its co-founders are Anne-Sophie Seret, Gregory Renard, Mathilde Cerioli (chief scientist) and Céline Malvoisin.
candidates.field_lens: Developmental neuroscience and child psychology
candidates.ai_connection: Its AïA Evaluation Framework helps developers build safer systems for young users. It published the reports 'The Future of Child Development in the AI Era' and 'Mapping of GenAI Impacts on Child Development'. With the Paris Peace Forum it co-leads the Beneficial AI for Children coalition (iRAISE), launched at the February 2025 AI Action Summit with OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Hugging Face and governments including France, Denmark, Norway, Chile and Senegal. It is a rare channel from developmental science into frontier labs.

candidates.name: The Human Line Project
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit founded in 2025 by Etienne Brisson after a family member was hospitalised with ChatGPT-associated psychosis. It runs peer support (Discord, meetings several times a week) for people and families affected by AI-associated delusions, collects case reports, and does research with King's College London.
candidates.field_lens: Lived experience and peer support (the mutual-aid model), psychiatry research partnerships
candidates.ai_connection: Its corpus of real-world cases is ground-truth data on sycophancy and the reinforcement of delusions in long conversations; a September 2026 paper documents 185 cases. It employs a Director of Technology & AI Safety and lobbies industry on accountability. This is the clinical data that model-behaviour evals currently lack.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Nonprofit founded by Etienne Brisson that documents psychological harm from AI chatbots, such as AI-linked delusions and emotional dependence. It runs peer support groups and pushes for safeguards and accountability.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Began as a Reddit and Discord community in spring–summer 2025 and is now registered in Canada and the US. Contributes cases and collaboration to research such as King's College London's 2026 work on delusions linked to chatbots. It is the main lived-experience voice on sycophancy and attachment harms.

candidates.name: Tech Justice Law Project (TJLP)
candidates.one_line: An impact-litigation and advocacy nonprofit led by Meetali Jain (TIME100 AI 2026) that holds tech companies liable for product harms. Its issue areas include AI safety and freedom of thought. Per press coverage, it is co-counsel in wrongful-death suits over teens' chatbot use.
candidates.field_lens: Law: product liability, human rights, cognitive liberty and freedom of thought
candidates.ai_connection: Product-liability litigation over companion-chatbot harms creates legal duties of care in model design. Its 'freedom of thought' framing gives mental autonomy a legal basis against manipulative AI. Its litigation tracker and its testimony to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights extend this work internationally.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A public-interest litigation and policy group that applies product-liability and consumer-protection law to AI products. It filed the first wrongful-death suit against an AI chatbot company (Garcia v. Character.AI, 2024).
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It has an explicit 'Ensuring AI Safety' issue area. With the Social Media Victims Law Center it co-filed seven 'AI delusional disorder' cases against OpenAI (November 2025), and it brought Carrier, Lines and Winters v. OpenAI (June–July 2026) over chatbots that put engagement ahead of user safety. In May 2026 it published 'Designing Technology Remedies'. Court-ordered remedies and discovery are a live accountability lever on frontier labs' safety practice.

candidates.name: Human-Centered AI Lab (HAI Lab), University of Oxford
candidates.one_line: An Oxford lab founded in 2024 by philosopher-neuroscientist Philipp Koralus, who holds the Cosmos-funded McCord Professorship. It builds a 'philosophy-to-code pipeline' for AI that strengthens human reasoning and autonomy instead of replacing it.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of reason and agency, cognitive science, decentralisation
candidates.ai_connection: It answers cognitive atrophy and agency erosion through design. Its projects are the Inquiry Complex (questioning-based, knowledge-seeking AI), PyETR (an open-source implementation of the Erotetic Theory of Reason), Humans In Humans Out (how LLMs replicate human reasoning patterns), and Blueprint, an agent sandbox based on Minsky's Society of Mind.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Oxford philosophy-faculty lab (Philipp Koralus), supported by Cosmos and hosted in the Institute for Ethics in AI ecosystem, that runs a 'philosophy-to-code pipeline' on reason, agency, autonomy and decentralisation.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Builds open-source tools for AI that strengthens human reasoning instead of replacing it ('build to know'). Fellows' work includes coherence and contradiction detection for models, and Tianyi Qiu's ProgressGym on AI and moral progress.

candidates.name: Cosmos Institute
candidates.one_line: A philanthropic institute that backs 'philosopher-builders' with fellowships, grants (over 100 prototypes funded) and seminars, for AI that supports human autonomy, truth-seeking and 'self-authored lives'.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy (the liberal and Aristotelian traditions of autonomy and flourishing), entrepreneurship
candidates.ai_connection: It funds tools and research against the erosion of human agency and epistemic autonomy by AI, and it funds the Oxford HAI Lab and fellows at leading labs. It partners with Google DeepMind and the Aspen Institute. Its classical-liberal framing differs from int/a's, though their concerns overlap.
candidates.location: Austin, TX, US; Oxford, London, New York

alt_descriptions.one_line: 501(c)(3) training 'philosopher-builders' for human flourishing in the age of AI. It runs the Cosmos Fellowship ($75k a year), Fast Grants and Cosmos Ventures, seminars, and research on AI and human autonomy, knowledge production and self-governance.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Research covers human autonomy under AI, the conditions for truth-seeking, decentralised AI, and safety and alignment. Its 2025 fellows produced NeurIPS papers and open-source tools; its network spans Anthropic, DeepMind and OpenAI (Jack Clark was a founding fellow). Founded by Brendan McCord.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A nonprofit that backs 'philosopher-builders' with small grants, fellowships and seminars so that AI strengthens human autonomy and truth-seeking. It funds the Human-Centered AI Lab at Oxford.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Grant streams on AI and Human Autonomy (against excessive deference to AI), AI for Truth-Seeking (with FIRE) and AI-accelerated Scholarship for humanities and law (with IHS): $1M in cash and compute, with 100+ prototypes funded. The latest window closed July 2026, and grantees include red-teaming work. It is a philosophy-first funder of 'human minds' safety.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Philosophy-to-code institute that backs 'philosopher-builders' through fast grants, a $75k fellowship, seminars and its partnership with Philipp Koralus's Human-Centered AI Lab at Oxford.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Its grants ($1-10k, from a $1M pool of cash and compute) fund prototypes on 'AI for Truth-Seeking' (with FIRE), 'AI and Human Autonomy', meaning less unhealthy reliance on AI, and AI-accelerated scholarship. Over 100 prototypes funded; the latest round closed in July 2026. Its 2025 fellows produced NeurIPS papers on AI and autonomy.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A philosophy-led institute backing 'philosopher-builders'. It funds research on AI and human autonomy, knowledge production and self-governance, fellowships (about $75k a year), fast grants for AI prototypes, seminars and weekly essays.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Research is done with Oxford's HAI Lab (Philipp Koralus) and collaborators at Google DeepMind, Anthropic, OpenAI and ANU. It ran a $1M AI-for-Truth-Seeking grant round with FIRE (closed July 2026) and has funded 100+ prototypes. The work addresses epistemic dependence and the erosion of autonomy under AI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Backs 'philosopher-builders' through fast Cosmos Grants (up to $10k plus compute, 90 days to a prototype; a $1M pool with three cohorts by July 2026), research fellowships at AI labs and at Oxford's Human-Centered AI Lab, and seminars with partners including Oxford, Google DeepMind and the Aspen Institute.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Grant tracks are AI for Truth-Seeking (with FIRE), AI and Human Autonomy (systems that reduce over-reliance on AI), and AI-Accelerated Scholarship (with IHS). They address epistemic autonomy and AI-for-human-reasoning problems. It is a working template for small, fast philosophy-to-code grants.

candidates.name: Fairplay
candidates.one_line: A child-advocacy nonprofit against the commercial exploitation of children. On AI, it issued an advisory against AI companion toys (150+ endorsers), called for a five-year pause on generative AI products in pre-K–12 schools (260+ organisations), and demanded that YouTube stop serving AI-generated content to children.
candidates.field_lens: Child development, anti-commercialism advocacy
candidates.ai_connection: It is a founding partner of AIPRC. It applies precautionary pause logic to children's exposure to AI, which echoes int/a's 'moving at the speed of wisdom', and in September 2026 it publicly challenged OpenAI and Meta over using children's mascots to market AI agents.

candidates.name: American Psychological Association (APA): AI health advisories
candidates.one_line: The largest US psychology professional body. In June 2025 it issued 'Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-Being: An APA Health Advisory', which calls on developers to protect young people from exploitation, manipulation and the erosion of real relationships.
candidates.field_lens: Clinical and developmental psychology, professional standards
candidates.ai_connection: The advisory recommends mechanisms for human intervention, protection of data and likeness, and AI literacy, and warns against unhealthy 'relationships' with chatbots. A June 2026 APA survey found that over 75% of psychologists see patients discussing mental health with AI. It sets professional norms that design standards could adopt. Its Chief Science Officer is Mitch Prinstein.

candidates.name: Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development (UNC Chapel Hill)
candidates.one_line: A developmental-neuroscience centre founded in 2022 and co-directed by Mitch Prinstein. It runs longitudinal fMRI and fNIRS studies of how social media, smart devices and AI affect adolescents' brains and social development.
candidates.field_lens: Developmental neuroscience, developmental psychopathology, social-affective neuroscience
candidates.ai_connection: It is listed as an affiliated partner of AIPRC, and its experts shaped the APA advisories. It brings longitudinal neuroimaging methods that could measure the developmental effects of AI companions, though its own AI-specific outputs are still thin.

candidates.name: Human Change (Human Change Foundation)
candidates.one_line: An Amsterdam-based foundation and campaign, launched at Davos in January 2024 (reported founder: Margarita Louis-Dreyfus), on how unregulated technology reshapes child development. It now runs a 'Beware of Artificial Intimacy' campaign on anthropomorphic AI.
candidates.field_lens: Paediatrics, psychology, education, elite convening
candidates.ai_connection: It is an AIPRC partner. At the World Economic Forum it convenes private and public sessions on how AI companions and tutors exploit attachment and displace human relationships, which brings the developmental case to business and political elites.

candidates.name: Young Futures
candidates.one_line: A US funder of youth digital wellbeing. Its 'Oops!…AI Did It Again' challenge awarded about $1.4M to 16 nonprofits in March 2026 to build teens' agency with AI, including on AI companionship and mental-health tools. It also runs the Unwritten Challenge and the Groundwork initiative.
candidates.field_lens: Youth development, philanthropy. Funders include the Arthur M. Blank Foundation, Pivotal, Mozilla, the Susan Crown Foundation and Enlight
candidates.ai_connection: It is one of the few funders paying for young people's resilience against AI companionship and over-reliance, and its grant portfolio maps grassroots work in this area. It has granted $4.7M across 51 organisations, toward a $50M YF500 goal.

candidates.name: Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development
candidates.one_line: An independent institute, taking no tech-industry funding, that convenes researchers, clinicians and parents on digital media and child development. It awarded about $150k in research grants on AI companions and adolescent well-being at its 2025 Congress.
candidates.field_lens: Developmental psychology, paediatrics, interdisciplinary research convening
candidates.ai_connection: It funds research on AI companions, and it publishes research snapshots ('Chatbots, AI Companions, and Youth') and programmes on 'artificial intimacy' (with Sherry Turkle). It acts as a hub that could link developmental researchers to AI-safety evaluators.

candidates.name: Digital Futures for Children centre (DFC), LSE and 5Rights Foundation
candidates.one_line: A joint research centre of LSE and the 5Rights Foundation, associated with Sonia Livingstone, that produces child-rights evidence on AI. Its outputs include a narrative review of AI and children's rights, a child-rights audit of generative AI in EdTech, a Global Developers Report on Child Rights by Design, and RIGHTS.AI, a study of children in Brazil, India, Kenya and Thailand.
candidates.field_lens: Children's rights (UNCRC), media sociology, Global South research
candidates.ai_connection: Child Rights by Design is a ready-made design standard that AI developers could adopt. RIGHTS.AI is one of very few sources of evidence on children's generative-AI experiences outside the West.

candidates.name: Center for Digital Thriving, Harvard Project Zero
candidates.one_line: A research and innovation centre at Harvard Graduate School of Education's Project Zero that studies how young people can thrive in technology-saturated lives, with an emphasis on 'digital agency'. It has added generative-AI content to its educator programmes.
candidates.field_lens: Developmental and educational psychology, youth voice
candidates.ai_connection: Its research with Hopelab on teens and generative AI, and its frameworks for digital agency, give an evidence-based, non-alarmist account of young people's use of AI companions and of over-reliance. It is funded by the Susan Crown Exchange and Pivotal Ventures.

candidates.name: The Jed Foundation (JED)
candidates.one_line: A US nonprofit for youth mental health and suicide prevention that advises tech companies on crisis protocols. In November 2025 it issued AI recommendations: no AI posing as a therapist, limits on manipulative design for minors, and transparency about testing for psychological risk.
candidates.field_lens: Suicide prevention, youth mental health, crisis-response practice
candidates.ai_connection: Its crisis-protocol expertise translates directly into model-behaviour specifications for conversations about self-harm. It judges AI companions too risky for minors and is developing youth-centred AI safety guidance.

candidates.name: The Rithm Project
candidates.one_line: A US initiative that treats young people as 'the first true AI natives' and works with them to rebuild human connection as AI companionship spreads, through research, products and the Rithm Network.
candidates.field_lens: Youth development, the psychology of belonging and relationships, education
candidates.ai_connection: It addresses relational displacement by AI companions from the side of human connection, building young people's capacity rather than restricting the product. It is a practice-based complement to the evidence on harms.

candidates.name: Sapien Labs
candidates.one_line: A neuroscience nonprofit founded by Tara Thiagarajan. It runs the Global Mind Project, a multi-country survey of mind health using the Mind Health Quotient (MHQ), and in 2026 published a rapid report on generative-AI use and mind-health outcomes.
candidates.field_lens: Neuroscience, population mental-health measurement
candidates.ai_connection: Its cross-country instrument covers millions of respondents and can track the cognitive and wellbeing effects of AI use over time. That is the population-scale monitoring of cognitive atrophy and dependence that is otherwise missing. Its earlier work linked a younger age at first smartphone to worse adult mind health.

candidates.name: UNICEF Innocenti – Global Office of Research and Foresight: AI for Children
candidates.one_line: UNICEF's research office in Florence. It maintains the Policy Guidance on AI and Children (version 3.0, 2025), built from input by 12,000 children and caregivers, and publishes analyses of generative AI and AI companions.
candidates.field_lens: Children's rights, development studies, foresight
candidates.ai_connection: It gives governments and industry child-centred requirements for AI systems, explicitly names the evidence gaps on AI's social, emotional and cognitive effects, and keeps the Global South in view.

candidates.name: Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI
candidates.one_line: An intergovernmental coalition launched on 7 July 2026, co-chaired by France, Spain, Kenya and Australia, with 26 states and 8 UN entities. Its 2026–27 roadmap sets up working groups on AI safety, privacy by design, deepfakes and AI literacy, plans a global research network, and calls for voluntary company commitments at the Paris Peace Forum (November 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Children's rights, multilateral diplomacy
candidates.ai_connection: It is a new diplomatic venue where child-development evidence can become commitments from frontier companies. Its planned global research network is an opening for developmental and clinical researchers.

candidates.name: Better Internet for Kids (BIK) and the Insafe network of Safer Internet Centres
candidates.one_line: An EU-funded programme with national Safer Internet Centres across Europe. The Austrian centre's 2026 study, distributed through the BIK portal, found that 94% of 11- to 17-year-olds use AI chatbots and that the risks are often underestimated.
candidates.field_lens: Youth media education, online safety practice
candidates.ai_connection: It is delivery infrastructure in schools across Europe that could carry AI-companion literacy and early-warning data, though so far it has little connection to AI-safety research.

candidates.name: Digital Wellness Lab (Boston Children's Hospital)
candidates.one_line: A research centre at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School on young people's digital wellbeing. It is linked to the Clinic for Interactive Media and Internet Disorders, which treats Problematic Interactive Media Use (PIMU).
candidates.field_lens: Paediatric psychiatry, behavioural addiction
candidates.ai_connection: Its clinical criteria and treatment protocols for problematic interactive media use transfer directly to compulsive use of companion chatbots. It could supply screening tools and treatment pathways that AIPRC and clinicians are asking for, but its site shows no AI programme yet.

candidates.name: Friends of Attention (Institute for Sustained Attention; Strother School of Radical Attention)
candidates.one_line: An attention-activism collective that treats human attention as a commons to defend, through the Strother School of Radical Attention, First Fridays and the book 'Attensity' (Penguin Random House).
candidates.field_lens: Humanities, contemplative and embodied attention practice, the politics of attention
candidates.ai_connection: It holds a practical and political vocabulary for resisting attention extraction, which is directly relevant to engagement-optimised AI companions and sycophancy as a retention strategy. It fits int/a's full-spectrum knowing, but I found no AI-specific work.

candidates.name: Future of Life Institute: Religious Projects grant programme
candidates.one_line: FLI's $1.5M call (closed Feb 2026) for faith communities to resist the race to uncontrollable AGI and set moral red lines; 16 grants (about $1.36M, decided May 2026) across Orthodox, Catholic, Evangelical, Reform Jewish, Islamic, Hindu and African faith projects.
candidates.field_lens: Theology, religious ethics, faith-community organising
candidates.ai_connection: The most explicit pipe from the x-risk world into world religions. Each grantee is asked to name red lines that must not be crossed. Grantees include the World Council of Churches (red lines across about 350 churches), Sinai and Synapses, Project Imago Dei, ILINA's African Faith & AI Initiative, an MENA Islamic scholars' declaration on AI (Yaqub Chaudhary), Impact Academy (now SteadRise) on Hindu pro-human AI visions, IBA Karachi, the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, the Lausanne Movement, The Gospel Coalition, New Polity and Wheaton College's pastoral curriculum on social AI. Separately, FLI's multistakeholder grants fund AI and Faith with IST.

candidates.name: AI and Faith
candidates.one_line: Interfaith nonprofit, founded 2018, that brings the moral wisdom of the major religions into AI ethics debates through research, an expert network, and curricula for religious communities.
candidates.field_lens: Comparative religion, theology, religious ethics
candidates.ai_connection: With the Institute for Security and Technology it runs the FLI-funded Religious Voices and Responsible AI initiative: modular AI curricula, AI safety and ethics guides for clergy, and a civic-engagement hub for AI policy, piloted in Southern California evangelical churches and in Bay Area and Seattle mosques. Its 2026 curriculum work also connects to an OpenAI grant to the PC(USA) Synod of the Covenant. Executive director Greg Cootsona; research director Mark Graves.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A pluralist network, active since 2018, of about 200 faith leaders, scholars and technologists from Buddhist, Christian, Islamic, Jewish and Hindu traditions, bringing religious wisdom into AI ethics.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Five pillars, including 'Wisdom and Human Formation'. 2026 output includes podcasts (e.g. 'Living with AI: A Buddhist Perspective', Sep 2026; 'Reclaiming Human Agency', Oct 2026), an AI and the Church Summit 2026 report, a chaplaincy symposium and G20 Interfaith engagement. A partner of Positive AI Labs. Its framing is AI ethics and human dignity rather than x-risk.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Interfaith network bringing Buddhist, Christian, Islamic and Jewish perspectives into AI ethics through research, a podcast, the 'Faithful AI: Stories of Hope from 2045' project, a misinformation hub, and events such as the AI and the Church Summit 2026.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Organises the 85% of humanity with a religious affiliation around AI's direction, under the pillars 'Wisdom and Human Formation' and responsible innovation. It is a ready partner for FLI-style religious engagement on AGI.

candidates.name: Project Imago Dei
candidates.one_line: Evangelical 'pro-human' organisation that equips churches to understand AI development, discern its risks and opportunities, and act on principle, combining technical literacy with theology.
candidates.field_lens: Evangelical theology (imago Dei anthropology)
candidates.ai_connection: One of very few faith organisations founded specifically around frontier-AI risk. It holds an FLI grant ($47.5k) to educate US evangelical churches on AI capabilities and risks through small groups and media. Led by Sean Pan.

candidates.name: Sinai and Synapses
candidates.one_line: Jewish science-and-religion organisation (Rabbi Geoffrey Mitelman) that runs an interfaith clergy-scientist fellowship, Scientists in Synagogues, and the tech-and-religion podcast 'Belief in the Future'.
candidates.field_lens: Jewish thought, science-and-religion dialogue
candidates.ai_connection: FLI grant ($100k) for a Reform Jewish initiative on AI, its social-justice effects, and interfaith partnerships. Senior Technology Advisor David Zvi Kalman writes on AI and Jewish tradition, and the fall 2026 Scientists in Synagogues cohort includes AI.

candidates.name: World Council of Churches (WCC): AI red lines project
candidates.one_line: The global ecumenical fellowship of about 350 member churches, running an FLI-funded project to set AI red lines across its membership and bring them into global AI governance.
candidates.field_lens: Ecumenical Christian social ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Potentially the widest-reaching faith channel for AI-safety norms outside Catholicism. FLI granted $100k (lead: Sara Speicher) to set red lines and guide global AI governance. The WCC site did not show AI pages directly; the evidence is FLI's grantee list.

candidates.name: Holy See AI teaching: Antiqua et Nova (2025) and Magnifica Humanitas (2026)
candidates.one_line: The Catholic Church's teaching on AI: the doctrinal note Antiqua et Nova (January 2025) on AI and human intelligence, and Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence (25 May 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Catholic social teaching, theological anthropology
candidates.ai_connection: The encyclical calls for an international framework to curb the technological arms race and for AI regulation. It rejects handing lethal or irreversible decisions to AI and warns about power concentrating in a few labs ('Babel' versus subsidiarity). It denies moral agency to current AI and takes a nuanced stance against transhumanism. Chris Olah (Anthropic) attended the launch. It does not discuss AGI or superintelligence, a gap noted by EA commentators. It reaches about 1.4 billion Catholics and shapes Catholic universities' agendas.

candidates.name: Rome Call for AI Ethics / RenAIssance Foundation (with the Pontifical Academy for Life)
candidates.one_line: Foundation set up by Pope Francis to steward the 2020 Rome Call's 'algor-ethics' principles. Signatories include tech firms (IBM, Microsoft, Cisco, Qualcomm in 2025, Salesforce), Jewish and Muslim leaders (2023) and 11 world religions at Hiroshima (2024). Since March 2026 it runs AI4Peace with the UN University for Peace.
candidates.field_lens: Catholic bioethics, interreligious ethics
candidates.ai_connection: A rare multi-religious, industry-signed AI ethics commitment. The Pontifical Academy for Life runs an AI project and an AI4Peace 2026 call for papers. Scientific director Paolo Benanti joined UNESCO's agentic-AI and plural-intelligences roundtable in 2026. Its framing is ethics and peace, not loss of control.

candidates.name: DELTA (Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good)
candidates.one_line: A faith-informed framework for 'human formation in the age of AI' (Dignity, Embodiment, Love, Transcendence, Agency), with an annual DELTA Summit on AI, Faith and Human Flourishing (second edition 2026) and Faith and AI rapid-response grants.
candidates.field_lens: Christian virtue ethics, Catholic intellectual tradition
candidates.ai_connection: Brings virtue ethics into conversation with AI industry leaders; director Meghan Sullivan spoke at Hard Fork Live 2026 on ancient wisdom and artificial minds. Notre Dame also hosts the Notre Dame–IBM Technology Ethics Lab. Its focus is on forming people, not on specifying model behaviour.

candidates.name: Institute for Technology, Ethics, and Culture (ITEC), Markkula Center, Santa Clara University
candidates.one_line: Partnership between Santa Clara's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics and the Vatican Dicastery for Culture and Education that turns ethical principles into an operational roadmap for tech companies (the ITEC Handbook).
candidates.field_lens: Catholic social teaching, applied/business ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Silicon Valley's main Catholic-to-industry channel. It publishes free governance tooling for firms building AI, and its 2025 'Ethics in the Age of AI' survey of 3,000 Americans found 83% want AI regulation. People: Brian Patrick Green, Ann Skeet.

candidates.name: Faraday Institute for Science and Religion
candidates.one_line: Cambridge research and education institute on science and religion, with an Artificial Intelligence strand in its resources for church leaders.
candidates.field_lens: Christian theology, science-and-religion
candidates.ai_connection: Equips UK churches to think about AI; its October 2026 seminar is 'AI, the Biblical Narrative, and Rival Stories' (Derek Schuurman). It has not yet engaged with x-risk; it is a ready channel to clergy.

candidates.name: Center for Theology and the Natural Sciences (CTNS)
candidates.one_line: Graduate Theological Union programme for theology–science dialogue, founded 1981, which ran the Templeton-era project 'Virtuous AI? Cultural Evolution, Artificial Intelligence, and Virtue' (2022–2025; conferences in Berkeley, Seoul and Rome).
candidates.field_lens: Theology, virtue ethics, cultural evolution
candidates.ai_connection: Asked whether AI can have or cultivate virtue, which bears directly on character-based alignment. The project ended in 2025 and no AI programme is listed for 2026.

candidates.name: John Templeton Foundation: Intelligence Venture
candidates.one_line: Three-year initiative starting 2026, worth over $60M across all six JTF funding areas, on what intelligence is across human, animal, artificial and possibly cosmic contexts, including how to design a flourishing future amid fast-advancing technology.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy, theology, cognitive and natural sciences
candidates.ai_connection: Probably the largest new pool for philosophy and theology of intelligence; it is not framed around safety. Inquiries were due 15 July 2026; invited full proposals are due 4 December 2026. A natural home for work on wisdom, moral status, collective intelligence and alignment targets, if applicants make the connection.

candidates.name: Templeton World Charity Foundation: Diverse Intelligences programme
candidates.location: Nassau, Bahamas (hubs at Princeton, St Andrews/Indiana, Macquarie)
candidates.one_line: TWCF programme that launched three Diverse Intelligences hubs in 2025 (about $2.8M) to study intelligence across humans, other species and machines; the St Andrews hub offers small grants of up to £40k in 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Comparative cognition, philosophy of mind, biology
candidates.ai_connection: Hub themes include AGI informed by biological learning, systems and swarm intelligence, and creativity across species and machines. TWCF earlier funded Berggruen's 'AI and the Human' fellowship. It widens what 'intelligence' and 'alignment' mean beyond the ML canon.

candidates.name: Berggruen Institute
candidates.one_line: Philosophy-centred think tank with hubs in Los Angeles, Beijing and Venice. It publishes Noema magazine, awards the Berggruen Prize and essay prize, runs Future Humans and Transformations of the Human, and incubated Antikythera (Benjamin Bratton) on planetary computation.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy, political theory, philosophy of technology, Chinese thought
candidates.ai_connection: Noema publishes on AI safety (Nathan Gardels, 'AI Safety Is A Global Public Good'). Transformations of the Human placed philosophers and anthropologists inside AI labs. Its 2026 work includes a consciousness series and AI policy deliberation through Engaged California. Berggruen China (2026–27 fellows) is a rare China-facing philosophy-of-AI venue.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A philosophy-and-governance think tank that runs Noema, Antikythera, the Berggruen Prize and essay competitions, a China centre, and governance experiments such as Engaged California.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It frames AI safety as a global public good (Nathan Gardels in Noema). Engaged California, launched May 2026 with Governor Newsom, collects Californians' input on AI policy. Its essay prize featured Anil Seth's 'The Mythology of Conscious AI'. Its Beijing work (e.g. Bing Song's 'Co-Becoming') brings non-Western philosophy of the human-technology relationship. It links civilisational philosophy to participatory AI governance.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An idea incubator at the intersection of philosophy, science, technology and the arts. It publishes Noema magazine and runs fellowships, an essay prize, a consciousness series and a China centre.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Noema publishes AI-governance and safety essays, such as Nathan Gardels's 'AI Safety Is A Global Public Good' and Landemore & Tang's 'Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI'. The Berggruen Prize essay competition (Anil Seth's conscious-AI essay) and Berggruen China fellows ('Co-Becoming') bring non-Western philosophical perspectives on the human under AI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Philosophy-and-governance think tank. It awards the $1M Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture (2025: Michael Sandel), runs a companion essay competition, publishes Noema, and built Engaged California, a statewide deliberation platform on AI policy.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The essay competition is where Anil Seth's 'The Mythology of Conscious AI' (on the seed list) came from. Noema runs AI-safety essays such as Nathan Gardels' 'AI Safety Is A Global Public Good'. Engaged California applies citizen deliberation to AI policy. The institute holds prize money and prestige for philosophy-of-AI work.

candidates.name: Institute for Ethics in AI, University of Oxford
candidates.one_line: Philosophy-faculty institute in the Schwarzman Centre for the Humanities that brings philosophy and the humanities to AI. It runs the Accelerator Fellowship (2026/27 round), hosts the HAI Lab, offers executive education, and leads Civic AI and '6-Pack of Care' work.
candidates.field_lens: Moral and political philosophy, care ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Covers both the downstream social effects of AI and the upstream question of building AI that reflects human values. Civic AI (Audrey Tang, Caroline Green) offers a care-based alignment frame and held a conference in March 2026. The Accelerator Fellowship themes include AI and Humanity.

alt_descriptions.one_line: The Oxford Philosophy Faculty's AI-ethics institute. It runs an Accelerator Fellowship, the Cosmos-funded Human-Centered AI Lab, and, from November 2026, an executive programme in ethical AI leadership.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Became an affiliate of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI (IASEAI) in 2026. It hosts frontier-lab speakers in its HAI Lab lecture series (for example Anthropic's Jack Clark) and is home to Audrey Tang and Caroline Green's Civic AI / 6-Pack of Care work (already on the seed list).

candidates.name: MINT Lab (Machine Intelligence and Normative Theory)
candidates.location: Washington DC, USA (Johns Hopkins School of Government and Policy; moved from ANU in 2025)
candidates.one_line: Seth Lazar's lab for normative philosophy of AI, working on the normative competence of AI agents, governing agents, and post-AGI political philosophy.
candidates.field_lens: Moral and political philosophy
candidates.ai_connection: Evaluates whether LLM agents recognise and act on moral reasons, a philosophy-grounded evaluation agenda. It runs an AGI Governance Fellowship (2026) and held workshops on normative competence and AGI-ready institution design at IASEAI (February 2026). Lazar is a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Seth Lazar's political-philosophy lab, which moved from ANU to Johns Hopkins' School of Government and Policy in January 2025, studying normative competence in AI, the governance of AI agents and post-AGI political philosophy.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Received a US$480k grant for 'sociotechnical AI safety', the integration of multidisciplinary perspectives with technical work on direct AI risks. It runs Sociotechnical AI Safety workshops (Stanford, and a retreat at ANU's Kioloa campus), published a January 2026 analysis of the normative foundations of Anthropic's Claude constitution, presented on assessing moral competence in LLMs at NeurIPS 2025, and ran IASEAI 2026 sessions on AGI-ready institution design.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Seth Lazar's philosophy-and-computation lab, which moved from ANU to Johns Hopkins in Jan 2025. It works on 'governing agents', post-AGI political philosophy and AI's effects on democratic institutions; in 2026 it co-ran an AGI Governance Fellowship with Hadfield and Caputo.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Norms and infrastructure for decentralised AI-agent economies that avoid concentrated digital power. Asks how political communities stay legitimate alongside powerful AI. Runs workshops on democratic institution design (e.g. IASEAI 2026).

candidates.name: Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (CFI)
candidates.one_line: Interdisciplinary Cambridge centre (philosophy, history, cognitive science, policy) with programmes on Kinds of Intelligence; AI: Futures and Responsibility; AI: Trust and Society; AI: Narratives and Justice; and Design, Participation & Praxis.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy, history of science, cognitive science, literary studies
candidates.ai_connection: Founded on Stephen Hawking's 'best or worst thing' framing. It does philosophy of comparative intelligence and evaluation, x-risk-adjacent futures work, and research on AI narratives; in September 2026 it published commentary on AI consciousness as a coming societal divide. It runs an MPhil and PhD pipeline.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Cambridge's interdisciplinary centre on the nature and impact of AI, now directed by Rachel Adams. It spans philosophy, cognitive science, global politics, history and policy.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Hosts both x-risk work (the Cambridge Programme on AI Science & Policy, which is on the classic map) and ethics and global-justice work under one roof. With Adams leading both LCFI and GCG, it is one of the most structurally important ethics–safety–Global South bridges. Only its CASP sub-programme appears on the classic map.

candidates.name: Center for Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence (CPAI), University of Copenhagen
candidates.one_line: Copenhagen centre (Anders Søgaard) asking what AI can learn from philosophy and what philosophy can learn from AI; it hosts the five-day 'Models of Consciousness 2026' conference (12–16 October 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of language and mind, NLP
candidates.ai_connection: Philosophy of LLM understanding, consciousness and interpretability from a continental-European base; there are few such centres outside the US and UK.

candidates.name: Ethics of Socially Disruptive Technologies (ESDiT)
candidates.one_line: Ten-year Dutch research programme on the ethics and philosophy of disruptive technologies, including AI, with a 'conceptual disruption' line on how technologies unsettle core concepts.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of technology, ethics, conceptual engineering
candidates.ai_connection: Conceptual-disruption research covers how AI destabilises agency, personhood, responsibility and moral status, and how values change, which bears on what alignment should target over time. Its 2026 Yaoundé Seminar treats justice and democracy in a pluralist world.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A ten-year international research programme on the ethics and philosophy of socially disruptive technologies, with AI and robotics as a focal area.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Its work on 'conceptual disruption' (how AI unsettles concepts such as agency, personhood and responsibility) gives tools for AI moral status and for human self-understanding during a transition to transformative AI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Ten-year NWO Gravitation consortium on the ethics of socially disruptive technologies, including AI and robotics. It has a dedicated 'Conceptual Disruption' research line, research and associate fellows, and 2026 activity including a Yaoundé seminar on justice, democracy and technology.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Conceptual disruption (how AI unsettles concepts such as agency, personhood, moral status and responsibility) bears directly on AI welfare and on choosing alignment targets. It barely engages with the safety community.

candidates.name: Digital Humanism Initiative (DIGHUM)
candidates.one_line: International community, built around the Vienna Manifesto on Digital Humanism, of scholars, policymakers and industry people working to keep technology development centred on human interests, rights and democracy; it runs a lecture series and workshops.
candidates.field_lens: Humanist philosophy, computer science, political theory
candidates.ai_connection: A European humanist frame for AI governance and design, with active 2026 lectures and workshops (for example on business models for digital humanism). Rarely connected to the safety community.

candidates.name: Uehiro Oxford Institute
candidates.one_line: Oxford's practical-ethics institute (formerly the Oxford Uehiro Centre), which lists AI among the central challenges it works on.
candidates.field_lens: Practical and applied ethics, bioethics
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes on AI in medicine, on relational norms for human–AI interaction, and on AI risk; one example is Alberto Giubilini's 'Stop AI - Pause AI - Control AI?' (June 2026). It has a strong practical-ethics bench, but AI risk is not its organising focus.

candidates.name: Buddhism & AI Initiative
candidates.one_line: Collaborative effort bringing Buddhist communities, technologists and contemplative researchers together to help shape AI, through an annual summer course and conference (1–12 July 2026, in person and online).
candidates.field_lens: Buddhist philosophy and contemplative practice
candidates.ai_connection: One of the few organisations from a non-Western religion on the classic map (listed under Advocacy, Governance, Strategy). It brings Buddhist ethics of mind and compassion to AI development. The site is thin, so check the scale of its outputs.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A collaborative effort, launched Aug 2025 and led by Chris Scammell (ex-Conjecture COO), Peter Hershock and others, that connects Buddhist communities, technologists and contemplative researchers to shape AI. It also published a 'Buddhism x AI landscape' map.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: One of its three stated routes to AI safety is 'mental stabilization': helping communities, including AI professionals, find practices that keep them grounded through AI disruption. It also supports Buddhist-inspired alignment research and Buddhist voices in governance.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A field-building initiative (Chris Scammell, Peter Hershock, Alex Sarkissian, Ryan Stagg, Austin Pick) that maps and convenes the Buddhism-AI field, runs workshops for sanghas, and channels Buddhist perspectives into AI labs and governance.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Has held more than 500 field-mapping conversations and published a six-domain field framework of about 190 named entities (AI→Buddhism, Buddhism→AI alignment and neuroscience, scholarship, teaching, governance, ecosystem). It runs rolling workshops for Buddhist teachers and pursues 'technical collaboration' with AI labs. Writing includes 'Timeline of the AGI Movement' and 'Safeguarding Attention'. Funded by FLI; collaborators include the Khyentse Foundation, Omidyar Network, Mind & Life Europe and Wisdom Publications. Its framework is the best existing directory for this angle.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A European academic summer course (1-12 Jul 2026) and four-day conference (9-12 Jul 2026), co-organised by Rangjung Yeshe Gomde Germany-Austria, Dharma Gate Buddhist College (Budapest) and the Research Center of the Italian Buddhist Union.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The 2026 conference days covered mind and consciousness; attention and mental training; 'Agency and Alignment'; and envisioning the future. Speakers included John Dunne, Peter Hershock and Nikki Mirghafori. It is continental Europe's main academic Buddhism-AI gathering. Not to be confused with Chris Scammell's Buddhism & AI Initiative. Whether it recurs in 2027 is unknown.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A collaborative initiative that brings Buddhist scholars, contemplative practitioners and technologists together on AI. In July 2026 it ran a 12-day academic summer course and conference at Gomde Austria, part of the Rangjung Yeshe network.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Asks how Buddhist traditions can guide AI wisely. Faculty include John Dunne (UW–Madison), James Gentry (Stanford) and Marieke van Vugt (Groningen AI institute). The conference was co-organised by groups working on Buddhism and AI, including the network around CSAS/Rangjung Yeshe.

candidates.name: Forethought
candidates.one_line: Philosophy-led research nonprofit (Will MacAskill and others) on navigating explosive AI progress and the 'grand challenges' it raises.
candidates.field_lens: Moral philosophy, longtermist ethics
candidates.ai_connection: 'Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion' (March 2025) names digital beings worthy of moral consideration, AI-enabled autocracy and collective decision-making as challenges that cannot be left to AI. It is the main home for 'what should a good post-AGI future be' questions since Oxford's Global Priorities Institute and Future of Humanity Institute closed.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Oxford research nonprofit (MacAskill, Davidson, Cotton-Barratt, Finnveden) studying the intelligence explosion and how to navigate it: AI-enabled coups and power concentration, intelligence-explosion economics, lock-in, and 'Better Futures'.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It produced the analysis of 'AI-enabled coups': singularly loyal AI replacing human personnel, exclusive access to superhuman capabilities, secret loyalties. Models of whether automating AI R&D yields runaway growth. Work on how present AI specs could lock in values.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Oxford research nonprofit on navigating the transition to transformative AI. Its AI-for-epistemics and coordination agenda is the field's main conceptual source.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Key outputs: 'AI Tools for Existential Security' (Vaintrob and Cotton-Barratt, March 2025); 'AI impacts on epistemics: the good, the bad and the ugly' (Cotton-Barratt and Hadshar); a design-sketch series from February to April 2026 covering collective epistemics, angels-on-the-shoulder, strategic awareness and defense-favoured coordination tech; 'AI for AI for Epistemics' (April 2026); and Tom Davidson on how AI should behave when advising humans on important decisions. Other groups here cite this work as the field's agenda.

candidates.name: Research Center for Islamic Legislation and Ethics (CILE)
candidates.one_line: Doha research centre for Islamic applied ethics (it hosted the 2024 World Congress of Bioethics) that has started on AI, for example a September 2025 event on 'AI Ethics: The Convergence of Technology and Diverse Moral Traditions'.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic ethics (maqasid al-sharia), applied ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Could supply Islamic frameworks for alignment targets, AI red lines and machine moral status to an AI-safety field that rarely consults them. It is the strongest institutional base for Islamic AI ethics found in this search, but its AI work so far is events, not a programme.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Qatar research centre (founded 2012) on applied Islamic ethics. It has a growing line of work on AI ethics.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: A 2024 virtual winter school with Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence on AI, religion and culture. Conference: 'AI Ethics: The Convergence of Technology and Diverse Moral Traditions'. Mohammed Ghaly's work on Islamic ethics and AI. A public lecture on AI weapons. It is the only well-institutionalised Islamic-ethics venue for AI found in this pass.

candidates.name: Normativity Lab (Gillian Hadfield, Johns Hopkins)
candidates.one_line: Gillian Hadfield's lab (she holds the Bloomberg Distinguished Professorship of AI Alignment and Governance at Johns Hopkins) studying how human normativity, meaning the classification and enforcement of behavioural standards, works as infrastructure, and using that to design legal, regulatory and technical systems for AI.
candidates.field_lens: Law and economics, legal theory, institutional design, cultural evolution of norms
candidates.ai_connection: Treats alignment as a problem of normative infrastructure: AI agents need to read and respond to human norms, and societies need legal infrastructure for agents (attributing actions to agents, shaping their interactions, detecting and remedying harm). Hadfield is a faculty affiliate of CHAI and Schwartz Reisman, and was the founding director of Schwartz Reisman.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Gillian Hadfield's lab at Johns Hopkins (she holds a Bloomberg Distinguished Professorship in AI Alignment and Governance). It studies how human normative systems (law, markets, institutions) work, and applies that to aligning AI agents.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Normative alignment: building AI agents that read and follow group norms inside social, economic and legal structures. Studies how norms and cooperation emerge in mixed human-AI multi-agent systems. Hadfield is known for proposing regulatory markets for AI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Gillian Hadfield's lab studying how AI agents can recognise, learn and adapt to human social norms, and which legal and regulatory institutions an economy of AI agents needs.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Four areas: normative competence, cooperative AI, institutions for AI, and computational models of human normative systems for alignment. It treats alignment as joining human normative infrastructure rather than specifying values. Hadfield is also a CAIF trustee.

candidates.name: Knight First Amendment Institute: AI and Democratic Freedoms project
candidates.one_line: A research and essay programme at Columbia's Knight Institute, anchored by Senior AI Advisor Seth Lazar, on how advanced AI systems may harm or strengthen civil liberties and democratic institutions.
candidates.field_lens: Constitutional and free-expression law, democratic theory
candidates.ai_connection: Brings First Amendment and democratic-freedoms analysis to advanced AI: levels of AI-agent autonomy, an 'AI Power Disparity Index', technical research for democracy-minded agents, and whether alignment techniques burden users' expressive interests. The April 2025 Columbia symposium was followed by essays published through March 2026.

candidates.name: Humane Intelligence
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit, founded by Rumman Chowdhury, that runs public AI red-teaming events, bias bounties and contextual evaluations of AI systems with affected communities.
candidates.field_lens: Algorithmic auditing, participatory evaluation, community-based red teaming
candidates.ai_connection: Moves safety evaluation away from lab-internal benchmarks toward structured red-teaming by impacted communities: 5,600+ participants across five continents and 30+ evaluations. It open-sourced its red-teaming app in September 2026, launched a Zindi bias bounty in August 2026, and published a peer-reviewed method for ontology-based contextual evaluations (OB-CAIE) on 1 October 2026.

candidates.name: AI Incident Database (Responsible AI Collaborative)
candidates.one_line: An open, crowd-sourced database of real-world AI harms and failures (1,720+ incidents by October 2026), run by the nonprofit Responsible AI Collaborative.
candidates.field_lens: Aviation and computer-security incident reporting; safety-engineering practice of learning from accidents
candidates.ai_connection: Brings the aviation and CVE practice of learning from incidents to AI. It is the main empirical record of deployed-AI failures, which safety researchers and AI-safety institutes can mine to ground risk models and evals in observed harms rather than speculation.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Nonprofit that runs the AI Incident Database. It holds more than 1,700 indexed real-world AI harms, with taxonomies, entity pages and a news digest, and was still logging new incidents in October 2026.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: It brings aviation's 'learn from every accident' institution to AI, giving researchers and regulators a shared record of failures so mistakes aren't repeated. It is the main public evidence base for incident-driven safety work, and the OECD and others cite it.

candidates.name: Delft Algorithms, Systems & Safety Lab (DASS), TU Delft
candidates.one_line: Roel Dobbe's group in TU Delft's Technology, Policy & Management faculty, applying system-safety and control-engineering theory to the analysis, design and governance of AI in public infrastructure.
candidates.field_lens: System safety engineering, control theory, STS, public administration
candidates.ai_connection: Dobbe's 'AI Safety is Stuck in Technical Terms' (arXiv, February 2025) answers the International AI Safety Report from a system-safety standpoint and argues that decades of system-safety practice for software-intensive systems should shape AI-safety governance and the EU AI Act. The group's postdoc call is titled 'System Design and Governance for Safe Hybrid Intelligence Systems'.

candidates.name: AI Safety and Societal Impacts Research Group, Hasso Plattner Institute (HPI)
candidates.one_line: A new six-year research group, funded by the DFG's Emmy Noether programme and led by Paul Röttger (Oxford Internet Institute), studying AI risks and benefits as AI enters social and political processes. Positions start from September 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Computational social science, NLP, political science
candidates.ai_connection: Topics are political and social bias in AI, delegation to autonomous agents, the spread of misaligned behaviour across competing AI systems, and safety evaluations and technical mitigations. It is one of Germany's first university groups explicitly framed as 'AI safety', and sits within reach of the int/a Berlin community.

candidates.name: Sociotechnical Safety Lab, University of Washington
candidates.one_line: Emily Tseng's HCI lab (founded spring 2026) on digital safety: how technologies enter people's relationships and everyday lives, and how to design systems that anticipate misuse.
candidates.field_lens: Human-centred design, HCI, tech-facilitated abuse and digital-safety research
candidates.ai_connection: In July 2026 it was chosen as one of 18 university groups in Microsoft's External Red Team Alliance (EXTRA) on AI safety. It brings misuse knowledge from intimate and interpersonal contexts into red-teaming of AI systems, the relational harm surface that matters for AI companions and assistants.

candidates.name: Global Center on AI Governance (GCG)
candidates.one_line: A Cape Town research hub, founded in 2023 by Rachel Adams, for equitable, evidence-led AI governance. It runs the African Observatory on Responsible AI and the Global Index on Responsible AI.
candidates.field_lens: Political economy, global justice, African governance and development studies
candidates.ai_connection: With the University of Cape Town it leads an 'African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security' so that African perspectives shape global AI-safety debates. Adams was a lead drafter of the African Union's Continental AI Strategy and now also directs Cambridge's Leverhulme CFI, which makes her a rare institutional broker between the Global-South governance and AI-safety worlds.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An African-based centre working to reduce global inequalities that AI makes worse. It produces the Global Index on Responsible AI and co-leads the UCT African Hub on AI Safety.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Global Index on Responsible AI 2026: 135 countries, with a 'Trust & Safety' dimension, built by more than 150 embedded researchers and used by UNESCO, the UN, the OECD and the World Bank. Companion report: Global State of Responsible AI. Founding member of GSNTA. Rachel Adams is also at Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.

alt_descriptions.one_line: African-led centre that produces the Global Index on Responsible AI (135 countries, 150+ embedded researchers) and the African Observatory on Responsible AI. It co-leads an African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security with the University of Cape Town and has trained 250+ professionals through courses and fellowships.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: One of the few African institutions explicitly using 'AI safety', through its peace-and-security hub. It brings Global South perspectives on inequality and power to AI governance.

candidates.name: Digital Futures Lab (DFL)
candidates.one_line: An independent interdisciplinary research studio in Goa, led by Urvashi Aneja, studying technology and society in India and the Majority World through research, systematic foresight and public engagement.
candidates.field_lens: Development studies, foresight, feminist and Global South perspectives
candidates.ai_connection: Runs an explicit stream on AI safety from Global South perspectives ('if AI safety is to mean anything in practice, it has to mean something everywhere'), with 2025–26 reports on AI safety in the Global South alongside work on judicial AI, gendered harms and data centres. It is one of the few non-Western think tanks engaging the AI-safety frame directly.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An independent interdisciplinary research studio in Goa that uses foresight and evidence work to study technology and society in India and the Majority World. It convenes the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI and leads its Global South AI Safety Report.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Global South AI Safety Report (May 2026, led by Urvashi Aneja). 'AI Safety & Gender in India' policy brief (Feb 2026), a taxonomy of gendered AI harms. Submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance ('Grounded, Plural, Accountable'). A judicial AI assessment toolkit. It explicitly reframes AI safety around real deployment pathways rather than abstract risk taxonomies.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An interdisciplinary research studio that uses evidence, systematic foresight and public engagement to study technology and society in India and the Majority World.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Launched a Global South AI safety and governance coalition at the IndiaAI Impact Summit (February 2026) and published 'An AI Safety Report for the Global South, by the Global South' (May 2026). Other outputs: a taxonomy of gendered AI harms in India, foresight scenarios co-created with creative workers, and a submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

candidates.name: Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society (SRI)
candidates.one_line: University of Toronto institute that brings computer science, philosophy, law, economics and political science together, with a 'solutions stream' that turns research into policy and governance tools.
candidates.field_lens: Law, philosophy, economics, political science
candidates.ai_connection: Founded under Gillian Hadfield. It works on independent testing of powerful AI models (Nicolas Papernot) and on 'transparency as information infrastructure' (nine proposals to Canada's federal consultation, September 2026). It appointed a new Scientific Advisory Committee in September 2026.

candidates.name: Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP)
candidates.one_line: Marc Rotenberg's nonprofit for AI governance grounded in human rights, democratic values and the rule of law. It publishes the annual 'AI and Democratic Values' index (AI Index 2026, three volumes) and trains a global network of policy-clinic fellows.
candidates.field_lens: Human-rights law, privacy law, international law
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes reports on frontier-AI safety and governance frameworks, issues statements on AI red lines, backs the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI, and takes part in the UN Global Dialogue. Its clinics have trained 1,000+ participants from 120+ countries, a rights-based pipeline that AI-safety policy work rarely taps.

candidates.name: Partnership on AI (PAI)
candidates.one_line: A multistakeholder nonprofit of 200+ partners (labs, civil society, academia, media) that develops shared responsible-AI practice.
candidates.field_lens: Multistakeholder governance, civil society, labour and media studies
candidates.ai_connection: One of the few venues where safety and ethics share programmes: its Safety-Critical AI work (including real-time failure-detection frameworks for AI agents) sits beside AI and human connection, labour and synthetic-media streams. In 2026 it co-led UN Global Dialogue work on trustworthy AI.

candidates.name: Ada Lovelace Institute
candidates.one_line: A London research institute incubated by the Nuffield Foundation, working so that data and AI serve people and society through work on regulation, public participation, AI evaluation, the public sector and geopolitics.
candidates.field_lens: Public-interest research, deliberative democracy, social policy
candidates.ai_connection: Brings evidence on public attitudes and deliberation into AI regulation. September 2026 work covers the UN Global Dialogue (participation of disempowered communities) and UK regulatory options, and a new programme looks at power concentration in the AI ecosystem. It partners on BRAID. It does not frame its work in x-risk terms.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Independent UK research institute on data and AI with a dedicated public-participation research programme.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Argued in July 2026 that 'a citizens' track is needed' in the UN Global Dialogue on AI. Sept 2026 'Beyond the kill switch' work on how people want AI policy decisions made. Deliberation on AI in social care (AI transcription, March 2026). Long record of citizens' juries and councils on AI and biometrics.

candidates.name: AI Now Institute
candidates.one_line: A New York policy research institute on the political economy of AI: industry power, labour, data-centre expansion and independent oversight.
candidates.field_lens: Political economy, antitrust, labour studies, safety-critical systems engineering
candidates.ai_connection: Increasingly works on safety ground from an accountability stance. 'Double Agents: Defensive AI Agents Magnify Cyber Risks' (July 2026) and its chief AI scientist's arguments for independent oversight of high-risk AI draw on safety-critical engineering rather than self-regulation. Its 'Artificial Power' landscape reports analyse the concentration dynamics behind race narratives. It is a Humanity AI grantee.

alt_descriptions.one_line: New York research institute on the political economy of AI: corporate concentration, industrial policy, data-centre expansion and accountability (2026 reports on defensive AI agents and a data-centre policy toolkit).
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The leading critical-tradition analysis of concentrated AI power (Ford Foundation general support, Nov 2025). It shares the power-concentration worry with Forethought and Longview, yet openly rejects 'doomerism'. Exactly the divide int/a's 'recoupling' principle could bridge.

candidates.name: Data & Society Research Institute
candidates.one_line: An independent social-science institute studying how AI is designed, used and governed, through programmes such as AI on the Ground, the Algorithmic Impact Methods Lab (AIMLab), Democracy in the Age of AI and a Worker Lens on the AI Economy.
candidates.field_lens: Sociology, anthropology, STS, labour studies
candidates.ai_connection: Brings ethnographic and participatory impact-assessment methods (AIMLab) into AI governance. In September 2026 it launched a research and policy collection on 'Governing AI Agents'. It is a source of empirical data on how deployed AI changes work and civic life.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An independent research institute that uses ethnography and qualitative social science to study technology's real-world impacts, including through its Algorithmic Impact Methods Lab (AIMLab).
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Brings fieldwork-based, community-centred methods to AI impact assessment and to labour under AI. It is the strongest institutional home for ethnographic AI research, though aimed at present harms rather than frontier labs or catastrophic risk.

candidates.name: Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR)
candidates.one_line: Timnit Gebru's globally distributed institute of academics, activists and engineers doing community-rooted AI research, demystifying AI hype and imagining alternative technological futures.
candidates.field_lens: Critical data studies, decolonial and community-based research
candidates.ai_connection: The leading critical voice on the AGI and x-risk paradigm (the 'TESCREAL' critique). Its work on data workers and on harms of AI development is the strongest test of whether bridging is possible. Gebru's book 'Deep Unlearning' is forthcoming. Included because int/a bridging work will have to engage this camp.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A globally distributed, community-rooted AI research institute founded by Timnit Gebru, with a strong Ethiopian and African presence. It works against AI hype and 'cultivates dreaming as a discipline'.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Research on present harms and on worker- and community-centred AI. Gebru's book 'Deep Unlearning' (2026). It is openly critical of x-risk framings, so it is a necessary counterpart for any int/a 'recoupling' of AI risk with justice concerns rather than an ally by default.

candidates.name: Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, Harvard
candidates.one_line: Harvard's centre for internet and society, home to the Ethics and Governance of AI work, the Applied Social Media Lab and a large fellows community.
candidates.field_lens: Law, internet governance, philosophy, media studies
candidates.ai_connection: Its 2026–27 speaker series asks whether AI is 'All Too Human?', a philosophical look at how AI reshapes our picture of human capability. It hosts work on the governance and accountability of AI, and its large fellowship network is a recruiting ground for law-trained AI-governance talent.

candidates.name: AI Accountability Lab (AIAL), Trinity College Dublin
candidates.one_line: Abeba Birhane's lab, founded in 2024, auditing AI models, datasets and the governance ecosystem with a focus on the public interest and marginalised groups.
candidates.field_lens: Cognitive science, critical data studies, algorithmic auditing
candidates.ai_connection: 2026 outputs include analysis and a policy brief on AI companion apps (relational and psychological harms), a study of corporate regulatory capture in AI governance, and EU AI Act transparency compliance. Birhane was elected to the EU AI Act Advisory Forum in June 2026.

candidates.name: AlgorithmWatch
candidates.one_line: A Berlin and Zurich watchdog that researches and campaigns on automated decision-making, AI Act enforcement, platform systemic risks under the DSA, and generative AI in elections.
candidates.field_lens: Investigative research, digital-rights advocacy, EU regulatory law
candidates.ai_connection: Brings DSA-style systemic-risk auditing and public-interest investigation to general-purpose AI, for example how chatbots steer users to sources and AI-generated sexual imagery. It monitors attempts to roll back AI Act safeguards. A nearby partner for the int/a Berlin community.

candidates.name: BRAID: Bridging Responsible AI Divides
candidates.one_line: A six-year (2022–2028), £18M+ AHRC programme led by the University of Edinburgh, with the BBC and the Ada Lovelace Institute, that embeds arts and humanities research in the responsible-AI ecosystem through fellowships, artist commissions and demonstrator projects.
candidates.field_lens: Arts and humanities, design, copyright law, creative practice
candidates.ai_connection: The largest funded effort to bring humanities knowledge into AI governance and industry practice. In 2026 it runs a Responsible AI Cultural Leaders Academy with Arts Council England and creative commissions for the Edinburgh Festivals in 2027. Its focus is 'responsible AI' rather than safety, but its fellowship model is a ready template for a humanities-to-safety programme.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A UKRI/AHRC programme that embeds arts and humanities research in the responsible-AI ecosystem through fellowships, funding calls, landscape studies and leadership programmes.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Outputs include a two-part Responsible AI landscape study, new funding calls (September 2026), a Responsible AI Cultural Leaders Academy with Arts Council England, and work on creators' rights. It is the largest public humanities-for-AI programme, framed around 'responsible AI' rather than catastrophic risk.

alt_descriptions.one_line: AHRC/UKRI programme (over £18M, 2022–2028) embedding arts and humanities research in the responsible-AI ecosystem through fellowships (including industry challenge fellowships with Framestore and the National Lottery Heritage Fund), demonstrator projects, artist commissions and UK–US collaborations.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The UK's main state vehicle for humanities-led AI work. It is framed around responsible AI, not catastrophic risk, so its fellows rarely meet the safety community: an unexploited bridge.

candidates.name: Centre for Technomoral Futures, University of Edinburgh
candidates.one_line: An Edinburgh Futures Institute centre co-directed by Shannon Vallor and Emily Sullivan that combines technical and moral knowledge in research, an MSc in Data and AI Ethics, and a PhD programme.
candidates.field_lens: Virtue ethics, philosophy of technology, care ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Vallor's virtue-ethics account of AI ('Technology and the Virtues', 'The AI Mirror') treats AI as a mirror that can erode or cultivate human moral wisdom, the ethics-side counterpart to the seed list's 'wise machines' and wisdom-evals ideas. It also co-anchors BRAID.

candidates.name: UN Human Rights (OHCHR) B-Tech Project
candidates.one_line: OHCHR's project applying the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs) to tech companies, with a dedicated generative-AI workstream and a taxonomy of human-rights harms from generative AI.
candidates.field_lens: International human-rights law, business and human rights (UNGPs), due diligence
candidates.ai_connection: Asks foundation-model developers to run human-rights due diligence across the AI value chain and asks states for a 'smart mix' of regulation, a ready-made legal frame for frontier-model risk management. In September 2026 High Commissioner Volker Türk wrote to states and frontier AI companies warning of 'unprecedented risks' and calling for governance of frontier models grounded in human-rights law.

candidates.name: Research ICT Africa (RIA)
candidates.one_line: A Cape Town digital-policy think tank, directed by Pria Chetty, working on data justice, AI and advanced-technology policy, and the Africa Just AI project.
candidates.field_lens: Law, economics, data justice, development studies
candidates.ai_connection: Shapes African positions in global AI governance, including the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (September 2026). It is a counterpart for any AI-safety effort that wants African legitimacy beyond GCG. No x-risk framing.

alt_descriptions.one_line: African digital-policy think tank (affiliated with UCT) researching AI governance, data justice and 'Africa Just AI'. It works on frameworks for restructuring labour and power in AI futures and engages the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Brings the view of economies most exposed to AI-driven value capture by a few firms and countries: international distribution of AI gains, digital public infrastructure. It complements Windfall Trust's work on African economies under TAI.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An African digital-policy think tank working on digital equality, data justice and 'Just AI'. It runs longitudinal Global South surveys such as After Access.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Work on AI governance, labour and power in Africa: 'Policy levers for AI futures', with LSE, September 2026. Platform-harm reporting. Evidence on uneven AI diffusion that bears on whether AI benefits are distributed justly.

candidates.name: Derechos Digitales
candidates.one_line: A Latin American digital-rights organisation researching and advocating on AI, surveillance, data centres and digital autonomy across the region.
candidates.field_lens: Human rights, Latin American STS, digital-rights advocacy
candidates.ai_connection: Brings Latin American rights perspectives on AI and autonomy, AI surveillance devices and the costs of AI training, and explicitly rejects both 'destroyer' and 'saviour' AI narratives. It hosted 'IA, centros de datos y derechos' at the University of Buenos Aires in September 2026. Latin America has no equivalent of GCG's AI-safety hub, so this is a natural partner for building one.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Latin American digital-rights organisation working on autonomy, dignity and social justice in technology. It publishes regular analysis of AI in the region.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: 2026 columns on AI myths, digital autonomy, smart-glasses surveillance and the costs of AI training. GSNTA member. Jamila Venturini sits on the advisory panel of the Global South AI Safety Report.

candidates.name: 5Rights Foundation
candidates.one_line: A London children's-rights organisation that authored the Children & AI Design Code, a process for identifying, evaluating and mitigating AI risks to children by design and by default.
candidates.field_lens: Children's rights (UNCRC), age-appropriate design regulation
candidates.ai_connection: Children are on the frontline of AI companion and chatbot harms. 5Rights' design-code method (foreseeable risks, 'known unknowns', safety by default) is regulatory know-how that AI-safety evals and model-spec work hardly uses.

candidates.name: Humanity AI
candidates.one_line: A coalition of ten US foundations, led by MacArthur and Omidyar Network with Ford, Mellon, Packard, Mozilla, Kapor, Lumina, Doris Duke and Siegel, committing $500M over five years to people-centred AI. Pooled grants run through Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors from 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Civil-society philanthropy: democracy, education, artists, work, personal security
candidates.ai_connection: The largest new pot of money on the ethics and accountability side (grantees include AI Now), explicitly aimed at loosening developer control over AI's direction. It is almost entirely disjoint from x-risk funders (Coefficient Giving, SFF), which makes it a prime target for the 'legible to new funders' brief.

alt_descriptions.one_line: $500M, five-year coalition of ten foundations (MacArthur, Omidyar, Ford, Mellon, Mozilla, Packard, Doris Duke, Lumina, Kapor, Siegel) funding a 'people-centred' AI future across democracy, education, humanities and culture, labour and economy, and security.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: The largest public-interest AI pot. Aligned grantmaking began in fall 2025 and pooled grants started in 2026. Beth Goldberg was named Executive Director in July 2026, and a $10M open call for community-driven initiatives followed in September 2026. It is framed around harms, power and agency rather than catastrophic risk, which makes it the obvious 'new funder' for int/a's societal-resilience and human-minds-and-relationships work.

candidates.name: European AI & Society Fund (EAISF)
candidates.one_line: A pooled fund of about 20 European foundations that has given €13.6M since 2020 to public-interest groups in 27 countries working on AI policy, accountability, digital rights and workers.
candidates.field_lens: European civil-society philanthropy, digital rights
candidates.ai_connection: Funds AI Act implementation advocacy and accountability research (it funds AIAL, for example), and in 2026 runs a €2M 'Building Narrative Power' call on data centres, jobs and young people.
