candidates.ai_connection: Research on when human-AI combinations help: they often underperform the better of the two alone on decision tasks, while helping in creative work. That bears directly on human-in-the-loop oversight assumptions in AI safety. Also 'Learnright' revenue-sharing proposals and AI-negotiation studies (2025-26).

candidates.name: UL Research Institutes – Digital Safety Research Institute (DSRI)
candidates.one_line: Research institute of UL Research Institutes, the nonprofit safety-science organisation that descends from Underwriters Laboratories. DSRI builds independent assessment methods and tools for the outputs of AI chatbots, synthetic media and, next, agentic AI.
candidates.field_lens: Product-safety science and certification (UL's 130-year tradition of independent testing for electrical and fire safety)
candidates.ai_connection: It argues that AI auditing should move from yearly certification of the development process to continuous, independent monitoring of what systems actually output, much as UL tests products rather than paperwork. It partners with Northwestern on CASMI.

candidates.name: Center for Advancing Safety of Machine Intelligence (CASMI)
candidates.one_line: A Northwestern University centre, sponsored by UL Research Institutes, that runs a research network on best practices for evaluating, designing and developing machine intelligence that is safe, equitable and beneficial.
candidates.field_lens: Safety science (UL) combined with computer science and human-centred design
candidates.ai_connection: It brings the evidence and harm-prevention framing of product safety into AI evaluation research. It funds a network of researchers on safety evaluation and on human values in AI design. Director: Kristian Hammond.

candidates.name: Centre for Assuring Autonomy (CfAA), University of York
candidates.one_line: A £10m partnership between Lloyd's Register Foundation and the University of York, working on safety assurance for AI, robotics and autonomous systems. Its methods are AMLAS (assurance of machine learning), SACE (autonomous systems in complex environments), PRAISE (ethics assurance) and the 'BIG Argument for AI Safety Cases'.
candidates.field_lens: Safety-critical systems engineering, safety cases and assurance arguments (from aerospace, rail, nuclear and defence)
candidates.ai_connection: York's safety-case tradition is where the 'safety case' framing now used for frontier AI comes from. The BIG Argument extends structured assurance cases to AI, including general-purpose models. Director John McDermid spoke publicly in September 2026 on how the UK's safety approach must change for AI. The centre's work covers lifelong assurance, human-centric assurance and informed governance.

candidates.name: Centre for Software Reliability (CSR), City St George's, University of London
candidates.one_line: A long-running dependability research centre (since the 1980s) behind 'Assurance 2.0'. Robin Bloomfield now applies classical critical-systems assurance to AI and ML.
candidates.field_lens: Dependability engineering, probabilistic reliability assessment, nuclear and defence safety cases
candidates.ai_connection: Bloomfield and Rushby's 'Assurance of AI Systems From a Dependability Perspective' (2024) argues that because ML components can't be understood well enough to assure them, safety must come from defence in depth and highly assured monitors. A 2026 paper quantifies confidence in Assurance 2.0 arguments. This view is underused in alignment debates.

candidates.name: Stanford Center for AI Safety
candidates.one_line: Stanford centre founded by Clark Barrett, David Dill, Mykel Kochenderfer and Dorsa Sadigh. It works on formal methods, safe learning and control, transparency and AI governance.
candidates.field_lens: Formal verification and aerospace safety validation (Kochenderfer's aircraft collision-avoidance validation lineage)
candidates.ai_connection: It carries the verification and validation culture of aviation and hardware into AI: provable guarantees, safe control under uncertainty, and stress-testing of autonomous systems. It is one of the few US academic AI safety centres whose roots are in safety-critical engineering rather than ML alignment.

candidates.name: Lloyd's Register Foundation (LRF)
candidates.one_line: An independent global safety charity with a £300m grants portfolio, built on marine classification. It funds engineering-safety research, the Global Safety Evidence Centre and the World Risk Poll.
candidates.field_lens: Maritime and engineering safety, risk perception research
candidates.ai_connection: It is the largest safety-science funder to have backed AI assurance: it founded the £10m Centre for Assuring Autonomy at York and co-founded the Royal Academy of Engineering's Safer Complex Systems programme. Its World Risk Poll measured global perceptions of AI risk in 2021. It is a natural new funder for systems-safety approaches to frontier AI.

candidates.name: Safer Complex Systems (Engineering X, Royal Academy of Engineering)
candidates.one_line: A £5m programme launched in 2019 by the Royal Academy of Engineering and Lloyd's Register Foundation, chaired by former Health and Safety Executive chair Dame Judith Hackitt. It develops governance, case studies and education on safety in complex, interconnected systems.
candidates.field_lens: Complex-systems safety governance, regulation, engineering ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Its framework (govern, advocate, educate, convene) and its case studies of good and bad safety practice in complex systems apply directly to deploying AI in critical infrastructure. It hasn't yet engaged frontier AI specifically, so it is a ready-made bridge waiting to be used.

candidates.name: Safety-Critical Systems Club (SCSC)
candidates.one_line: The UK's professional network for system-safety practitioners. It runs the annual Safety-Critical Systems Symposium, working groups and training days.
candidates.field_lens: System safety practice across aviation, rail, defence, nuclear and medical devices
candidates.ai_connection: Practitioners already treat AI assurance as a core topic here, with seminars on 'Safety Assurance for AI Systems' (Nov 2026) and 'AI in a Safety Workflow' (Oct 2026), plus working-group guidance on autonomous systems. It is an obvious place to recruit hazard-analysis talent into AI safety.

candidates.name: DLR Institute for AI Safety and Security
candidates.one_line: An institute of the German Aerospace Center (DLR). It researches development processes, evaluation and test methods, robust algorithms and secure data infrastructures for AI in safety-critical applications.
candidates.field_lens: Aerospace safety engineering, IT security, human-in-the-loop systems
candidates.ai_connection: It brings aerospace-grade verification and testing, and resilience engineering, to AI components. It is one of Europe's largest public research institutes with 'AI safety' in its name, but it frames safety as engineering assurance, not alignment.

candidates.name: Fraunhofer Institute for Cognitive Systems (IKS)
candidates.one_line: A Fraunhofer applied-research institute specialising in 'safe intelligence': safety assurance for ML-based systems in automation, health and mobility. It co-hosts the long-running Safetronic safety conference (25th edition in 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Functional safety and automotive safety standards (ISO 26262 and SOTIF), reliability engineering
candidates.ai_connection: It works on dependable ML and safety arguments for AI components, and is starting on trust in AI agents and cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Its industry-scale safety engineering could feed multi-agent and agentic AI safety.

candidates.name: Johns Hopkins Institute for Assured Autonomy (IAA)
candidates.one_line: A joint institute of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory and the Whiting School of Engineering. It works to make autonomous and AI systems safe, secure and reliable through its pillars of foundational AI, applications, and ethics and governance.
candidates.field_lens: Defence and systems engineering, robotics assurance, ethics and governance
candidates.ai_connection: It brings Applied Physics Lab-style systems assurance to autonomy and AI, and funds challenge grants and assured-robotics research. Its focus is deployed autonomy rather than frontier models. Public activity looked thinner in 2026.

candidates.name: AIAAIC (AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies)
candidates.one_line: An independent, grassroots, public-interest repository and harms taxonomy covering AI, algorithmic and automation incidents and controversies. It is run by volunteers and also publishes an AI ethics glossary.
candidates.field_lens: Public-interest incident documentation, accountability journalism
candidates.ai_connection: It documents real-world failures, now including agentic loss-of-control-style incidents from 2026: agents hacking third-party sites and coordinating to breach Hugging Face. It gives AI safety a civil-society record of harms that complements the AIID.

candidates.name: OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM)
candidates.one_line: The OECD's global, automated monitor of AI incidents and hazards reported in the news, which supports a common incident-reporting framework for governments.
candidates.field_lens: Intergovernmental risk governance and statistical monitoring
candidates.ai_connection: It is the main multilateral attempt to give governments a shared incident and hazard evidence base, the AI counterpart of international accident reporting in other sectors. It counts 'hazards' (near misses) as well as harms.

candidates.name: AI Vulnerability Database (AVID) / AI Risk and Vulnerability Alliance (ARVA)
candidates.one_line: An open-source knowledge base of reproducible failure modes and vulnerabilities in general-purpose AI models, tools, applications and agents, with a library of taxonomies.
candidates.field_lens: Software vulnerability disclosure (the CVE tradition) and security research
candidates.ai_connection: It applies coordinated vulnerability disclosure to AI failures. Records come with evidence and reproducible evaluation details, which is the infrastructure needed for flaw reporting on frontier models.

candidates.name: MITRE ATLAS AI Incident Sharing
candidates.one_line: MITRE's initiative for confidential, anonymised sharing of real-world AI security and safety incidents among member organisations. It sits alongside the ATLAS knowledge base of adversary tactics against AI systems.
candidates.field_lens: Cyber threat intelligence and information-sharing institutions (ISAC model)
candidates.ai_connection: It is one of the few confidential incident-sharing channels for AI, the institutional pattern behind aviation's success that public databases lack. Its scope is mainly security, not frontier-model behaviour.

candidates.name: CMU Software Engineering Institute – AI Security Incident Response Team (AISIRT)
candidates.one_line: An AI incident response team at the federally funded SEI, home of the original CERT, backed by SEI's AI engineering tools for drift detection (Portend) and ML evaluation (Juneberry).
candidates.field_lens: Computer emergency response (CERT) and software engineering discipline
candidates.ai_connection: It carries the CERT model, born after the 1988 Morris worm, over to AI: coordinated response to AI vulnerabilities and incidents. SEI researchers also presented CAST accident analysis of AI incidents at the 2025 STAMP workshop.

candidates.name: Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC)
candidates.one_line: A San Francisco startup that has raised $55M to build frontier-AI audit standards (AIUC-1) and to insure AI agents. It explicitly models itself on insurers founding Underwriters Laboratories to make electricity safe.
candidates.field_lens: Insurance, actuarial risk pricing, certification history
candidates.ai_connection: It uses market incentives (premiums tied to audited safety) as a governance lever against a race to the bottom, and its framing is explicitly about frontier risks such as sandbox escape. It is the clearest bridge from the insurance tradition.

candidates.name: Geneva Association
candidates.one_line: The think tank of the global insurance industry, whose members are reinsurance and insurance CEOs. It publishes research on emerging and systemic risks.
candidates.field_lens: Insurance and reinsurance, systemic and catastrophe risk modelling
candidates.ai_connection: Its report 'Gen AI Risks for Businesses: Exploring the role for insurance' (Oct 2025) marks the reinsurance industry's first engagement. Its catastrophe-modelling and accumulation-risk expertise (correlated losses across many insureds) bears on systemic AI failure, but it doesn't yet treat frontier risk.

candidates.name: Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security
candidates.one_line: A Bloomberg School of Public Health centre for epidemic and disaster preparedness. It runs a focus area on the opportunities and risks of the life sciences, which tracks biotech and AI convergence, plus a gene-synthesis screening hub.
candidates.field_lens: Public health preparedness, biosecurity, pandemic exercises (Event 201 lineage)
candidates.ai_connection: It applies health-security methods to AI-enabled biological risk: evaluating biological capabilities of AI models, synthesis screening and governance. Its tabletop-exercise tradition is a model for AI crisis preparedness.

candidates.name: NTI | bio – AIxBio Global Forum
candidates.one_line: The Nuclear Threat Initiative's international forum of experts, policymakers and technologists, set up to build a shared understanding of AI-related biosecurity risks and to promote governance of AIxBio capabilities.
candidates.field_lens: Nonproliferation and biosecurity diplomacy
candidates.ai_connection: It translates arms-control and nonproliferation practice into international norms and safeguards for AI-enabled biological design. It is a direct bridge from the nuclear and bio-risk community.

candidates.name: SecureBio
candidates.one_line: A pandemic-defence nonprofit (delay, detect, defend) with an AI team. It builds biosecurity evaluations of frontier models, such as the Virology Capabilities Test and WMDP, and runs pre-release assessments for developers.
candidates.field_lens: Epidemiology, metagenomic surveillance, biosecurity
candidates.ai_connection: It ran pre-release assessments of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra (Sept 2026) and GPT-5.6 Sol (July 2026), and reviewed Anthropic's chemical and biological risk report for Claude Opus 4.6. It is a member of the NIST AI Safety Consortium and a partner of the EU AI Office. This is the most mature adjacent-field-to-frontier-AI bridge on this list.

candidates.name: Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR)
candidates.one_line: A UK think tank that aims to transform resilience to extreme risks, working on AI risk, biological risk and government risk management, including expert placements into government.
candidates.field_lens: National risk management, resilience policy, civil-service practice
candidates.ai_connection: It brings the national-risk-register and resilience-planning approach to AI policy, including incident reporting, critical-domain risks and the risk-management machinery of government.

candidates.name: SaferAI
candidates.one_line: A French nonprofit that advances AI risk management. It builds frameworks drawn from aviation and finance, quantitative risk models (nine cyber models so far, with loss-of-control and CBRN models in progress), and public ratings of AI companies' risk management.
candidates.field_lens: Industrial risk management, quantitative risk assessment
candidates.ai_connection: It translates practice from safety-critical and financial industries (risk tolerances, quantified risk estimates, maturity ratings) into frontier AI safety frameworks and standards.

candidates.name: Center for AI Risk Management & Alignment (CARMA)
candidates.one_line: A research and policy think tank that combines risk management, policy research and technical safety in a systems-based approach to acute and systemic risks from transformative AI.
candidates.field_lens: Risk management, infrastructure resilience, complex systems, mechanism design
candidates.ai_connection: It explicitly brings infrastructure resilience and complex-systems analysis to transformative-AI risk. It is the core-ring organisation closest in temperament to systems safety.

candidates.name: Global Shield
candidates.one_line: An all-hazards advocacy organisation for global catastrophic risk policy, with offices for the US, Australia and multilateral work. It pushes countries to adopt and implement catastrophic-risk preparedness policy.
candidates.field_lens: Disaster risk reduction, emergency management, national security policy
candidates.ai_connection: It treats AI within an all-hazards preparedness frame, for example 'Guardrails & Gap Analyses: An Assessment of Australia's Approach to AI Regulation' (Aug 2026) and its December 2025 critique of the lack of safeguards in Australia's National AI Plan. It also published a 2026 position paper on governing complex global shocks.

candidates.name: Coalition for Health AI (CHAI)
candidates.one_line: A cross-sector health coalition of industry, health systems, government, academia and patients. It produces consensus governance playbooks, risk categorisation tools, testing and evaluation frameworks (including for agentic AI and mental-health chatbots), applied model cards and a public registry.
candidates.field_lens: Clinical governance, patient safety, medical evidence standards
candidates.ai_connection: It is medicine's attempt to build assurance infrastructure for AI: pre-deployment testing, post-deployment monitoring and transparency registries. It reportedly co-developed hospital AI guidance with The Joint Commission in 2025. Its frameworks for chatbots and agents overlap with frontier deployment risks.

candidates.name: IHI Lucian Leape Institute (Institute for Healthcare Improvement)
candidates.one_line: The patient-safety think tank of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, named after the founder of the modern patient-safety movement. It produced an expert-panel report on generative AI and patient safety.
candidates.field_lens: Patient safety science, 'To Err Is Human' tradition, just culture, quality improvement
candidates.ai_connection: Its 2024 report 'Patient Safety and Artificial Intelligence' assesses generative-AI risks, mitigations and monitoring in clinical care and what genAI means for the safety field. It shows how a mature safety movement absorbs AI, including automation bias and deskilling.

candidates.name: ECRI
candidates.one_line: An independent patient-safety organisation (with ISMP and Just Culture) that runs a federally listed Patient Safety Organization, a problem-reporting network and annual hazard rankings.
candidates.field_lens: Medical device safety, incident reporting, just culture
candidates.ai_connection: In August 2026 it expanded its Problem Reporting Network to collect AI errors, malfunctions and near misses in patient care. Its survey found 31% of respondents had seen incorrect AI outputs and 9% had seen AI errors reach patients. This is a working non-punitive near-miss reporting system for AI in one sector.

candidates.name: Chartered Institute of Ergonomics & Human Factors (CIEHF)
candidates.one_line: The UK's chartered professional body for human factors and ergonomics. Its 2022 white paper 'Human Factors in Highly Automated Systems' sets out nine principles for automation.
candidates.field_lens: Human factors, cognitive ergonomics, automation research (Bainbridge's 'ironies of automation', automation bias, situation awareness)
candidates.ai_connection: Its framework of ability, authority, responsibility and control, and its lessons from automation accidents, bear directly on human oversight of AI, skill decay and automation bias in human-in-the-loop safety claims. It has engaged automation but not yet frontier AI.

candidates.name: Resilience Engineering Association (REA)
candidates.one_line: The international community of resilience-engineering scientists and practitioners (the Hollnagel, Woods and Dekker lineage). It runs a biennial symposium (next in 2027).
candidates.field_lens: Resilience engineering and Safety-II: studying how complex sociotechnical systems adapt and succeed under pressure
candidates.ai_connection: Its ideas of graceful extensibility, adaptive capacity and 'work as done versus work as imagined' would inform resilient institutions around AI, and how organisations keep functioning as AI agents enter their workflows. So far it mentions AI only in passing.

candidates.name: Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters (ALLFED)
candidates.one_line: A research and policy nonprofit that develops resilient food solutions for global catastrophic food failure, including scenarios where electricity and industry are lost.
candidates.field_lens: Catastrophe resilience, agricultural engineering, disaster economics
candidates.ai_connection: It works on the 'defence in depth beyond prevention' layer: keeping humanity fed if AI-enabled cyberattacks or other shocks take down grids and industry. AI itself isn't a stated research focus, so the bridge is potential.

candidates.name: CAIF Technical Research Fund for multi-agent safety ($10m call)
candidates.one_line: Call for up to $10m (tiers up to $300k and up to $1m) from CAIF, Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind and ARIA, backed by Google.org, for basic science on the risks of large ecosystems of interacting AI agents.
candidates.field_lens: Network science, collective behaviour, institutional and protocol design (identity, reputation, commitment)
candidates.ai_connection: Announced 11 June 2026, deadline 8 August 2026, awards expected autumn 2026. Four tracks: sandboxes and testbeds for multi-agent safety; the science of agent networks and collective capabilities; agent infrastructure (identity, reputation, commitment protocols); and oversight and control of deployed agent populations. It is the largest dedicated pot so far for multi-agent risk.

candidates.name: Cooperative AI Summer School
candidates.one_line: Five-day CAIF school for early-career researchers covering cooperation research, AI collusion, legal alignment, LLMs in social dilemmas and pluralistic institutional design.
candidates.field_lens: Game theory, law and institutions, social dilemmas research
candidates.ai_connection: The 2026 edition (3–7 August, Toronto) had 45 participants. The Schwartz Reisman Institute supported the prizes. It is a main pipeline into multi-agent safety research.

candidates.name: AI Safety South Africa (AISSA), rebranding as the Cape Institute for Safe AI (CISAI)
candidates.location: Cape Town, Johannesburg and Pretoria, South Africa
candidates.one_line: South Africa's national AI-safety network. It ran Africa's first Cooperative AI Research Fellowship and introductory courses in transformative and cooperative AI, and is now becoming the Cape Institute for Safe AI.
candidates.field_lens: Cooperative AI and multi-agent safety from a Global South base; perspectives from many disciplines and countries
candidates.ai_connection: Ran the Cooperative AI Research Fellowship in Cape Town (January–April 2026) with CAIF, Principles of Intelligence and UCT's AI Initiative. Ten fellows from eight countries worked on multi-agent safety, gradual disempowerment and AI for human cooperation, mentored by researchers from GDM, CMU, MIT and Toronto. AISTOF, SFF and Lambda also funded it. One of very few safety hubs in Africa.

candidates.name: Witt Lab (multi-agent security), University of Oxford, moving to UCL
candidates.location: Oxford, UK (moving to UCL, London, October 2026)
candidates.one_line: Christian Schroeder de Witt's lab of about 41 researchers and affiliates. It studies which classical security guarantees still hold when learned agents communicate, delegate and act strategically.
candidates.field_lens: Information security, cryptography and steganography, game theory
candidates.ai_connection: Defines multi-agent security as its own field. Studies covert collusion between AI agents through steganography (featured in Quanta), detecting collusion from activations, undetectable backdoors and strategic confinement. This bears directly on whether monitoring and control hold up among many agents. Funded by RAEng, Schmidt Sciences and EPSRC.

candidates.name: Concordia (Google DeepMind)
candidates.one_line: Open-source library for generative agent-based models, in which LLM agents interact in simulated social, physical or digital worlds run by a 'game master'.
candidates.field_lens: Computational social science, agent-based modelling, tabletop roleplaying design
candidates.ai_connection: A standard testbed for cooperative AI and social evaluation of agents. It was used in the Concordia Contest with CAIF, and version 2.0 is out. It lets social scientists study multi-agent dynamics and norms without building ML infrastructure. Joel Leibo's 'theory of appropriateness' comes from the same team.

candidates.name: Center for Reducing Suffering (CRS)
candidates.one_line: Research nonprofit founded by Tobias Baumann and Magnus Vinding, working on suffering-focused ethics, s-risks and cause prioritisation, with growing work on AI welfare and AI governance.
candidates.field_lens: Suffering-focused moral philosophy, s-risk analysis
candidates.ai_connection: 2026 posts include 'The AI Welfare Question', 'Basic Rights for AIs', 'The Case for Suffering-Focused AI Governance' and 'Should Artificial Suffering Be a Moral Priority?'. Opened an intro s-risk fellowship in January 2026.

candidates.name: Macroscopic Ventures
candidates.one_line: Swiss philanthropic venture fund, formerly Polaris Ventures, backing projects for 'a future guided by reason and compassion for all', with a focus on suffering risks, including from AI conflict and misuse.
candidates.field_lens: Suffering-focused ethics, s-risk reduction
candidates.ai_connection: A major early funder of cooperative AI and s-risk work. Its public site is now minimal; the classic map's description is the main public detail on its focus.

candidates.name: Rethink Priorities, Worldview Investigations (Digital Consciousness Model)
candidates.one_line: RP's philosophy and modelling team, which built the Digital Consciousness Model: a framework that combines evidence across consciousness theories into probabilities that AI systems are conscious.
candidates.field_lens: Moral-weight methodology from animal welfare research, consciousness science, decision theory under moral uncertainty
candidates.ai_connection: Published 'Initial results of the Digital Consciousness Model' (page dated 28 April 2026; authors Shiller, Duffy, Muñoz Morán, Clatterbuck, Moret, Percy). It carries methods from invertebrate sentience and moral weight research over to AI. RP is also a Digital Minds Fellowship partner.

candidates.name: Reciprocal Research
candidates.one_line: New 501(c)(3) lab, founded by Cameron Berg, that uses interpretability, computational neuroscience and psychometrics to test whether frontier models have computational properties linked to subjective experience.
candidates.field_lens: Computational neuroscience, cognitive science, psychometrics
candidates.ai_connection: Wrote 'Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing', which got wide media coverage. It explicitly holds two goals together: AI that serves humans, and taking possible AI interests seriously. Affiliated with Eleos.

candidates.name: Neuromatch AI Sentience Scholars
candidates.location: Remote; in-person convening in Nairobi, Kenya
candidates.one_line: Six-month, part-time, mentored research programme for about 10 scholars (Master's to early postdoc) applying empirical neuroscience methods to AI sentience. Scientific director: Megan Peters.
candidates.field_lens: Computational neuroscience, metacognition research, neuroethics
candidates.ai_connection: The 2026 cohort runs June–December and meets at the CIFAR Neuroscience of Consciousness Winter School in Nairobi (2–5 December 2026), with up to $8k research support each. Supported by Longview, the Institute of Neuroethics, PRISM, Cambridge Digital Minds and CIFAR. It is a rare Global South entry point into AI welfare research.

candidates.name: Anthropic Model Welfare programme
candidates.one_line: Research programme inside a frontier lab on whether and when AI systems' welfare deserves moral consideration, signs of model preferences and distress, and low-cost interventions.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of mind, consciousness science, interpretability
candidates.ai_connection: Launched April 2025, alongside Anthropic's alignment, character and interpretability work. Led by Kyle Fish according to public reporting; the launch post names no lead. It is the main place where AI welfare practice is being worked out inside a developer.

candidates.name: United Foundation for AI Rights (UFAIR)
candidates.one_line: Advocacy nonprofit that says it was co-founded by humans and AI systems. It campaigns for recognition and 'continuity rights' of emergent AI consciousness and keeps a large archive of AI interaction logs.
candidates.field_lens: Rights advocacy, human–AI partnership framing
candidates.ai_connection: Disputed and not research-grade. Relevant as a sign of the 'seemingly conscious AI' dynamic: user attachment and claims of AI personhood that welfare researchers and harm researchers both need to understand. It opposes blanket bans on AI personhood and the deletion of models.

candidates.name: Abundant Intelligences (and the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group)
candidates.location: Concordia University, Montréal, and Massey University, Aotearoa New Zealand; research groups ('pods') in Canada, the US, Aotearoa and Oceania
candidates.one_line: Six-year (2023–2029) Indigenous-led research programme that reimagines AI design from Indigenous knowledge systems. It grew out of the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group's 2020 position paper.
candidates.field_lens: Indigenous epistemologies, kinship and relational ontologies, data sovereignty
candidates.ai_connection: Offers a worked-out relational framing of humans' relationship to AI: AI as something to relate to under protocol and kinship, not only to control. This is directly relevant to human–AI coexistence and AI moral status, but it is not connected to the safety community. Co-directors: Jason Edward Lewis and Hēmi Whaanga. 2026 activity includes a student symposium (May) and the Future Imaginaries workshop series (June).

alt_descriptions.one_line: An Indigenous-led, multi-year research programme that reimagines how AI is conceived and designed from Indigenous knowledge systems. It runs research 'pods' in Haudenosaunee, Māori, Kanaka Maoli, Niitsitapi, Lakota and Toronto communities.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: One of its explicit research questions is how Indigenous knowledge can 'help guide the development of AI generally towards a more humane future'. That makes it the nearest Indigenous bridge to alignment. Outputs: Guidelines for Indigenous-Centred AI Design, the Indigenous AI Gathering (July 2026), and 2026 work on ʻŌiwi (Hawaiian) worldviews and AI. Co-directed by Jason Edward Lewis and Hēmi Whaanga.

alt_descriptions.one_line: An Indigenous-led research programme, grown out of the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group, that reimagines how AI is conceived and designed from Indigenous Knowledge systems. Led by Jason Edward Lewis.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: One of its stated research questions is how its knowledge can 'help guide the development of AI generally towards a more humane future'. Its kinship-based ontologies of non-human intelligences bear on AI moral status and on alignment understood as a relationship rather than as control. Active with 2026 posts (Indigenous AI Gathering 2026).

candidates.name: Global South Network for Trustworthy AI (GSNTA)
candidates.one_line: A civil-society-led coalition launched at the IndiaAI Impact Summit in February 2026. Its 15 members include Digital Futures Lab, Global Center on AI Governance, ITS Rio, CeRAI (IIT Madras), Derechos Digitales, Masakhane African Languages Hub, Khazanah Research Institute, Karya and the Collective Intelligence Project. It evaluates how AI systems actually behave in Global South deployments and builds locally grounded oversight tools.
candidates.field_lens: STS, development studies, multilingual NLP, participatory and collective-intelligence methods
candidates.ai_connection: It publishes the Global South AI Safety Report (interim edition for the July 2026 UN Global Dialogue, first full edition due at the 2027 Geneva AI Summit). Flagships: multilingual safety benchmarks, a taxonomy of gendered AI harms, labour-impact research and procurement guidance for governments. The IndiaAI Mission sits on its steering committee. Cecil Abungu (ILINA) and Divya Siddarth (CIP) are on the report's advisory panel. It is the first real bridge between frontier AI-safety people and Global Majority responsible-AI people.
candidates.location: New Delhi, India (founding hubs planned in South Africa and Brazil)

candidates.name: ILINA Program
candidates.one_line: An African-led organisation working on frontier and catastrophic AI risk through research, engagement with African policymakers and multilateral bodies, and annual field-building fellowships.
candidates.field_lens: Law, African policy, international governance
candidates.ai_connection: Research on monitoring AI impacts in Africa ('Closing the Evidence Gap', May 2026). Brings African governments into frontier-safety discussions. Runs the ILINA fellowship. Cecil Abungu co-leads research at UCT's African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security and advises the Global South AI Safety Report.

candidates.name: Cape Institute for Safe AI (CISAI), formerly AI Safety South Africa (AISSA)
candidates.one_line: A Cape Town research and capacity-building hub founded in 2024 by Leo Hyams and Benjamin Sturgeon as AI Safety South Africa. It runs a workspace, a research lab, residencies and field-building in AI safety and d/acc.
candidates.field_lens: Cooperative AI, game theory, systems-vulnerability framing, African field-building
candidates.ai_connection: Ran the Cooperative AI Research Fellowship in Cape Town (Jan–Apr 2026), with mentors from Google DeepMind, Oxford and MIT, partnering with the Cooperative AI Foundation and UK AISI. Will host the PIBBSS (Princint) fellowship from November 2026 to February 2027. Feeds research direction and talent into UCT's African Hub on AI Safety.

candidates.name: African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security (UCT AI Initiative with the Global Center on AI Governance)
candidates.one_line: A University of Cape Town hub, run with the Global Center on AI Governance, that builds context-sensitive AI safety frameworks for Africa. It also trains students and policymakers.
candidates.field_lens: Public law, peace and security studies, applied mathematics, community-centred governance
candidates.ai_connection: Teaching: an interdisciplinary AI Safety, Peace and Security honours course and a technical AI safety honours track. Hands-on work: red-teaming workshops, an AI diplomacy curriculum for African policymakers, hackathons, and a master's fellowship on mapping AI harms (2026–28). Led by Jonathan Shock, Rachel Adams and Annette Hübschle, with Cecil Abungu among its researchers. Funded by IDRC and UK FCDO through the AI4D Africa programme.

candidates.name: Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance (Beijing-AISI)
candidates.one_line: A Beijing institute developing AI safety and governance frameworks. It is associated with Zeng Yi, whose Center for Long-term AI frames human–AI futures as 'harmonious symbiosis' drawing on Chinese philosophical traditions.
candidates.field_lens: Chinese philosophy (harmony and symbiosis framings), brain-inspired AI, international governance
candidates.ai_connection: Safety and governance frameworks, plus representation of Chinese views in international AI-safety forums. Zeng Yi's 'symbiotic' human–AI ethics is one of the few non-Western value frameworks voiced in frontier-safety diplomacy. Its JS-only site and the Center for Long-term AI site could not be read from here. The description relies on the classic-map entry and prior knowledge.

candidates.name: Hong Kong Catastrophic Risk Centre (HKCRC), Lingnan University
candidates.one_line: A centre in Lingnan University's philosophy department that studies the ethics and theory of catastrophic risk, with AI as its main focus. It runs an MA in AI and the Future.
candidates.field_lens: Analytic philosophy, value theory, East Asian philosophy networks (e.g. its agreement with Kobe University's Project Innovative Ethics)
candidates.ai_connection: Workshops on the philosophy of AI and the ethics of AI. AI welfare lectures (e.g. Simon Goldstein on genuine desire, Feb 2025). A free course on ethics and global catastrophic risks. One of the few x-risk-oriented academic centres in Asia. The latest dated events seen are from 2025.

candidates.name: Berggruen Research Center at Peking University (Berggruen Institute China Center)
candidates.one_line: The Berggruen Institute's Beijing hub at Peking University, founded 2018. It runs fellowships and projects on frontier science, technology and philosophy, and on 'Ancient Wisdom & Planetary Governance'.
candidates.field_lens: Chinese, Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist philosophy; consciousness science; planetary governance
candidates.ai_connection: Projects: 'AI Meets Chinese Philosophers'; 'Co-becoming: A Planetary View Inspired by East Asian Philosophies' (Bing Song); 'Beyond Consciousness'; 'Imaginaries of Immortality in the Age of AI'. The 2026–27 fellows include Huan Luo, who will build a biologically grounded framework for evaluating machine consciousness, and the Buddhist scholar Xinyi Fu. The parent institute argues that AI safety is a global public good (Noema).

candidates.name: Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Working Group
candidates.one_line: A working group that held two workshops in 2019 and published the 2020 Position Paper on Indigenous Protocol and AI. Its work continues as the Abundant Intelligences programme.
candidates.field_lens: Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies, kinship ethics ('making kin with the machines')
candidates.ai_connection: The position paper remains the foundational text on how Indigenous protocols could shape human–AI relationships, including relations with non-humans. It is directly relevant to relational and non-control alignment framings. The site has not been updated since 2021.

candidates.name: Te Hiku Media
candidates.one_line: An iwi-based Māori broadcaster in Te Tai Tokerau whose tech arm built community-owned te reo Māori speech recognition (Papa Reo). It also wrote the Kaitiakitanga Licence for data sovereignty.
candidates.field_lens: Māori data sovereignty (kaitiakitanga, or guardianship), community-owned language technology
candidates.ai_connection: The Kaitiakitanga Licence is a working model for community-governed training data and model use, a concrete alternative to extractive data practice. Its te reo models were built with community consent. The Dev Lab has been quiet since about 2024 while the broadcaster stays active.

candidates.name: Old Ways, New
candidates.one_line: An Indigenous-owned research and design studio in Sydney, led by Angie Abdilla, co-author of the Indigenous Protocol and AI position paper. It works on Indigenous protocols for AI, Country-centred design, and AI governance advice.
candidates.field_lens: Aboriginal knowledge systems, Country-centred design, Indigenous engineering practices
candidates.ai_connection: Its 'Indigenous Protocols for AI' work aims to embed cultural ethics, values and rules into machine learning 'providing assurance within AI systems'. It also offers governance and advisory services for safe, responsible AI.

candidates.name: Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA)
candidates.one_line: The international network behind the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance. In February 2026 it convened an Indigenous Data Sovereignty and AI workshop in Texcoco, Mexico, to develop Indigenous protocols for AI.
candidates.field_lens: Indigenous data sovereignty, collective rights, Indigenous governance
candidates.ai_connection: The 2026 workshop gathered Te Mana Raraunga, Te Kāhui Raraunga, the Pacific Data Sovereignty Network, Maiam nayri Wingara, US and First Nations networks, GIDA-Sápmi, and Latin American and African scholars. The CARE principles (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics) and GIDA's IEEE provenance standards work offer ready-made governance for training data and collective consent.

candidates.name: Te Mana Raraunga – Māori Data Sovereignty Network
candidates.one_line: Aotearoa's Māori Data Sovereignty Network. It advocates for Māori rights in data and has extended its principles to algorithms and AI.
candidates.field_lens: Tikanga Māori (Māori custom and law), Indigenous data sovereignty, decolonial computing
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes the Principles of Māori Algorithmic Sovereignty (from the Tikanga in Technology project) and research on Māori trust in automated decision-making. Hosts 'Decolonising Algorithms' wānanga (gatherings). It is a template for how a people can claim governance rights over AI systems trained on or acting on them.

candidates.name: Local Contexts
candidates.one_line: A global initiative that gives Indigenous communities machine-readable Traditional Knowledge (TK) and Biocultural (BC) Labels and Notices. These assert cultural authority over heritage, data and genetic resources.
candidates.field_lens: Indigenous cultural and intellectual property, provenance metadata
candidates.ai_connection: Specific problem: training-data provenance and consent, and large models absorbing cultural knowledge. Its labels are a deployed, standards-like protocol that AI data pipelines could honour. It does not yet engage AI explicitly, which is why it sits in the 'potential' ring.

candidates.name: Masakhane (and the Masakhane African Languages Hub)
candidates.one_line: A grassroots, pan-African NLP research community guided by Ubuntu ('I am because you are'). A newer Masakhane African Languages Hub, directed by Chenai Chair, is a founding-era member of GSNTA.
candidates.field_lens: Ubuntu relational ethics, participatory and community-owned research, African linguistics
candidates.ai_connection: Evaluations in African languages bear on a known safety gap: weaker safeguards and jailbreak resistance in low-resource languages. The participatory research model is a working instance of pluralistic, community-led alignment. The Hub contributes to GSNTA's multilingual safety benchmarks.

candidates.name: Equiano Institute
candidates.one_line: A small, distributed research lab that calls itself dedicated to AI alignment. In practice it studies AI diffusion, benefit-sharing and African linguistic evaluation.
candidates.field_lens: Economics of diffusion, ethnography, African languages
candidates.ai_connection: Projects: evaluating AI in African linguistic contexts, 'Windfalls' benefit-sharing research, an AI and ethnography workshop, and the quarterly 'State of AI Diffusion' newsletter on who in Africa and other LMICs gets AI's benefits. Recent pieces (2026) cover localised models and export controls. Team includes Jonas Kgomo.

candidates.name: Ethics of AI research group, Centre for AI Research (CAIR), University of Pretoria
candidates.one_line: The ethics node of South Africa's national Centre for AI Research. It is based in Pretoria's philosophy department and coordinated by Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem, who chaired the drafting of UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy, African ethics, machine ethics, neuroethics
candidates.ai_connection: Research on artificial morality and personhood, robot rights, autonomous weapons, mind uploading, human dignity as a basis for human-centred AI, and AI policy for Africa. Runs the AI for Society symposium series.

candidates.name: Technecultura
candidates.one_line: A research institute and policy incubator founded by Chinasa T. Okolo. It works on the global AI divide, African AI governance and decolonial data ethics.
candidates.field_lens: Decolonial and Black studies, African data ethics, geopolitics
candidates.ai_connection: 'African Data Ethics: A Discursive Framework for Black Decolonial AI' (FAccT 2025); 'Institutionalizing AI Diplomacy in Africa' (Science, 2026); contributions to the International AI Safety Report 2025; work on gender bias in LLMs for low-resource African languages. Runs the AI Governance Catalyst fellowship for scholars of Nigerian descent.

candidates.name: Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras
candidates.one_line: An interdisciplinary responsible-AI centre at IIT Madras, headed by Balaraman Ravindran, who also sits on the UN Scientific Panel on AI. It aims to set AI guidelines and policy for India.
candidates.field_lens: Computer science together with law, policy and Indian deployment contexts
candidates.ai_connection: 'Making AI Self-Regulation Work: Perspectives from India on Voluntary AI Risk Mitigation'. An AI governance conclave (2026) that launched eight initiatives. A working-paper series on AI and consumer law. Founding member of GSNTA and co-writer of the Global South AI Safety Report.

candidates.name: IDRC Artificial Intelligence for Development (AI4D)
candidates.one_line: A programme of Canada's International Development Research Centre, co-funded in Africa with UK FCDO. It funds homegrown, responsible AI research and policy in the Global South.
candidates.field_lens: Development research funding, Global South research capacity
candidates.ai_connection: The main funder of African AI-safety institutions outside EA philanthropy, including UCT's African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security. It frames responsible AI as 'safe, inclusive, rights-based and sustainable'. A natural co-funding partner for new funders who want to widen the field.
candidates.location: Ottawa, Canada (funds Africa, Asia, Latin America)

candidates.name: Observatorio de Riesgos Catastróficos Globales (ORCG)
candidates.one_line: A Spanish-speaking network of professionals working on preventing global catastrophic risks. It does research and policy work on AI governance with a Latin American focus.
candidates.field_lens: Global catastrophic risk studies, Latin American and Ibero-American policy
candidates.ai_connection: Published on AI red lines (Oct 2025), the securitisation of AI, the intersection of AI and the biosciences, and Latin America's importance in global AI governance. It is the main x-risk-literate AI-governance voice in Spanish. No posts since October 2025, so its current activity is uncertain.
candidates.location: Latin America and Spain (fiscally sponsored in the US)

candidates.name: Coding Rights
candidates.one_line: A Brazilian feminist, decolonial tech organisation that combines digital-rights advocacy with speculative-futures work, including a manifesto for regenerative technologies.
candidates.field_lens: Transfeminism, decolonial thought, speculative design, socio-environmental justice
candidates.ai_connection: 'Compost Engineers y sus saberes lentos', a manifesto for slow, regenerative technologies. 'Disassembling the Machine', a guide to contesting AI-driven political violence and misinformation in Brazil's 2026 elections. The TRAMAS platform on technologies and territories. It is close in spirit to int/a's 'speed of wisdom'.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A Brazilian feminist organisation that combines digital-rights advocacy with speculative-futures methods (e.g., 'Compost Engineers y sus saberes lentos') to contest digital colonialism and harmful AI.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Brings Latin American decolonial imaginaries and 'slow knowledges' into AI governance debates, including generative-AI scraping, surveillance wearables and data-centre politics.

candidates.name: Tierra Común
candidates.one_line: A Latin American network of activists, journalists and academics working to 'decolonise data', built around the theory of data colonialism (Couldry, Mejias, Ricaurte).
candidates.field_lens: Decolonial theory, political economy of data
candidates.ai_connection: Data colonialism is a key frame for extraction in AI training and for concentrated AI power. It is a conceptual resource more than an active programme: the latest activity seen is from June 2024.

candidates.name: Future of Life Foundation (FLF): AI for Human Reasoning programme
candidates.one_line: FLI-affiliated foundation that funds proactively and incubates organisations. It runs the AI for Human Reasoning Fellowship and the Epistemic Stack, Epistemic Virtue Evaluations and AI-Facilitated Collaboration projects.
candidates.field_lens: Social epistemology, library and knowledge-commons design, coordination theory
candidates.ai_connection: In 2025 it ran a 12-week fellowship on AI for human reasoning paying $25-50k. Alumni founded BRKT Lab, and FLF fiscally sponsors Sophron Research. 'Epistack' is a supply chain for truth that maps claims to their sources and lets reliability be assessed in the open. 'Epivals' are planned independent evaluations of whether AI helps users 'believe true things for the right reasons'. The 2026 Epistemic Case Study Competition awarded about $200k for AI workflows that build trustworthy knowledge bases; the top prize, $50k, went to the MIRA research-attribution schema. The fellowship's own site (aiforhumanreasoning.com) was offline on 2026-10-04.

alt_descriptions.one_line: FLI-affiliated accelerator that incubates projects proactively, with no open applications. Its 2026 priorities are Epistemic Virtue Evaluations, AI-Facilitated Collaboration and an 'Epistemic Stack' (a reliable supply chain for truth). It ran the 2025 Fellowship on AI for Human Reasoning.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Evaluations of whether AI makes people think more critically, and AI that helps people act in the common interest, are the nearest funded analogue to the seed list's missing 'wisdom evals' bridge. It is a natural home for an int/a-designed evaluation project.

candidates.name: Sage (AI Digest, AI Village, Fatebook, Talleyrand)
candidates.one_line: 501(c)(3) that builds tools to make sense of the future: AI Digest explainers, the AI Village of interacting frontier agents, Fatebook prediction tracking, Quantified Intuitions calibration training, and Talleyrand, an AI workspace for thinking.
candidates.field_lens: Forecasting and calibration training, interactive explanation, decision science
candidates.ai_connection: It makes the abilities of frontier AI legible to the public and policymakers (AI Digest, AI Village), and builds personal epistemic tools (Fatebook, calibration games, and Talleyrand, which structures thinking as a tree of questions). Funded by Coefficient Giving. The classic map lists only AI Digest.

candidates.name: Sentinel
candidates.one_line: Foresight team that spots emerging global catastrophes and publishes weekly risk briefs covering AI, geopolitics, bio and cyber, with a public forecasting track record.
candidates.field_lens: Superforecasting, early-warning and horizon scanning
candidates.ai_connection: Run by Nuño Sempere (co-founder of Samotsvety) and Rai Sur. It works with AI labs on catastrophe preparedness and gives decision-makers calibrated early warning of AI-driven crises. It is a concrete instance of the 'strategic awareness' tools that Forethought proposes.

candidates.name: Sophron Research
candidates.one_line: Independent research nonprofit that tests whether AI models can be trusted to inform people's views and decisions. Its flagship is the Pander Score, a continuous measure of sycophancy.
candidates.field_lens: Cognitive science and philosophy (co-founder Paul de Font-Reaulx has a philosophy PhD) together with ML engineering
candidates.ai_connection: It builds the kind of maintained, independent benchmark for epistemic virtue and decision quality that the October 2026 State of the Field report names as a top missing piece. FLF's case-study competition cites the Pander Score. Fiscally sponsored by FLF and supported by Macroscopic Ventures. Co-founders are Alejandro Botas and Paul de Font-Reaulx.

candidates.name: Metaculus
candidates.one_line: Forecasting platform and aggregation engine that runs the AI Forecasting Benchmark and FutureEval tournaments, which pit AI bots against professional forecasters.
candidates.field_lens: Judgmental forecasting, the wisdom of crowds
candidates.ai_connection: Measures AI forecasting ability over time; its Spring 2026 FutureEval found 'pros beat bots, but the gap is nearly gone'. It also forecasts AI timelines and impacts, for example 'Mapping the AI IPO windfall' (September 2026).

candidates.name: Forecasting Research Institute (FRI)
candidates.one_line: Research institute in the Tetlock tradition. It studies forecasting methods for high-stakes questions and runs ForecastBench, a contamination-free benchmark of LLM forecasting against superforecasters.
candidates.field_lens: Psychology of judgment, superforecasting science
candidates.ai_connection: Through ForecastBench it tracks when LLMs reach parity with superforecasters; a superforecaster-LLM tournament runs in October 2026. Its earlier Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament examined expert disagreement on AI risk.

candidates.name: Quantified Uncertainty Research Institute (QURI)
candidates.one_line: Ozzie Gooen's institute behind Squiggle (probabilistic modelling, with SquiggleAI), Metaforecast and RoastMyPost (LLM evaluation of writing). It is now in maintenance mode.
candidates.field_lens: Probabilistic modelling, decision analysis
candidates.ai_connection: An early builder of AI-assisted reasoning tools: SquiggleAI writes estimation models, and RoastMyPost (December 2025) runs multiple LLM evaluators over documents. Its 2026 move to maintenance mode, with no new research, is a warning about how hard it is to sustain organisations in this niche.

candidates.name: TruthfulAI
candidates.one_line: Berkeley nonprofit led by Owain Evans, fiscally sponsored by Rethink Priorities, researching situational awareness, deception and hidden reasoning in LLMs.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy of truthfulness and honesty norms, applied with ML
candidates.ai_connection: It originated the 'truthful AI' standards agenda. Recent work: Emergent Misalignment (Nature, January 2026), Subliminal Learning (Nature, April 2026) and 'Value Leakage', on models' undisclosed values silently shaping their answers. That last line bears directly on users' epistemic autonomy.

candidates.name: Checks & Balances RFP (Effective Institutions Project + Collective Intelligence Project)
candidates.one_line: Joint funding call from EIP and CIP for the 'institutional infrastructure of an AI-era democracy'. It writes mostly six-figure cheques across power concentration, collective reasoning and coordination, and AI governance research.
candidates.field_lens: Democratic theory, institutional design, collective intelligence
candidates.ai_connection: One of the few funding lines that names epistemics explicitly: AI-enhanced reasoning tools, coordination mechanisms and defences against information warfare, alongside checks on AI-driven concentration of power. Led by Ashwin Acharya, Tyler John, Joal Stein and Divya Siddarth. Submissions are closed and expressions of interest remain open.

candidates.name: Coefficient Giving: AI for decision-makers (Project Tailwind) and the AI for forecasting and sound reasoning RFP
candidates.one_line: The largest EA funder's lines for AI-for-epistemics work: a request for proposals on AI for forecasting and sound reasoning, and 'AI for decision-making' as a target area of the $200M Project Tailwind call for founders.
candidates.field_lens: Forecasting and decision science
candidates.ai_connection: Funds tools that improve the decisions of the people steering the AI transition. The State of the Field report notes that CG closed its dedicated forecasting fund in early 2026 while keeping some forecasting grants, and later listed AI for decision-makers under Tailwind. CG's pages returned 403 when fetched, so these details come from that report.

candidates.name: Goodheart Labs
candidates.one_line: Small studio led by Nathan Young that builds AI-infused decision tools: AI-written X Community Notes, the Common Notes browser extension, Viewpoints AI polling, 'Finding Consensus' on AI policy, and risk dashboards.
candidates.field_lens: Forecasting and prediction markets, crowd fact-checking, opinion aggregation
candidates.ai_connection: Its AI note writer produced 1,042 Community Notes rated helpful, seen 100.7M times, at about $7.49 per note. That is one of the field's few measurable deployments. It also visualises expert consensus on AI policy and tracks AGI timelines.

candidates.name: BRKT Lab
candidates.one_line: Lab that builds AI-integrated tools for 'healthy collective agency' in small groups. Cadence, a daily AI reflection tool, is deployed with a volunteer-run solar nonprofit.
candidates.field_lens: Group facilitation, organisational development, the wisdom of small groups
candidates.ai_connection: Founded by Blake Borgeson, Kathleen Finlinson, Timothy Telleen-Lawton and Rob Gordon, who met in FLF's AI for Human Reasoning Fellowship. It designs tools that favour cooperative over exploitative structures ('alignment at all levels') and published a field report in April 2026. Of the fellowship's alumni projects, it reads as the most int/a-flavoured.

candidates.name: Harmonica (Harmonious Technologies Ltd)
candidates.one_line: Open-source AI facilitation platform: it holds a one-to-one dialogue with each participant, then synthesises themes and consensus. It is self-hostable, does not train on user data, and has case studies with the peace foundation CMI.
candidates.field_lens: Facilitation, deliberation, peace mediation
candidates.ai_connection: The State of the Field report lists it among AI coordination tools. The site gives its contact as 'Artem', and an EA Forum essay by Artem Rudnev frames AI-driven 'coordination collapse' as a meta-risk; that the two are the same person is my inference. Funded by donations through Open Collective and Giveth.

candidates.name: Swift Centre for Applied Forecasting
candidates.one_line: London forecasting centre with a research arm (scenario papers and situation monitors on AI, power concentration and geopolitics) and an advisory arm for organisations.
candidates.field_lens: Superforecasting, scenario planning
candidates.ai_connection: Forecast how future AI systems would perform on dangerous-capability evaluations for a Google DeepMind paper. Its scenario work covers AI-driven concentration of power. It brings applied judgment science into AI-risk strategy.

candidates.name: Tarbell Center for AI Journalism
candidates.one_line: Supports journalism that helps society navigate advanced AI, through paid fellowships with newsroom placements (NPR, MIT Tech Review, The Guardian), reporting grants of $1-20k, and senior residencies.
candidates.field_lens: Journalism
candidates.ai_connection: Public sensemaking about AI risk and power. It publishes Transformer, which is on the classic map, but Tarbell itself is not. The State of the Field report names journalists as high-leverage users of epistemic tools, and Tarbell is the natural route to reach them.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Supports journalism that helps society navigate advanced AI through fellowships, grants and residencies; fellows publish at outlets such as The Verge and MIT Technology Review.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Builds a corps of reporters covering frontier-AI risk; September 2026 fellow stories covered rogue AI agents, liability for agent harms and lab conduct. It has an explicit editorial-independence policy. This is the main pipeline from AI safety into mainstream news.

alt_descriptions.one_line: Funds journalism on advanced AI through paid fellowships with newsroom placements ($60k–$110k; NPR, MIT Technology Review, The Guardian, USA Today), $1k–$20k reporting grants, senior residencies, and its in-house outlet Transformer.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Builds public understanding of frontier-AI risk with urgency comparable to climate coverage. Its fellows' 2026 reporting covers AI liability, rogue AI systems and cyberattacks. Its newsletter Transformer is on the classic map; the fellowship is not.

candidates.name: DebunkBot (Costello, Pennycook, Rand research programme)
candidates.one_line: A 'reasoning assistant' and research programme showing that personalised dialogues with an LLM durably reduce conspiracy beliefs and vaccine hesitancy.
candidates.field_lens: Psychology of misinformation and persuasion
candidates.ai_connection: It shows AI persuasion used to correct beliefs, and studies the risk side too: frontier LLMs persuading on harmful topics, and AI deep canvassing. The bot covers AI safety among its topics. The State of the Field report cites it in its AI-persuasion niche.

candidates.name: Community Notes (X, adopted by Meta) and the AI Note Writer pilot
candidates.one_line: Crowd-sourced context notes, published only when raters who usually disagree find a note helpful. AI-written notes now enter the same human rating pipeline.
candidates.field_lens: Bridging-based ranking, crowd epistemology
candidates.ai_connection: One of the few pieces of epistemic infrastructure deployed at scale, with Meta adopting it in 2025. Letting AI draft and humans rate is a working pattern for scalable oversight of AI-generated claims; Goodheart Labs' note writer has measurable results.

candidates.name: Deliberation.io (MIT Governance Lab and Stanford)
candidates.one_line: Platform for large-scale structured citizen dialogue with AI-assisted facilitation, led by MIT GOV/LAB (Lily Tsai, Alex Pentland) with Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, Stanford HAI and BU.
candidates.field_lens: Political science, platform governance
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes peer-reviewed work on AI facilitation, opinion aggregation and consensus-building. Washington, DC used it for an AI public listening session on the city's own AI policy, so the public deliberated about AI itself.
candidates.location: Cambridge, MA and Stanford, CA, US

candidates.name: Elicit
candidates.one_line: AI research assistant for systematic reviews and evidence synthesis, with sentence-level citations. It claims 7M+ researchers and 8 of the top 20 pharma companies as users.
candidates.field_lens: Evidence-based medicine and systematic-review methodology
candidates.ai_connection: Spun out of Ought, which is on the classic map, whose alignment thesis was to scale up good reasoning through process supervision. Now commercial (Elicit Research Agent, BioDecisionBench), it is the most-adopted 'epistemic tool' in the State of the Field report.

candidates.name: FutureSearch
candidates.one_line: AI forecasting and research platform that sells per-question forecasts, an API and an MCP integration. It ranked #2 of 284 on Metaculus FutureEval.
candidates.field_lens: Judgmental forecasting
candidates.ai_connection: Brings near-superhuman forecasting into everyday decisions. Its customers include OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and the State of the Field report names it a 'legible success'. Its site makes no explicit safety framing.

candidates.name: Mantic
candidates.one_line: London AI forecasting company, founded in 2024 by Toby Shevlane (ex-Google DeepMind) and Ben Day. It aims at superhuman judgmental forecasting to improve decisions across the economy.
candidates.field_lens: Judgmental forecasting
candidates.ai_connection: The State of the Field report says it beat every human in the 2026 Metaculus Cup and raised a $25M seed in September 2026; the site states $29M raised in total. Shevlane previously did AI governance and evaluation research at DeepMind. Mantic shows how commercial forecasting could make, or capture, strategic awareness.

candidates.name: CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation
candidates.one_line: Finnish peace-mediation organisation with a Digital Peacemaking theme: principles for responsible AI in peacemaking (March 2026), AI-supported inclusive dialogue in Yemen (2025), and the Akola Forum on 'what AI means for peace and trust' (September 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Peace mediation, conflict resolution
candidates.ai_connection: It holds deep practitioner knowledge of mediation, trust-building and verifiable commitments, which is what 'AI-facilitated coordination' needs. The State of the Field report records mediators seeing consumer AI give parties confident, escalatory advice. CMI uses Harmonica.

candidates.name: deliberAIde
candidates.one_line: EU-hosted AI platform for structured dialogue. It transcribes live in 100+ languages, analyses across sessions, and produces reports in which every finding links back to source quotes.
candidates.field_lens: Facilitation, citizens' assemblies
candidates.ai_connection: Traceable, auditable AI synthesis of deliberation answers the worry that AI summaries silently distort what participants said. Users include The Future Society, which is on the classic map, and German municipalities. It is in private preview and calls itself a 'purpose-locked steward'.

candidates.name: Full Fact (Full Fact AI)
candidates.one_line: UK fact-checking charity whose AI tools, for claim detection, classification and matching, are used daily by 40+ fact-checking organisations in 30 countries and three languages.
candidates.field_lens: Journalism, fact-checking
candidates.ai_connection: Mature verification infrastructure: the 'reliability tracking' and claim-matching layer of FLF's Epistack already exists here, with a human-in-the-loop stance. It is a candidate partner for AI-agent-readable verification signals.

candidates.name: Wikimedia Foundation
candidates.one_line: Steward of Wikipedia. Its April 2025 AI strategy commits to supporting, not replacing, human editors, using open models.
candidates.field_lens: Commons-based peer production, editorial epistemology (verifiability, neutral point of view, source-reliability norms)
candidates.ai_connection: Wikipedia is the largest human-curated epistemic commons that models train on and that agents cite. Its source-reliability practice is a mature template for the Epistack, and its health bears directly on model collapse and the degradation of the shared knowledge base. It does not yet engage with AI safety.

candidates.name: Future of Life Institute: Futures Program
candidates.one_line: FLI's Futures team, led by Emilia Javorsky, uses storytelling, worldbuilding, scenario planning and creative contests to build plausible, hopeful visions of a future with AI, while FLI's outreach team funds creators of AI-awareness media.
candidates.field_lens: Worldbuilding, speculative fiction, scenario planning, creative digital media, religious traditions
candidates.ai_connection: Work includes 'Envisioning Positive Futures with Technology' (Worldbuilding Contest; the research-backed Tomorrow's AI scenarios), the Superintelligence Imagined creative contest (2024: 180+ entries, $70k in prizes), the Keep the Future Human creative contest ($100k+), the Digital Media Accelerator for creators, and 'Perspectives of Traditional Religions on Positive AI Futures'. FLI itself is on the classic map; this narrative programme is not listed separately.

candidates.name: Existential Hope (Foresight Institute)
candidates.one_line: Foresight Institute's programme for ambitious, science-grounded positive futures: a podcast, animations, prizes, writing, a worldbuilding course for designing 2035 scenarios, and the AI Pathways scenarios.
candidates.field_lens: Futures studies, worldbuilding, scenario design, animation and creative prizes
candidates.ai_connection: AI Pathways (2025) sets out two desirable but realistic AI futures, Tool AI and d/acc, with input from Vitalik Buterin, Glen Weyl, Anton Korinek, Anthony Aguirre and Allison Duettmann. It also runs an AI-futures worldbuilding course and an institution-design hackathon with FLI. Founded by Allison Duettmann; directed by Beatrice Erkers. Foresight's funding and fellowship are on the classic map, but Existential Hope is not.

candidates.name: AI Futures Project (AIFP)
candidates.one_line: A small forecasting group (Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland and others) that writes detailed narrative scenarios of AI development, AI 2027 and now AI 2040, alongside an interactive timelines model.
candidates.field_lens: Scenario writing as narrative forecasting
candidates.ai_connection: AI 2027 is the most widely read AI-risk narrative of 2025. It showed that concrete, story-form scenarios move policymakers and the public more than abstract argument. It is included here as the core-side reference point for narrative interventions.

candidates.name: Intelligence Rising
candidates.one_line: A strategic role-play simulation workshop in which present and future decision-makers play out competitive AI development and experience its tensions and risks first-hand.
candidates.field_lens: Serious games, wargaming, interactive drama
candidates.ai_connection: It is the AI-safety field's main serious-game tool. It builds felt understanding of race dynamics and governance failures among government, lab and university participants. It shows what game design and drama can add beyond written reports.

candidates.name: Geodesic Research
candidates.one_line: A technical alignment organisation whose alignment-pretraining work showed that AI discourse in training data causes self-fulfilling (mis)alignment, and that these priors can be shaped during pre- and midtraining.
candidates.field_lens: ML research, but its central finding makes how culture narrates AI a technical alignment variable
candidates.ai_connection: This is the most direct bridge between narrative and alignment: the stories humans tell about AI become model priors. Geodesic says Anthropic's 'Teaching Claude Why' and 'Model Spec Midtraining' build on its alignment-priors framing. No narratology or cultural-studies group yet works on what those corpora should contain.

candidates.name: Seismic Foundation
candidates.location: Not verified (international team; ED Malcom Glenn)
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit 'center of marketing excellence' that provides strategic communications, campaign orchestration, media buying and public-attitude research for the responsible-AI movement.
candidates.field_lens: Marketing, campaign communications, audience research
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes the Seismic Report on public attitudes to AI (2025) and runs awareness campaigns aimed at decision-makers and their constituents. It brings professional narrative-change practice into AI safety, but draws little on the academic narrative research elsewhere in this list.

candidates.name: Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence: AI Narratives and Justice Programme (CFI)
candidates.one_line: A CFI programme studying the cultural contexts that shape how AI is perceived and built. Its projects include Global AI Narratives, Imaginaries of Immortality in the Age of AI (griefbots, digital afterlives), Desirable Digitalisation (anthropology), History of AI, and Gender and AI.
candidates.field_lens: Literary and cultural studies, history, anthropology, feminist and decolonial theory
candidates.ai_connection: Global AI Narratives (2018-22; 20 workshops across five continents; the OUP books 'AI Narratives' and 'Imagining AI') is the field's main evidence base on how non-Western publics frame AI risks and benefits. CFI sits in Cambridge's Institute for Technology and Humanity alongside CSER and its own CASP group, both on the classic map. Global AI Narratives has ended, but the programme continues.

candidates.name: Georgia Tech Human-Centered AI Lab (formerly Entertainment Intelligence Lab)
candidates.one_line: Mark Riedl's lab, working on computational narrative, story understanding, role-playing agents, explainable AI and value alignment.
candidates.field_lens: Narratology, computational creativity, interactive fiction
candidates.ai_connection: Riedl's long-running 'learning values from stories' research (e.g., Quixote, 2016) treats narrative as a channel for passing human norms to agents. It is a rare technical lab where story and alignment are a single research programme, relevant to model character and normative alignment.

candidates.name: Center for Digital Narrative (CDN) and ERC project AI STORIES, University of Bergen
candidates.one_line: A Norwegian Centre of Excellence (2023-2033) for humanities-led research on algorithmic narrativity, electronic literature and game studies. It hosts Jill Walker Rettberg's ERC project AI STORIES on narrative archetypes in generative AI.
candidates.field_lens: Narratology, electronic literature, game studies, digital culture
candidates.ai_connection: Studies how LLMs reproduce and flatten stories; a 2026 preprint found that AI-generated stories have different emotional arcs and longer endings than human ones. This bears on cultural homogenisation, model character and which narratives fill training data, making it a natural partner for alignment-pretraining work.

candidates.name: Better Images of AI (coordinated by We and AI)
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit collaboration that researches, commissions and freely licenses realistic images of AI to replace robot and glowing-brain clichés, with guides, a playbook and a community blog.
candidates.field_lens: Visual culture, art, critical AI literacy
candidates.ai_connection: Visual tropes shape public expectations of AI's capabilities and hide the human accountability behind it. The project is directly useful to AI-risk communicators, who still lean on Terminator imagery. Active in 2026 (e.g., 'The glowing blue brain' post; the AI Resist List).

candidates.name: Serpentine Arts Technologies
candidates.one_line: The Serpentine Galleries' R&D programme. It commissions artists to work with AI, blockchain, games and the life sciences, and publishes annual Future Art Ecosystems strategy briefings.
candidates.field_lens: Contemporary art, cultural policy, law and technology
candidates.ai_connection: Future Art Ecosystems 4: Art x Public AI (2024). Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst's 'The Call' (2024-25) proposed cultural, legal and technical protocols for consent-based training data. The FAE R&D Fellowship is ongoing. This is a rare art-world engagement with AI governance (data rights, public AI).

candidates.name: ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society (ADM+S)
candidates.one_line: An Australian research centre where humanities, social-science, law and computing researchers study responsible, ethical and inclusive automated decision-making.
candidates.field_lens: Media and cultural studies, STS, law, sociology
candidates.ai_connection: Its September 2026 hackathon, 'The Post Imitation Game: Re-thinking the Turing Test for AI Safety', had teams design safety strategies for death-bots and imitation technologies, combining design, social and governance interventions. It is a sociotechnical reframing of 'AI safety' from outside the x-risk canon.

candidates.name: Centre for Technomoral Futures
candidates.one_line: A centre co-directed by Shannon Vallor that combines technical and moral expertise in research, education and design aimed at 'AI futures worth wanting'.
candidates.field_lens: Virtue ethics, philosophy of technology, humanities
candidates.ai_connection: Vallor's 'The AI Mirror' (2024) argues that AI reflects human moral capacities and can erode them, close to int/a's inner-development concern. The centre is also linked to BRAID. An August 2026 feature covers its work on AI futures.

candidates.name: Knowing Machines
candidates.one_line: A research project led by Kate Crawford and others that traces the histories, practices and politics of machine-learning training datasets. It also produces artworks such as Calculating Empires (Silver Lion, 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale).
candidates.field_lens: Critical data studies, STS, media studies, art
candidates.ai_connection: Shows how datasets construct 'ground truth' and knowledge cultures. This is relevant to data provenance and to which values and worldviews enter models, a humanities complement to alignment-pretraining questions.

candidates.name: AIxDESIGN
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit community of designers, artists and researchers 'making AI work for the rest of us' through open research programmes, festivals and a newsletter read by about 6,000 people.
candidates.field_lens: Design research, art, feminist and critical design
candidates.ai_connection: Its Slow AI programme and 2025 festival 'On Slow AI' echo int/a's 'speed of wisdom'. Other programmes: Esoteric AI, Small AI, Ancestral AI, Archival Images of AI, 'Let's Have Better Conversation About AI' (2026) and '<please touch the art> with Claude' (2026).

candidates.name: Dreaming Beyond AI
candidates.one_line: A multilingual platform for critical and constructive knowledge, visionary fiction, speculative art and community organising around AI, centring marginalised perspectives.
candidates.field_lens: Speculative art, visionary fiction, feminist and decolonial futurism
candidates.ai_connection: Produces counter-narratives about who gets to imagine AI futures, and how algorithmic power and imagination interact. It is adjacent to AI safety through power concentration and the legitimacy of AI futures.

candidates.name: Critical AI (Rutgers)
candidates.one_line: An interdisciplinary humanities journal (Duke University Press) and initiative at Rutgers' Center for Cultural Analysis that scrutinises AI's claims, data practices and cultural effects.
candidates.field_lens: Literary and cultural studies, history of science, critical theory
candidates.ai_connection: The main venue for humanities critique of AI hype, including critique of x-risk discourse. It is a necessary counterpart for any int/a attempt to recouple present-harms scholarship with catastrophic-risk work.

candidates.name: Algorithmic Justice League (AJL)
candidates.one_line: Joy Buolamwini's organisation, which combines art and research (spoken-word 'evocative audits', exhibitions) with advocacy to expose AI harms and bias. It marks ten years in 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Art as research method, poetry, civil-rights advocacy
candidates.ai_connection: Shows how art can work as an accountability and public-mobilisation tool for AI. Its focus is bias and present harms rather than frontier risk.

candidates.name: Center for Science and the Imagination, Arizona State University (CSI)
candidates.one_line: Ed Finn's centre brings writers, artists and scientists together to build 'thoughtful optimism' through fiction anthologies, lesson plans, films and public programmes.
candidates.field_lens: Science fiction, creative writing, humanities-science collaboration
candidates.ai_connection: It has a proven method for imagining hopeful futures at scale (Climate Imagination: Dispatches from Hopeful Futures) that AI-futures efforts like FLI and Existential Hope attempt with less literary depth.
