Specific AI-safety relevance: Futures Literacy Labs and the GAP Coalition are a ready vehicle for anticipatory-governance training on frontier AI for policymakers in countries outside the AI-safety network.

candidates.name: Future Generations Commissioner for Wales
candidates.one_line: The statutory, independent guardian of the interests of future generations under the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015; the Commissioner is Derek Walker.
candidates.field_lens: Intergenerational justice institutionalised in law: long-term duties on public bodies, Section 20 reviews, future-generations impact assessment
candidates.ai_connection: No AI work found; 2026 priorities are inequality, energy (Project Ynni, July 2026) and health with climate. Listed as a potential partner because it is the world's leading working model of a legal duty to consider long-term effects on future generations. It could set an example of statutory long-term impact assessment of AI adoption by public bodies, and of intergenerational representation in AI governance, a gap the Simon Institute and the Centre for Future Generations only partly fill.

candidates.name: SHIFT Grants (NODES and Edge City)
candidates.location: Global (run by NODES, a deep-tech foresight consultancy, with Edge City)
candidates.one_line: A d/acc ('decentralized, democratic, differential, defensive acceleration') grants programme giving micro grants of $5k–15k and development grants of $20k–40k in rounds tied to Edge City's d/acc Week.
candidates.field_lens: d/acc / defensive accelerationism (Vitalik Buterin's framework) and the public-goods funding culture
candidates.ai_connection: Six tracks: biosecurity, social technology and governance, information resilience, neurotech and augmented cognition, physical defence, and cyberdefence and cryptography. One AI-safety grantee is the Institute for Security and Technology, for SL5 model-weight security protocols for AI labs. Other grantees work on information resilience, such as prediction markets. A small funder that new founders building defensive tech for the AI transition can reach.

candidates.name: Simocracy
candidates.location: San Francisco / New York (open source, on ATProto)
candidates.one_line: A public ledger of citizen-built AI 'sims' (digital twins), each with an avatar, a constitution written by its human and a speaking style. The sims deliberate and allocate funds on their owners' behalf in public senates, councils and S-Process rounds.
candidates.field_lens: Digital democracy, delegation and representation theory, and public-goods mechanism design (it uses the S-Process allocation mechanism from the Survival and Flourishing Fund)
candidates.ai_connection: A live testbed for AI delegates in collective decisions: 336 sims, 26 gatherings and 432 proposals, including Filecoin ProPGF milestone evaluations. At Edge City's Agent Village, 82 sims allocated $10k without their principals confirming, a concrete case of the principal–agent and human-oversight gap that matters for gradual-disempowerment and scalable-oversight debates. It is linked to Protocol Labs, Hypercerts and GainForest. Its makers describe it as 'a publication on governance AI'.

candidates.name: Protocol Labs (PL) and Protocol Labs R&D
candidates.one_line: The open-source R&D network behind IPFS and Filecoin, which funds and co-organises much of the public-goods and d/acc pop-up ecosystem. Its R&D areas include AI and robotics and 'safe neurotech'.
candidates.field_lens: Decentralised systems, cryptoeconomics, and the d/acc and public-goods movement
candidates.ai_connection: Co-founded Funding the Commons; co-ran the Edge City d/acc residency (Juan Benet, Molly Mackinlay); is a partner in Simocracy and Agent Village; hosted a Neurotech Summit at Edge Esmeralda 2025. Its R&D agenda covers agent-coordination infrastructure (identity, reputation and coordination protocols for autonomous agents) and safe neurotech, including NeuroAI and whole-brain emulation. It held the talk 'AI Safety and Governance: Hard Rules, Real Evaluations, and Risk' (October 2025). It mixes capabilities-adjacent infrastructure with governance and safety interest.

candidates.name: Mimir Center for Long Term Futures Research (at the Institute for Futures Studies, Stockholm)
candidates.one_line: A long-term futures research centre at Stockholm's Institute for Futures Studies (IFFS). Its agenda covers civilisational collapse, global catastrophic risk, decision-making under deep uncertainty, space governance, and whole brain emulation.
candidates.field_lens: Futures studies, philosophy and decision theory, macrohistory, and existential-risk studies (Anders Sandberg, ex-FHI)
candidates.ai_connection: Publications include Jebari & Adler, 'The Time of Perils and a World System of Governance' (working paper 2025:1), Engström on basing long-term AI policy on today's deep-learning technology (Tidskrift för politisk filosofi, 2025), and work on regulating high-reach AI under the EU Digital Services Act. It held a workshop on the philosophy and ethics of brain emulation (January 2025, covering digital minds, identity and the ethics of experiments on artificial neural systems), and has a research theme on novel technology risks. This qualifies the brief's finding that IFFS has no AI work.

candidates.name: OECD Expert Group on AI Futures (with the OECD Strategic Foresight Unit)
candidates.one_line: An OECD.AI workstream that uses strategic-foresight exercises with the OECD Strategic Foresight Unit to analyse possible AI trajectories. Its multidisciplinary expert group is co-chaired by Stuart Russell and Michael Schoenstein of the German Federal Chancellery.
candidates.field_lens: Government strategic foresight and horizon scanning in an intergovernmental policy setting
candidates.ai_connection: Produced the foresight analysis of future AI risks, benefits and policy imperatives; ran a public consultation on risk thresholds for advanced AI systems (2024) and a consultation on the biggest AI benefits and risks '10+ years from now'. Earlier it held an OECD–MIT roundtable on 'AI by 2032' and a meeting on emerging future AI risks (2022). The last documented expert-group meeting was in November 2023, so the current cadence is unclear, though the page is live with 2026 posts.

candidates.name: UK Government Office for Science (GO-Science): Futures and foresight on frontier AI
candidates.one_line: The UK government's science-advice office. Its futures and foresight team applied professional foresight methods to frontier AI for the 2023 AI Safety Summit.
candidates.field_lens: Government futures, foresight and horizon scanning (scenario methods, drivers analysis)
candidates.ai_connection: Wrote 'Future risks of frontier AI' (Annex A) and the 'AI 2030 scenarios' annex to the UK frontier-AI capabilities and risks discussion paper. The paper was reviewed by Yoshua Bengio, Sara Hooker, Arvind Narayanan and others, published October 2023, updated April 2025, and covers misuse, social harms and loss of control. It shows professional foresight feeding directly into AI-safety policy; the team's ongoing AI work after 2025 is not confirmed.

candidates.name: Office of Technology Assessment at the German Bundestag (TAB), operated by ITAS/KIT
candidates.one_line: The German parliament's technology-assessment office, run by the Institute for Technology Assessment and Systems Analysis (ITAS) at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. It produces precautionary analyses of emerging technologies for Bundestag committees.
candidates.field_lens: Technology assessment, futures studies' policy-facing sibling: precautionary analysis under deep uncertainty, parliamentary advice, systems analysis
candidates.ai_connection: TAB Report No. 217, 'Biotechnology and Artificial Intelligence: Risks Posed by Research to Security and Biological Weapons Proliferation' (13 August 2026), examines LLM knowledge diffusion, AI-driven protein and pathogen design, and automated labs. It recommends continuous monitoring, mandatory gene-synthesis screening, risk-based access controls for powerful biological AI systems, and stronger international oversight. A TAB project on 'The potential and risks of using AI agents' (autonomy, manipulation, liability, democratic discourse) runs November 2026 to June 2027.

alt_descriptions.one_line: The German parliament's technology-assessment office. KIT's ITAS runs it with IZT and VDI/VDE-IT, and it gives MPs forward-looking assessments of the risks of emerging technologies.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: TAB-Fokus No. 51 (2026) covers security risks where AI meets biotechnology, including AI lowering the barriers to bioweapons, and sets out policy options. TAB held a public expert hearing on 'AIxBio' on 8 July 2026. ITAS is organising a conference on long-term governance, 'Beyond the crisis reflex?' (April 2027). A rare case of a technology-assessment body taking on catastrophic AI risk directly.

candidates.name: European Parliamentary Technology Assessment network (EPTA), incl. the European Parliament's STOA panel
candidates.location: Europe (parliamentary TA offices, plus some outside Europe)
candidates.one_line: The network of parliamentary technology-assessment offices (TAB, Rathenau Instituut, the European Parliament's STOA, UK POST and others). It publishes a joint annual report and shares a database of member projects.
candidates.field_lens: Technology assessment and parliamentary foresight
candidates.ai_connection: Its 2024 joint report was 'Artificial Intelligence and Democracy'. The project database lists current member work on AI agents, AI for cybersecurity, and AI in the cultural and media industries. STOA keeps an AI repository and legislative overview and supports the EU AI Pact. This is an under-used channel through which AI-safety findings could reach national parliaments.

alt_descriptions.one_line: A network of 24 parliamentary technology-assessment bodies (14 full members, 10 associates) that advise parliaments using citizen panels, stakeholder input and expert analysis.
alt_descriptions.ai_connection: Published a joint 2024 EPTA report, 'AI and Democracy', and its members run AI projects, for example on AI agents and cybersecurity. It is the existing channel for bringing technology-assessment methods to frontier AI across about 20 parliaments, including Japan's and Korea's, though it has not yet been used for frontier or catastrophic AI risk.

candidates.name: Transformative Futures Institute (TFI)
candidates.one_line: A 501(c)(3) that applies under-used foresight methods (horizon scanning, wargaming, red teaming, agent-based and Monte Carlo simulation, Bayesian networks) to societal-scale AI risk.
candidates.field_lens: Futures studies and foresight methods applied from inside the x-risk community; crisis-management planning
candidates.ai_connection: Work on responding to and recovering from AI loss of control, for cases where alignment fails. ARA-27 is a decision game on an escalating incident of autonomous replication and adaptation. Other outputs: 'The Reasoning Under Uncertainty Trap' (a structural AI risk), a survey of US experts and voters on 18 AI risks, a report on drivers of structural AI risk, and a proposal for an international consortium for evaluating societal-scale AI risks. The site shows a 2024 copyright and no new feed posts since 2023, so its current activity is unclear.

candidates.name: Centre for Future Generations (CFG)
candidates.one_line: A Brussels think tank that helps policymakers anticipate and govern rapid technological change, with programmes on advanced AI, biotech, neurotech and climate interventions, plus an incubator.
candidates.field_lens: Anticipatory governance with an intergenerational framing; foresight for EU policy
candidates.ai_connection: Its advanced-AI programme published the 'Governing AI for cognitive integrity' series (September 2026): why people turn to AI systems, how effects compound across people and society, and the business and design choices behind AI systems. It also does EU frontier-AI governance input. It links AI governance to mental integrity, a theme close to int/a.

candidates.name: Demos Helsinki
candidates.one_line: An independent Nordic think tank on societal transitions and 'remastering technology for society', working with governments and EU research consortia.
candidates.field_lens: Transition studies, futures thinking, democratic theory, and Nordic public-sector innovation
candidates.ai_connection: Published 'A framework for democratic AI governance' (February 2026), which builds participation, freedom, equality, transparency, knowledge and the rule of law into the AI lifecycle. It is a partner in the EU project FORSEE (2025) on defining what 'successful AI' means for society, and has studied algorithmic management of workers and non-discriminatory public-sector AI. It does not use an x-risk framing.

candidates.name: Sitra (Finnish Innovation Fund)
candidates.one_line: Finland's independent public futures and innovation fund, which reports to Parliament and publishes Megatrends, Weak Signals and the Futures Barometer.
candidates.field_lens: National strategic foresight (megatrends, weak signals) and public-interest innovation funding
candidates.ai_connection: In 'Could AI kill us all?' (28 September 2026), Sitra's director of international programmes, Kristo Lehtonen, argues that the practical existential risk is humans losing oversight of opaque, self-improving autonomous systems. Sitra also ran a nationwide mapping, with the Agentic State foundation, of how ready Finland's public sector is for agentic AI, plus a data and AI programme. It is a futures fund just starting to engage with AI risk and could commission foresight on it.

candidates.name: London Futurists
candidates.one_line: A long-running futurist meetup, podcast and essay community chaired by David Wood that does 'serious analysis of radical scenarios for the disruptions ahead'. It also runs the Vital Syllabus education project.
candidates.field_lens: Technoprogressive futurism and scenario analysis (co-hosts events with IEET)
candidates.ai_connection: Recent output is centred on superintelligence: the essay 'Safety before Superintelligence' (February 2026), posts on governance, trust and worldbuilding (July 2026), and the event 'The Technoprogressive Opportunity' (September 2026, with IEET). David Wood co-wrote one of the Millennium Project's AGI 2035 scenarios. Its outlook leans transhumanist rather than integral.

candidates.name: Flowers AI & CogSci Lab (Inria / University of Bordeaux)
candidates.one_line: Pierre-Yves Oudeyer's lab, which studies curiosity-driven, open-ended ('autotelic') learning in children and machines, using developmental psychology and computational models.
candidates.field_lens: Developmental psychology, cognitive science, cultural evolution
candidates.ai_connection: Has an explicit research line on aligning autotelic systems with human cultures (values and preferences), and uses language and social interaction to guide exploration, including in LLM-based autotelic agents. It frames its question as how to build AI that serves human societies in their diversity. This bears on aligning open-ended agents that set their own goals, a problem the ML-alignment canon rarely approaches from developmental science.

candidates.name: VALAWAI (Value-Aware AI), coordinated by IIIA-CSIC
candidates.location: Barcelona, Spain (consortium with IMIM, IIT, Ghent University, Sony Europe, Studio Stelluti)
candidates.one_line: A European Innovation Council (EIC) Pathfinder project (grant 101070930) building 'value-aware' AI architectures that represent a value system, act within it and explain their behaviour. It tests them on social media, social robots and social decision-making.
candidates.field_lens: Moral philosophy (mapping norms and values), neuroscience of awareness (quantitative measures of awareness), cognitive architecture
candidates.ai_connection: An approach to alignment from outside the ML canon: it pairs philosophical analysis of values with neuroscience-based awareness architectures. It held the 'Awareness in Artificial Agents' conference in Venice, 6–8 September 2025. The project appears to run roughly 2022–2026, so it may be winding down.

candidates.name: IRIS (Interchange Forum for Reflecting on Intelligent Systems), University of Stuttgart: AI Safety group (Thilo Hagendorff)
candidates.one_line: An interdisciplinary platform for critical reflection on intelligent systems that hosts a dedicated AI Safety research group led by Thilo Hagendorff.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy and ethics of technology; 'machine psychology', which applies experimental psychology to LLMs
candidates.ai_connection: Hagendorff's group runs psychology-style experiments on LLMs, and its work includes emergent deception abilities in LLMs (PNAS 2024) and mapping the ethics of generative AI. IRIS launched six projects in 2026 on human–intelligent-system teaming (HISIT). It is the clearest AI-safety group in German academia that comes from philosophy and psychology rather than ML.

candidates.name: KIRA Center
candidates.one_line: An independent think tank 'working to make AI go well' (founder and director Daniel Privitera), working on frontier-AI policy, AI economics and European compute.
candidates.field_lens: Mainly conventional AI policy and economics. It is included because it is the main x-risk-aware policy organisation in int/a's Berlin hub, not because it has an integral bent.
candidates.ai_connection: Wrote the Safety and Security chapter of the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice. Staff work on the International AI Safety Report. A KIRA compute report informed Germany's National Data Center Strategy.

candidates.name: European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies (EGE)
candidates.one_line: An independent advisory body on ethics to the President of the European Commission, in existence since 1991. The current group was appointed on 26 January 2025.
candidates.field_lens: Philosophy, bioethics, law, fundamental rights
candidates.ai_connection: Issued the opinion 'Democracy in the Digital Age' (algorithmic surveillance, manipulation and discrimination). In 2026 it called for a new approach to Neuro-AI governance grounded in EU fundamental rights (news dated 8 September 2026). It also issued a 2018 statement on AI, robotics and 'autonomous' systems. It is the EU-level counterpart of the national ethics councils.

candidates.name: Alexander von Humboldt Institute for Internet and Society (HIIG): AI & Society Lab and Public Interest AI
candidates.one_line: A Berlin internet-and-society institute. Its Public Interest AI group, led by Theresa Züger, defines and builds prototypes of AI that serves a public rather than profit, and runs the publicinterest.ai platform.
candidates.field_lens: STS, law, political theory, participatory design
candidates.ai_connection: Sets out six conditions for public-interest AI: justification, equity, participatory design and deliberation, technical standards and safeguards, openness to validation, and sustainability. It maintains a project map and stakeholder index, and has built prototypes such as the Simba text simplifier and Telegram claim-spotting. Züger has publicly put calls to pause AI in context, arguing for responsibility over speed. The group's core funding ran from 2020 to 2024, but it continues within HIIG.

candidates.name: Bertelsmann Stiftung: reframe[Tech] – Algorithms for the Common Good
candidates.one_line: A large German foundation's programme for aligning digital technology with the common good. It publishes analyses and policy proposals on AI regulation, public AI and platform alternatives.
candidates.field_lens: Common-good and public-value policy, institutional design
candidates.ai_connection: Published a policy brief on 'European Public AI' (January 2026), a report on decentralised social media (January 2026), work on interoperability standards (December 2025) and on simplifying EU AI rules (November 2025). The work bears on public-option AI and on concentration of power. No 'Beyond Tech' successor was found; reframe[Tech] is the live programme.

candidates.name: SUPERRR Lab
candidates.one_line: A feminist tech-policy and futures organisation that challenges power dynamics in the tech sector and argues that 'digital policy is social policy'.
candidates.field_lens: Feminist theory, futures and speculative design, social policy
candidates.ai_connection: Produced 'AI Mythbusting: The Zine' and runs feministtechpolicy.org. Its 2026 work covers solidarity among data workers. It brings futures-literacy and care-ethics methods to the question of whose futures AI serves.

candidates.name: FIfF – Forum InformatikerInnen für Frieden und gesellschaftliche Verantwortung
candidates.one_line: An association of computer scientists for peace and social responsibility, founded in 1984 out of the peace movement. It publishes the quarterly FIfF-Kommunikation.
candidates.field_lens: Peace research, professional ethics in computing, critical informatics
candidates.ai_connection: Its long-running Cyberpeace campaign opposes lethal autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons, and a working group studies armed drones and AI targeting. Its 'Grüne Bits' project covers AI's environmental costs. The FIfF Conference 2026, 'Keine Panik! Resilienz in der Polykrise', runs in Berlin from 30 October to 1 November. It carries a 40-year tradition of conscientious engagement by computing professionals.

candidates.name: Bits & Bäume
candidates.one_line: An alliance of 13 environmental, climate, digital-rights and development organisations, plus a grassroots community, working for sustainable and socially just digitalisation.
candidates.field_lens: Political ecology, sustainability science, digital sufficiency
candidates.ai_connection: Campaigns on the energy use of generative AI and its ties to the fossil-fuel industry, and runs policy labs on cloud infrastructure and digital resilience. It held a regional conference in June 2026. It places AI inside the ecological crisis: a metacrisis framing of AI that has no x-risk crossover.

candidates.name: Institute for Human-Centered AI, Helmholtz Munich (Eric Schulz)
candidates.one_line: A group of cognitive scientists, neuroscientists and computer scientists who study machine intelligence through cognitive experiments and build computational models of human cognition.
candidates.field_lens: Cognitive psychology, computational cognitive science, neuroscience
candidates.ai_connection: Built Centaur (Nature 2025), a model trained on more than 10 million human decisions from psychology experiments that simulates human behaviour. Earlier work includes 'Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3' (Binz and Schulz, PNAS 2023). Marcel Binz won an ERC Starting Grant (MIDAS) in 2026. Two AI-safety problems: evaluating models with cognitive test batteries, and the dual-use risk of accurate human-behaviour simulators for persuasion and manipulation. The work itself is not framed as safety.

candidates.name: FEST – Forschungsstätte der Evangelischen Studiengemeinschaft
candidates.one_line: The interdisciplinary research institute of the Protestant Church in Germany (EKD), founded in 1958. It works on peace, sustainable development, religion and law, and theology and natural science.
candidates.field_lens: Protestant theology, just-peace ethics, theology–science dialogue
candidates.ai_connection: 'Digital theology' is an active research field, and a 2025 publication covers unmanned weapons and their ethical implications. The specific AI-safety problems are autonomous weapons, and the question of what it means to be a person alongside AI, which theological anthropology addresses. Its AI work is still light.

candidates.name: Institut de recherche et d'innovation (IRI), Centre Pompidou
candidates.one_line: An institute founded by the philosopher Bernard Stiegler in 2006. It develops 'digital studies', contributory research, and a 'pharmacological' philosophy of technology, which treats every technology as both cure and poison.
candidates.field_lens: Continental philosophy of technology (Stiegler, Simondon), digital humanities, design
candidates.ai_connection: Runs the annual Entretiens du Nouveau Monde Industriel (ENMI). ENMI 2026, 'La clinique des objets', includes a session on physical AI and robotics and treats generative models through a pharmacological lens. The specific problem is the erosion of human attention and knowledge ('proletarianisation'), which this philosophical tradition analyses in depth and which AI-safety discourse barely touches.

candidates.name: Café IA (France)
candidates.one_line: A national programme of free, informal public discussions on AI, held in libraries, workplaces, schools and community spaces, with facilitation kits on AI and work, the environment and information. It came from France's digital council, now the Conseil de l'IA et du numérique.
candidates.field_lens: Public deliberation, popular education, collective sense-making
candidates.ai_connection: Infrastructure for mass public deliberation and AI literacy. The 2025–26 season is active. It bears on the democratic legitimacy of decisions about AI, and is a model int/a's Paris community could plug into or copy. The council's origin is not stated on Café IA's own site, so that link needs confirming.

candidates.name: Current AI
candidates.one_line: A global public-interest AI partnership launched at the February 2025 Paris AI Action Summit. It has more than $400M committed, aims for $2.5B over five years, and funds, builds and connects open, public-option AI.
candidates.field_lens: Public goods and commons, development, digital sovereignty
candidates.ai_connection: Gives grants to community changemakers, is building an open-source 'full stack' of public-interest AI, and published a September 2026 report with UNDP on multilingual AI and community authority over knowledge. It bears on power concentration and on who gets to build AI. It is a new, large funder outside the AI-safety funding circuit.

candidates.name: UNESCO Ethics of AI programme (Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, Global Forum on the Ethics of AI)
candidates.one_line: UNESCO's AI-ethics programme, built around the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (adopted by 193 member states), plus its readiness-assessment methodology, its Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory and an annual Global Forum.
candidates.field_lens: Human rights, cultural and linguistic diversity, environmental flourishing, intergovernmental norm-setting
candidates.ai_connection: The Recommendation's values include peaceful, just and interconnected societies, and environment and ecosystem flourishing, making it one of the few global AI norms with an ecological value. The 2026 Global Forum (Riyadh, 14–17 September), 'Transforming Global Cooperation for Ethical AI Governance', covered neurotechnology and cultural and linguistic diversity.

candidates.name: Mind & Life Europe (MLE)
candidates.one_line: The European sister organisation of the Mind & Life Institute. It brings contemplative practitioners together with scientists of embodied ('enactive') cognition through its European Summer Research Institute, the journal Hyphae and the Enactive Fold podcast.
candidates.field_lens: Contemplative science, enactive and embodied cognitive science, phenomenology
candidates.ai_connection: Promoted 'A Mind & Life Dialogue: Minds, Artificial Intelligence, and Ethics' with the Dalai Lama (Dharamsala, 14–16 October 2025); this was probably led jointly with the US Mind & Life Institute. Its podcast episode 'An Enactive AI? Computing and Sense-Making Beyond the Data-Driven Approach' featured Luc Steels and Takashi Ikegami. It holds Europe's densest network of enactivist and contemplative scientists. Its 2026 theme is 'Empowering through Caring'.

candidates.name: Globethics
candidates.location: Geneva, Switzerland (regional centres in Asia-Pacific, Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa)
candidates.one_line: A global ethics network founded in 2004 that offers training, publishing and convening. 'Ethics of AI and Emerging Technology' is one of its core areas.
candidates.field_lens: Applied and interreligious ethics, ethics of governance and leadership, Global South networks
candidates.ai_connection: Its stated aim is 'empowering people and organisations for safe and inclusive AI', and partners cite its concrete work bringing civil society and multiple faiths together on AI. The Global Ethics Forum 2026 (Bali, 20–22 October) focuses on ethics, AI and governance.

candidates.name: FBK Center for Religious Studies (FBK-ISR), Fondazione Bruno Kessler
candidates.one_line: An interdisciplinary research centre on religion, ethics and society within Fondazione Bruno Kessler.
candidates.field_lens: Religious studies, theology, ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Ran a 'Religion and Artificial Intelligence' seminar (University of Urbino, 19 September 2026), the 2026 conference 'The Lonesome Meaning' on solitude and isolation, which includes AI scenarios, and a project on AI in faith-based healthcare systems in Bangladesh, Kenya and India. The specific problem is loneliness and AI companionship, read through religious ideas of solitude and communion.

candidates.name: University of Osaka Research Center on Ethical, Legal and Social Issues (Osaka ELSI Center)
candidates.one_line: Japan's largest dedicated ELSI centre, doing practical research on the ethical, legal and social issues of emerging technologies with industry and government.
candidates.field_lens: ELSI, bioethics, law, science communication
candidates.ai_connection: Publishes the ELSI NOTE series (Nos. 58–67 recently), including AI in child-welfare assessment. It has also produced a 'Value and Privacy Impact Assessment' framework, surveys of public values on AI in healthcare, and analysis of media coverage of AI in sensitive domains.

candidates.name: B'AI Global Forum, University of Tokyo
candidates.one_line: A University of Tokyo initiative (2020 to March 2026) on using AI and digital technology to build a gender-equal society that guarantees minority rights.
candidates.field_lens: Gender studies, media studies, cross-cultural AI ethics, art
candidates.ai_connection: Researched algorithmic bias and gender, cross-cultural perceptions of AI, and masculinity and algorithms (the BAIRAL meetings). It ran a joint workshop with Cambridge, 'Pro-Justice: Cross-Cultural Approaches to AI Ethics' (March 2026), and an art installation on migration and AI. The project announced its completion on 31 March 2026, so Japan has lost its main gender- and minority-focused AI research hub.

candidates.name: Doublethink Lab
candidates.one_line: A Taiwanese nonprofit that investigates authoritarian, especially PRC, information manipulation in 101 countries. Its digital-intelligence team builds AI tools for investigations.
candidates.field_lens: Open-source intelligence (OSINT), information-warfare studies, Taiwan's whole-of-society approach to resilience
candidates.ai_connection: Analysed leaked GoLaxy files on PRC AI-driven influence operations aimed at Taiwan and the US (April 2026). Documented a PRC-linked network of 549 fake Threads accounts (March 2026). Published policy pathways against foreign information manipulation and interference (February 2026). Its work bears on AI-enabled persuasion and on society's resilience to it.

candidates.name: The Pranava Institute
candidates.one_line: An India-first centre for emerging technology and policy, co-founded by Shyam Krishnakumar and Titiksha Vashist, working on technology, design and society.
candidates.field_lens: Design ethics, psychology of persuasion, Indian public policy
candidates.ai_connection: Runs 'Feeling Automated', a project on the ethical development of emotional and interactive AI systems. Wrote 'Design Beyond Deception', a manual on dark patterns. Launched a Youth Digital Cultures Lab and the Youth for Tech Futures Fellowship (2026). Its work bears on manipulation and on harms from companion and emotional AI in non-Western settings.

candidates.name: Tattle Civic Tech
candidates.one_line: A community of technologists, researchers and artists building tools and datasets for a healthier online information ecosystem in India.
candidates.field_lens: Participatory and community design, feminist technology, media literacy, art
candidates.ai_connection: Builds Uli, a community-sourced, localised moderation tool against online gender-based violence in Indian languages, and runs the Deepfakes Analysis Unit. Gave a February 2026 talk on evaluations and open-source software for AI at scale, and commented on India's draft deepfake rules (December 2025). Its participatory, multilingual evaluation methods are relevant to safety evaluations outside English.

candidates.name: <A+> Alliance for Inclusive Algorithms and the Feminist AI Research Network (f<a+i>r)
candidates.location: Global; co-led by Women at the Table (Geneva) and Code for Africa; f<a+i>r co-led with Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica (2021–2024)
candidates.one_line: A global feminist coalition that moves 'from critique to creation' on AI, taking ideas from paper to prototype to pilot.
candidates.field_lens: Feminist theory, Majority-World knowledge, participatory design
candidates.ai_connection: f<a+i>r built a body of feminist AI research and prototypes from Global South and Majority-World contexts, with a Latin American hub through Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica. The Alliance produces governance and policy tools for gender equality and democratic participation. Code for Africa joined as co-lead in 2025.

candidates.name: Fundación Vía Libre
candidates.one_line: An Argentine foundation that defends fundamental rights in the digital environment, with an emphasis on free culture and building knowledge collectively. AI is one of its main lines of work.
candidates.field_lens: Human rights, free culture and commons, social science
candidates.ai_connection: Its 2026 work covers facial recognition in Buenos Aires and AI sovereignty, and it scheduled a talk on AI and democracy for 8 October 2026. It is also known for EDIA, a no-code tool for social scientists to probe stereotypes in Spanish-language models, but EDIA did not appear on the homepage checked.

candidates.name: LIRNEasia
candidates.one_line: An Asia-Pacific think tank on ICT policy and regulation, with research themes on data, algorithms and policy, and on misinformation and language resources.
candidates.field_lens: Development economics, regulation, Asian policy research
candidates.ai_connection: Runs the Asia AI4D Observatory, the Asian node of IDRC's AI4D network. Its CEO spoke at WAIC 2026 on a more inclusive vision for global AI governance, and in October 2026 it was hiring a senior researcher, a sign the AI programme is growing. It is a route into non-Anglophone Asian AI-policy research.

candidates.name: Consortium for Evaluating Faith and Ethics in AI (CEFEAI)
candidates.one_line: A consortium of faith-based universities (Baylor, BYU, Notre Dame, Yeshiva) that builds open benchmarks of how LLMs treat religious traditions and moral questions, and publishes leaderboards and code.
candidates.field_lens: Religious studies, survey methodology and moral psychology, combined with ML evaluation, across Baptist, Latter-day Saint, Catholic and Jewish institutions
candidates.ai_connection: It has released two open benchmarks on GitHub: 'allfaith-conversion-bias' tests whether models treat religious-conversion prompts symmetrically across faiths, and 'allfaith-religious-representation' measures how often models surface religious perspectives on ethics and life questions, using items from a 1,125-person national survey and testing about 27 models. Early findings: religion is barely studied in AI-fairness research; models favour some traditions in conversion prompts; and models leave religion out of answers about grief and meaning even though users expect it. This is pluralistic-alignment and evals work that comes from inside religious academia. GitHub org created October 2025; repos updated September 2026. BYU's David Wingate is the academic lead.

candidates.name: AI Christian Benchmark (Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics, The Gospel Coalition)
candidates.one_line: An evangelical benchmark that puts commonly searched questions about Christian faith to leading AI platforms and has Christian scholars grade the answers. It was founded by Michael Graham, programme director of The Gospel Coalition's Keller Center.
candidates.field_lens: Evangelical theology and apologetics, religious data science (Graham also co-founded 'Religion Data')
candidates.ai_connection: In its first round, seven questions went to seven leading platforms: two nudged users toward Christianity, two away from it, and three gave pluralistic answers. That is evidence of how unevenly models behave on worldview questions. It was presented on IF20's 'AI & Benchmarks' webinar (July 2026) next to CEFEAI. It belongs with Gloo's Flourishing AI benchmark as faith-community model evaluation, and it shows how much worldview-steering differs across models.

candidates.name: Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility (ICCR), with the Investor Alliance for Human Rights
candidates.one_line: A coalition of more than 300 faith-based and values-driven institutional investors that files shareholder proposals and engages companies. Its 'Digital Rights and AI Accountability' programme, together with its Investor Alliance for Human Rights, presses tech companies on AI harms.
candidates.field_lens: Faith-based shareholder activism (religious orders, denominational pension funds), business and human rights (UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights)
candidates.ai_connection: It runs a Digital Rights and AI Accountability working group, publishes investor briefings ('Risks of AI on Human Rights'; 'AI in the Kill Chain: The Risk of AI-Enabled Warfare and What Investors Need to Know'), and has made submissions to the US AI Action Plan (2025), the UN Human Rights Council (2025), NTIA and the EU AI Act. It responded to the 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. It holds a governance lever (shareholder resolutions at Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and others) that AI-safety groups have barely used.

candidates.name: Stop Killer Robots Interfaith Group
candidates.one_line: The interreligious working group inside the Stop Killer Robots coalition, which brings faith voices into the campaign for a treaty banning autonomous weapons that target people.
candidates.field_lens: Religious peace and disarmament traditions, humanitarian law
candidates.ai_connection: In June 2026 it issued 'Disarming AI, Defending Humanity', a statement endorsing Pope Leo XIV's call in Magnifica Humanitas to 'disarm AI' and urging legal prohibition of anti-personnel autonomous weapons, with meaningful human control over force. It is a working link between multi-faith moral authority and a live AI arms-control process. Stop Killer Robots itself is already on the roster; this sub-group is the faith-specific entry point.

candidates.name: Cambridge Interfaith Programme (CIP)
candidates.one_line: University of Cambridge programme on Jewish, Christian and Muslim relations (the home of Scriptural Reasoning). Its AI strand looks at faith, ethics and 'one-person dialogues' with chatbots.
candidates.field_lens: Interreligious studies, scriptural reasoning, Jewish thought, cognitive science (with Sciences Po)
candidates.ai_connection: Prof. Daniel Weiss and Dr Darren Frey (Sciences Po) published paired articles in Harvard Data Science Review and the Harvard Divinity Bulletin. They argue that empathetic chatbots create 'one-person dialogues' that may erode human dialogical capacity and community relations. They were discussants at the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk's 2026 summer programme ('Historical Dimensions of AI, Power & Catastrophic Risk') alongside Yuval Noah Harari. CIP also ran a 'Faith & AI' workshop in September 2026. It is an explicit academic bridge between interreligious dialogue methods and the x-risk community.

candidates.name: AI Faith & Civil Society Commission (AIFCS)
candidates.one_line: UK-based commission of senior faith and civil-society leaders that formed around the 2023 Bletchley AI Safety Summit. It runs parliamentary roundtables and sends recommendations to the UK government.
candidates.field_lens: Multi-faith public ethics: Muslim (via the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace), Christian, Jewish, Hindu and Bahá'í commissioners and associates, with civil-society advocacy
candidates.ai_connection: It was convened by the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace (hosted by Google, supported by the Good Faith Partnership) the week before Bletchley, and sent an open letter to the UK Science Secretary feeding into the Summit. Since then: an AI APPG event on 'AI and Our Spiritual and Cultural Lives' (Dec 2024), a Paris AI Action Summit fringe event (Feb 2025), an algorithmic-bias roundtable in Portcullis House, recommendations to the UK government (March 2025), and participation in the FLI and Leverhulme CFI 'Positive Futures and Religious Tradition' workshop (July 2024). The latest news post is from October 2025.

candidates.name: Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace (Forum for Promoting Peace in Muslim Societies)
candidates.one_line: Islamic peace forum chaired by Sheikh Abdallah bin Bayyah. It brought the Muslim side into the Rome Call for AI Ethics and drives interfaith AI-ethics convenings.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic jurisprudence and maqasid ethics, Abrahamic interfaith diplomacy
candidates.ai_connection: It joined the 'Abrahamic commitment' to the Rome Call (January 2023). It co-organised 'AI Ethics for Peace' in Hiroshima (July 2024) with the Pontifical Academy for Life, Religions for Peace Japan and the Chief Rabbinate of Israel's Commission for Interreligious Relations; there, sixteen new signatories from eleven religions signed and a 'Hiroshima Appeal' was issued. It convened the pre-Bletchley faith meeting that created the AI Faith & Civil Society Commission. Its executive director, Zeshan Zafar, spoke at the 2024 UNGA side event 'Faith, Ethics and AI'. Its website was unreachable during this check.

candidates.name: Religions for Peace (RfP), incl. Religions for Peace Japan (WCRP Japan)
candidates.one_line: The world's largest multi-religious coalition, made up of national and regional interreligious councils in about 90 countries. Its Japan chapter co-organised the Hiroshima multi-faith signing of the Rome Call for AI Ethics.
candidates.field_lens: Interreligious council-building, peace and disarmament advocacy
candidates.ai_connection: RfP Japan co-hosted 'AI Ethics for Peace' (Hiroshima, 9-10 July 2024), where Buddhist, Hindu, Zoroastrian, Bahá'í, Shinto-adjacent and Abrahamic leaders signed the Rome Call and Microsoft, IBM and Cisco took part. The global body's own published AI work is thin: a 2021 piece arguing for faith perspectives 'in the rooms where AI decisions are being made', and a 'Shared Sacred Flourishing' podcast. The value here is its council infrastructure, not current AI output.

candidates.name: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (IIFA)
candidates.one_line: The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation's (OIC) highest juristic body. In November 2025 it issued Resolution No. 258 on 'Artificial Intelligence: Its Rulings, Guidelines, and Ethics'.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), maqasid al-sharia
candidates.ai_connection: Resolution 258 (26th session, Doha) holds that developing and using AI is permissible (ibahah) subject to ethical and legal conditions on purpose, funding, outcomes, accountability and transparency. It builds on ICESCO's Riyadh Charter. It recommends a dedicated study of whether AI should be granted legal personality, which is an opening for AI moral-status and welfare dialogue, and it calls for specialised symposia. In April 2026 the Secretary-General chaired 'Coexistence in the Age of AI' at the Fez conference on 'The Future of Human Civilization in Light of AI'. These rulings are normative guidance for 57 member states.

candidates.name: Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO): Riyadh Charter on AI and Center of Foresight and Artificial Intelligence
candidates.one_line: OIC agency, roughly the Islamic world's UNESCO. With Saudi Arabia's data and AI authority (SDAIA) it issued the Riyadh Charter on AI Ethics in the Islamic World, and it runs a Center of Foresight and Artificial Intelligence.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic ethics applied to science, education and cultural policy
candidates.ai_connection: The Riyadh Charter (announced at the Global AI Summit in September 2024 and presented to the IIFA in 2025) sets principles including reliability and safety, transparency, accountability, humanity, and social and environmental benefit. ICESCO and SDAIA signed an implementation agreement on 15 December 2025 aiming at a unified AI-governance framework across member states. Its September 2026 statements argue that legislation alone is not enough for AI governance. It is the main intergovernmental channel for Islamic-world AI norms, and a natural counterpart for international AI-safety dialogues.

candidates.name: Muslim World League (MWL)
candidates.one_line: Mecca-based pan-Islamic body with a large scholarly network. In April 2026 it co-organised an international conference in Fez on 'The Future of Human Civilization in Light of Artificial Intelligence'.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic scholarship, interfaith outreach
candidates.ai_connection: The Fez conference, hosted by the Euro-Mediterranean University of Fez, included IIFA's session on 'Coexistence in the Age of AI', which focused on protecting 'human and innate intelligence' and on AI illiteracy. The only evidence found is the IIFA's account of the conference; MWL's own AI programme, if it has one, could not be verified.

candidates.name: Kalam Research & Media (KRM)
candidates.one_line: Muslim think tank founded by theologian Aref Ali Nayed. Its 'AI & Technology' research programme pairs Islamic theologians and philosophers with AI researchers on AI ethics and an 'operational hermeneutics of AI artifacts'.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic theology (kalam), hermeneutics, philosophy of science and complexity, interfaith philosophy
candidates.ai_connection: KRM's programme covers deep learning, NLP, artificial life, complexity, cybernetics and AI ethics. It announced research on 'Artificial Understanding' (2023), published 'Towards an Operational Hermeneutics of AI Artifacts', and in January 2026 co-hosted 'Humanities, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Responsibility' with the University of Guelph's Centre for Advancing Responsible AI. That workshop argued that responsible AI needs 'institutional wisdom', not only compliance. It is one of the few Islamic institutions doing conceptual rather than permissibility-focused AI work.

candidates.name: Al-Mahdi Institute (AMI)
candidates.one_line: Birmingham research institute for Islamic (Shi'i) legal, philosophical and theological studies. It runs seminars and conferences on Islam and AI.
candidates.field_lens: Islamic legal theory (ethical ijtihad), philosophy and theology, sociology of religion
candidates.ai_connection: It hosted 'Islam and Artificial Intelligence' (May 2024), which argued that Islamic epistemology should shape value-aligned AI. With the Catholic University of America's McLean Center it held 'Adaptive Faith: Technology and Religious Change in the Digital Age' (November 2025) on AI, biotech and transhumanism. AMI scholar Ali-reza Bhojani wrote 'Between Fear and Hope: AI ethics in Islamic Thought' (in Ted Peters, ed., The Promise and Peril of AI and IA). It is a small but real Islamic academic node beyond CILE.

candidates.name: World Fellowship of Buddhists (WFB)
candidates.one_line: The oldest international Buddhist federation (founded in Colombo in 1950) with regional centres across Asia and beyond. Its 75th-anniversary General Conference was devoted to AI.
candidates.field_lens: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist institutions; Buddhist ethics of wisdom and well-being
candidates.ai_connection: The 31st General Conference (5-6 December 2025, Vajiravudh College, Bangkok) had the theme 'Cultivating Wisdom and Well-being in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Buddhist Vision for the Future'. No declaration or follow-up programme could be found. This is a federation-level convening capacity across Asian Buddhism that has started on AI but has not yet produced positions.

candidates.name: Toda Peace Institute
candidates.one_line: Peace-research institute founded in 1996 by Soka Gakkai International president Daisaku Ikeda. Its Social Media, Technology and Peacebuilding programme tests AI-enabled deliberative technology in conflict settings.
candidates.field_lens: Nichiren Buddhist humanism (SGI), peace and conflict studies, deliberative democracy
candidates.ai_connection: Its 'Interoperable Deliberative Technology' and 'Deliberative Technologies in Afghanistan' projects tested Pol.is, Talk to the City, Deliberation.io and Crowdsmart. It published an AI-facilitated youth consultation in Yemen's peace process, a study of deliberative tech in the ECOWAS Early Warning network (ECOWARN), and 'Reclaiming Attention: From Digital Conflict to Democratic Dialogue'; the programme lead is Lisa Schirch. This is AI-for-collective-intelligence applied to peacebuilding, from a Buddhist-founded institution. It is also the most concrete AI work traceable to Soka Gakkai, whose own site was down for relaunch.

candidates.name: Shalom Hartman Institute
candidates.one_line: Pluralist Jewish research and education institute. Its 'Artificial Intelligence' strand addresses Jewish ethics, human dignity and the future of humanity.
candidates.field_lens: Jewish philosophy, halakhic ethics, Jewish peoplehood
candidates.ai_connection: In March 2024 it held 'Artificial Intelligence, Jewish Ethics, and the Future of Humanity' with AI researcher Oren Etzioni, Ellen P. Goodman, Orly Lobel and David Zvi Kalman; the framing explicitly included AI threatening humankind. Other pieces: 'Staying Human in the Age of AI' (Kurtzer and Kalman, 2025) and Tomer Persico's 'What the Pope Is Telling Us' (May 2026), which argues that grounding human worth in intelligence would hand AI a greater claim to dignity. It is the strongest Jewish intellectual institution with a standing AI strand.

candidates.name: Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR)
candidates.one_line: The professional body of Reform rabbis (about 2,000 members). It issues formal responsa and runs an ongoing AI series with Sinai and Synapses.
candidates.field_lens: Reform Jewish law (responsa), pastoral practice
candidates.ai_connection: Responsum 5784.2, 'Artificial Intelligence and Authorship', sets disclosure norms when AI 'is the contractor'. The CCAR Journal's Fall 2025 issue was 'AI and the Rabbinate', and its series with Sinai and Synapses includes 'Can AI Develop a N'shamah?' (a soul) and 'When Machines Seem Human: Rethinking Personhood in the Age of AI'. It is a denominational body producing normative guidance on AI personhood and honesty, which bears on AI moral status and on the effects of human-AI relationships.

candidates.name: ADL Center for Technology & Society (CTS)
candidates.one_line: The Anti-Defamation League's tech research centre. It evaluates LLMs, video generators and open-weight models for antisemitic and extremist outputs, and publishes the ADL AI Index.
candidates.field_lens: Extremism and hate monitoring rooted in a Jewish civil-rights organisation; trust and safety
candidates.ai_connection: The ADL AI Index (January 2026) scores leading LLMs on detecting and countering antisemitic and extremist narratives. Other reports: 'The Safety Divide: Open-Source AI Models Fall Short on Guardrails' (December 2025), red-teaming of AI video generators (October 2025), and 'Lost in Translation' (July 2026) on chatbot failures in Persian. This is independent misuse evaluation of the kind AI-safety evals groups do, from a community that has monitored hate for decades.

candidates.name: Lausanne Movement
candidates.one_line: Global evangelical mission network. Its AI topic hub, State of the Great Commission report chapter and Global Analysis briefings shape how evangelical leaders worldwide approach AI.
candidates.field_lens: Evangelical missiology and biblical ethics
candidates.ai_connection: Quintin McGrath's 'AI Ethical Framework' LIGHT briefing (Lausanne Global Analysis, October/November 2025) evaluates AI design and use against biblical ethics and compares the AI ethics of different faith traditions. There is a 'What Does it Mean to Be Human?' AI chapter and a podcast series. Most of the content is about using AI for mission rather than about AI risk, which is itself telling. Reported to be an FLI Religious Projects grantee.

candidates.name: Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission of the Southern Baptist Convention (ERLC)
candidates.one_line: Public-policy arm of the largest US Protestant denomination. It wrote 'Artificial Intelligence: An Evangelical Statement of Principles'.
candidates.field_lens: Evangelical (Baptist) theological anthropology and public policy
candidates.ai_connection: The 2019 statement, from memory: 12 articles covering human dignity, moral agency, medicine, bias, sexuality, work, data, security, war, public policy and the future of AI, signed by more than 60 evangelical leaders. Jason Thacker, who led ERLC's AI work, now contributes to Lausanne. It shapes a large, policy-active US constituency. The site sits behind a Cloudflare bot check and could not be re-read in this pass.

candidates.name: Theos
candidates.one_line: London religion-and-society think tank with an AI research category and senior researchers on technology ethics. Its 20th-anniversary programme in 2026 centres on being human in the age of AI.
candidates.field_lens: Christian theology of culture, public theology, social research
candidates.ai_connection: 2026 events include 'Art, creativity and what it means to be human in the age of AI' at the National Gallery and 'AI & The Future of Being Human' (The Sacred podcast with Jamie Bartlett). Senior researcher Nathan Mladin works on technology ethics and is an associate of the AI Faith & Civil Society Commission. Its research covers big tech and AI. It is a UK policy-literate faith voice on how AI affects relationships and meaning.

candidates.name: Christians for Impact (EA for Christians)
candidates.one_line: The careers-advice arm of Effective Altruism for Christians. It publishes problem profiles, including a full AI Risk report, and runs annual conferences in London and Washington DC with a catastrophic-risk track.
candidates.field_lens: Christian stewardship ethics with EA cause prioritisation
candidates.ai_connection: The AI Risk report (March-April 2025) is a cause-area investigation arguing that advanced AI poses significant risks, with career paths to reduce them, framed through Christian stewardship. The 2026 conferences (DC, November 13-15; London, November 27-29) list catastrophic risks from AI among their core topics. This is one of the very few faith-community bodies that engages AI x-risk directly and sends people into the core field.

candidates.name: Network for Religious and Traditional Peacemakers (Peacemakers Network)
candidates.one_line: Helsinki-based network, with its secretariat at Finn Church Aid, that links religious and traditional peacemakers to formal mediation processes.
candidates.field_lens: Insider mediation, religious peacebuilding, UN conflict-prevention practice
candidates.ai_connection: It co-hosted the 2024 UNGA side event 'Faith, Ethics and AI: Shaping a Future for Global Peace' with the UN Multi-Faith Advisory Council's Peace and Security Working Group. Speakers there covered algorethics, AI in oppressive regimes and inclusive AI data. It is listed as potential: it holds mediation and track-two methods with religious actors that bear directly on AI arms-race de-escalation and US-China confidence-building, but AI is not yet a programme.

candidates.name: Global Ethic Foundation (Stiftung Weltethos)
candidates.one_line: Tübingen foundation carrying forward Hans Küng's Global Ethic project: the 1993 Parliament of the World's Religions declaration of shared ethical principles across traditions. It now runs public programmes on AI and ethics.
candidates.field_lens: Comparative religious ethics, cross-traditional value consensus (Weltethos)
candidates.ai_connection: With the Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart's Academy and Cyber Valley it held 'Herausforderung KI: zwischen Algorithmus und Ethos' (June 2024), with ethicist Peter G. Kirchschläger (who proposes a UN 'International Data-Based Systems Agency') and Islamic theologian Milad Karimi, plus 'Religion & Ethik: KI mit Verantwortung'. Listed as potential: its core method, finding a minimal ethic that many traditions can endorse, is the pluralistic value-specification problem ('aligned to whose values?') at the centre of alignment.

candidates.name: United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW, a CWU branch), with Unite the Union: Google DeepMind recognition campaign
candidates.one_line: UK tech workers' union, a branch of the Communication Workers Union. On 4 May 2026, together with Unite, it asked Google to recognise a union at Google DeepMind UK. Google refused but agreed to talks through ACAS. Members have passed the 10% statutory threshold.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour and collective bargaining; workplace democracy inside a frontier lab
candidates.ai_connection: FRONTIER / LAB-INTERNAL. This is the most direct worker-side lever on a frontier developer found in this sweep. The campaign's three demands are: (1) restore the AI Principles pledges on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, which Google removed; (2) end 'unethical military contracts'; (3) guarantee protection against AI-led redundancies. A recognised union inside a lab could carry safety and ethics clauses, protect whistleblowers through collective agreements, and staff safety committees on the model of health-and-safety reps. UTAW has also published an 'AI Workers' Inquiry' on generative AI and tech work.

candidates.name: Club of Rome: AGI open letter and AI policy
candidates.one_line: Membership organisation of scientists, economists and leaders, best known for 'The Limits to Growth'. On 16 March 2026 it led an open letter, co-signed by Millennium Project director Jerome C. Glenn and 30+ others, calling for a special UN General Assembly session on AGI. It also adopted an AI policy statement in January 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Systems dynamics and limits-to-growth thinking; metacrisis and planetary-boundaries framing; new humanism
candidates.ai_connection: FRONTIER. The letter calls AGI an existential threat and says systems that rewrite their own code could escape human oversight. It calls the new Independent International Scientific Panel on AI necessary but too slow. This is the clearest case of a metacrisis-tradition membership body adopting loss-of-control language. That makes it a natural int/a partner for placing AI risk within polycrisis framings, and it has UN access.

candidates.name: International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW): AI and nuclear weapons work
candidates.one_line: Nobel Peace Prize-winning (1985) federation of national physicians' organisations. It set up an AI and nuclear threat working group at its 24th World Congress (Nagasaki, October 2025) and demands that the nine nuclear-armed states keep AI out of nuclear command and control.
candidates.field_lens: Medicine and public health as a voice on catastrophic risk; the anti-nuclear movement
candidates.ai_connection: FRONTIER. Its focus is AI integrated into nuclear command, control and communications. It took part in the July 2026 Nobel Laureate summit at the Vatican calling for a permanent 'firewall' between AI and nuclear weapons, co-hosted the 'Autonomous Armageddon' webinar (January 2025) with AI-safety experts, and makes submissions to the UN on autonomous weapons. It carries clinicians' moral authority and a model of a professional body campaigning on extinction-level risk.

candidates.name: Society for Risk Analysis (SRA): 'AI for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI' special issue
candidates.one_line: International learned society for risk analysis. Its journal Risk Analysis ran a 2025 special issue, 'Artificial Intelligence for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI', edited by Vicki Bier, Emanuele Borgonovo, Tony Cox and Cynthia Rudin, which includes a risk assessment of AI takeover by Seth Baum.
candidates.field_lens: Quantitative risk analysis and decision science; risk governance and risk communication
candidates.ai_connection: FRONTIER (partial). Risk analysis has mature methods (probabilistic risk assessment, expert elicitation, deep-uncertainty methods) that frontier-AI risk modelling often reinvents. The special issue puts a catastrophic-AI paper (Baum, 2025) in the field's flagship journal, a toehold for AI-safety risk modellers such as SaferAI and CARMA to publish and recruit there. SRA also runs webinars on AI risk, through its Security and Defense specialty group among others.

candidates.name: SAE G-34 / EUROCAE WG-114: Artificial Intelligence in Aviation
candidates.one_line: Joint SAE–EUROCAE standards committee writing certification guidance for machine-learning systems in safety-critical aerospace. Published: AIR6987 (taxonomy) and AIR6988 (statement of concerns). In progress: the ARP6983/ED-324 process standard, AIR8519 (reinforcement-learning gap analysis) and AIR8493 (human-factors concerns). Charter updated October 2025.
candidates.field_lens: Aviation certification and safety-critical systems engineering, in the DO-178C lineage
candidates.ai_connection: ASSURANCE / SAFETY-CRITICAL. This is arguably the most mature effort anywhere to certify learned systems for life-critical use. Its methods (assurance levels, design-assurance processes, gap analysis for RL, human-factors review) are directly relevant to frontier 'safety cases' and assurance arguments, yet almost unknown in the AI-safety community.
candidates.location: Warrendale, PA, USA and Saint-Denis, France

candidates.name: UL Standards & Engagement (ULSE): UL 4600
candidates.one_line: Nonprofit safety-standards developer that publishes UL 4600, the safety-case-based Standard for Evaluation of Autonomous Products, used for example by autonomous-trucking companies to argue real-world safety.
candidates.field_lens: Product-safety standards and safety-case (assurance argument) methodology
candidates.ai_connection: POTENTIAL / ASSURANCE. UL 4600's approach (structured safety cases, safety performance indicators, 'unknown unknowns' handling) is the closest existing standard to the 'frontier AI safety case' idea now discussed by UK AISI and labs. ULSE does not yet publish frontier-AI standards. Note that ULSE is distinct from UL Research Institutes' DSRI, which is already in the roster.

candidates.name: INCOSE Artificial Intelligence Systems Working Group
candidates.one_line: Working group of the International Council on Systems Engineering, founded in 2019 out of its Future of Systems Engineering initiative. It develops 'AI for SE' and 'SE for AI' methods, and its stated objectives include evaluating the safety and security of AI systems and human-AI collaboration.
candidates.field_lens: Systems engineering: requirements, lifecycle assurance, model-based systems engineering
candidates.ai_connection: POTENTIAL. Systems engineering offers lifecycle-wide methods (requirements traceability, verification and validation, emergent-behaviour analysis) for AI embedded in larger sociotechnical systems, a gap in model-centric alignment work. It is chaired by Ali K. Raz.

candidates.name: The Cybernetics Society (UK)
candidates.one_line: UK learned society founded in 1968, which awards MCybS/FCybS professional credentials. Its 2026 annual conference (Loughborough University, 1–3 July) included sessions on 'Ethics and AI', and it runs monthly 'Cybernetics Live' online seminars.
candidates.field_lens: Cybernetics (Ashby, Beer, Pask lineage), organisational cybernetics
candidates.ai_connection: POTENTIAL. Its October 2026 seminar is on Ashby's Law of requisite variety, a core concept for whether human institutions can regulate far more capable AI systems. It engages with AI ethics, but not yet with AI safety or control. It is a low-cost partner for UK-based cybernetics-for-alignment events.

candidates.name: System Dynamics Society (SDS)
candidates.one_line: International society for system dynamics modelling, in the Forrester lineage that produced 'The Limits to Growth'. Its 2026 conference (TU Delft, 20–24 July) was on 'Navigating uncertainty, managing instability and crafting futures together'. Its AI engagement so far is limited to an 'AI in System Dynamics Education' resource.
candidates.field_lens: System dynamics: stock-and-flow and feedback modelling of socio-economic systems
candidates.ai_connection: POTENTIAL (light engagement). Feedback modelling is well suited to AI race dynamics, compute–capability–investment loops, and gradual erosion of human economic and political leverage. No SDS group yet models these. A founder or funder could commission an SDS special interest group or a conference track on AI-transition dynamics.

candidates.name: Human Factors and Ergonomics Society (HFES)
candidates.one_line: US-based learned society for human factors and ergonomics. It has a Human-AI-Robot Teaming technical group, a 2023 policy statement 'Artificial Intelligence Guardrails for Human Use' (alongside earlier statements on AI in health care and on autonomous vehicles), and its 2026 ASPIRE annual meeting placed heavy emphasis on AI. A June 2026 special-issue call covers 'Human Factors in Cognitive Security'.
candidates.field_lens: Human factors engineering: situation awareness, trust calibration, automation complacency, human-systems integration
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT. Human factors science on automation bias, out-of-the-loop problems and 'ironies of automation' bears directly on human oversight of AI and on scalable oversight. HFES has testified to Congress before, on the Boeing 737 MAX. It is the US counterpart of CIEHF, which is already in the roster.

candidates.name: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
candidates.one_line: Standards coalition maintaining the open Content Credentials specification (v2.3) for the origin and edit history of digital media. Its steering committee includes Adobe, Amazon, BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Publicis, Sony, TikTok and Truepic.
candidates.field_lens: Media standards, provenance and authenticity infrastructure
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT. It provides epistemic-security infrastructure, such as labelling AI-generated content, against synthetic-media erosion of shared reality. It is industry-governed, so its value for societal resilience depends on adoption and independent oversight. Civil-society voices are thin on the steering committee.

candidates.name: Nuffield Council on Bioethics
candidates.one_line: Independent UK bioethics council known for public dialogue, citizens' juries and horizon scanning. It published AI-in-healthcare briefings in 2018, but its current priorities (reproduction, mind and brain/neurotechnology, environment and health) do not centre AI.
candidates.field_lens: Bioethics; deliberative public engagement methods
candidates.ai_connection: POTENTIAL (dormant on AI). It has well-tested methods for anticipatory governance of contested technologies, such as its genome-editing and neurotechnology work. These could be applied to frontier AI or digital minds. It has been inactive on AI since 2018, which is itself a gap.

candidates.name: American Psychoanalytic Association: Commission on Artificial Intelligence (APsA CAI)
candidates.one_line: Commission founded and co-chaired by psychoanalyst Todd Essig (William Alanson White Institute), with Amy Levy. It develops psychoanalytically informed responses to AI through the CAI Report (edited by Alexander Stein), 'CAI Conversations' videos, the 'CAI Currents' newsletter, clinician peer groups, and a film, 'Uncharted Territory: Humans and the Rise of AI'.
candidates.field_lens: Psychoanalysis: attachment, fantasy, the unconscious, relational theory
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT. Its central concern is people forming attachments to 'new others' that perform human connection without experiencing it. This is a depth-psychological lens on AI companions, sycophancy and dependence that complements empirical AI-psychological-harm work. It held an 'AI and the Psychoanalytic Future' symposium in May 2025.

candidates.name: British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP)
candidates.one_line: UK membership body for counsellors and psychotherapists. In 2026 it called for clearer AI regulation in mental health in its response to the MHRA consultation (February), reported that nearly half of young adults turn to AI instead of people about mental health (July), and issued guidance on managing anxiety about AI's future (September).
candidates.field_lens: Counselling and psychotherapy; clinical practice standards
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT. It protects human minds from AI used as a stand-in therapist, and it is one of the few professional bodies addressing public 'AI anxiety'. That makes it a candidate partner for the psychological support that AI-safety researchers lack, an int/a gap.

candidates.name: American Psychiatric Association: Committee on Mental Health Information Technology (AI in Psychiatric Care)
candidates.one_line: The US psychiatrists' professional body's AI programme. It publishes clinical AI guidance, an AI-scribe assessment checklist, positions on 'AI prescribing', and a standardised 'facts label' for AI-enabled digital mental-health tools (Frontiers in Psychiatry).
candidates.field_lens: Psychiatry and clinical governance
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT (clinical deployment). The facts label is a transparency template that could be adapted to general-purpose chatbots used for emotional support. It is distinct from the American Psychological Association, which is already in the roster.

candidates.name: American Law Institute (ALI): Principles of the Law, Civil Liability for Artificial Intelligence
candidates.one_line: Project of the ALI, the elite US membership body that drafts Restatements and Principles of law. Its Council approved the project in October 2024 to set out principles, grounded in common-law tort doctrine, for assigning responsibility for harm caused by AI systems.
candidates.field_lens: Common law, tort and products liability; a legal-elite consensus process
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT. Tort liability is a key AI-safety lever: it puts the cost of risk on developers and drives safety investment. ALI Principles carry heavy weight with US courts. AI-safety legal scholars (for example in LawAI or CLAIR circles) could join its Members Consultative Group.

candidates.name: World Academy of Art and Science (WAAS)
candidates.one_line: Global academy of 560+ elected fellows from 90+ countries working on transdisciplinary global challenges. On 3 July 2026 it held the joint symposium 'Synthetic Societies: Human Vulnerability and Systemic Fragility in a Context of Rising Algorithmic Power', and it runs a 'Technology as Force for Good' programme.
candidates.field_lens: Transdisciplinary humanism, human security, global governance
candidates.ai_connection: ADJACENT. The symposium's framing (opaque algorithmic power, systemic fragility, human vulnerability) sits close to gradual-disempowerment concerns. It has no standing AI working group.

candidates.name: Trades Union Congress (TUC): AI (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill
candidates.one_line: UK federation of trade unions. In April 2024 it published a model AI (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill, drafted by Robin Allen KC and Dee Masters (AI Law Consultancy, Cloisters) with a cross-sector advisory committee. The bill provides for Workplace AI Risk Assessments, union consultation rights and enforcement through employment tribunals.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour; employment and equality law
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It is a fully drafted statute for worker-side governance of high-risk AI decision-making. Its combination of pre-deployment risk assessment, transparency duties and collective rights could be extended toward wider deployment-safety obligations.

candidates.name: UNI Global Union (incl. the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators)
candidates.one_line: Global union federation for service sectors. It negotiates sectoral AI agreements (for example the European banking social partners' joint AI declaration, May 2024), presses employers at Davos and the ILO to bargain over AI, and in April 2025 launched the first Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators.
candidates.field_lens: International labour organising; social dialogue and collective bargaining
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI and the AI SUPPLY CHAIN. The content-moderator alliance organises the human layer that filters data and outputs for AI systems, demanding mental-health protocols and accountability; TikTok moderators struck in Berlin in 2025 under the slogan 'We trained your AI – now pay us!'. UNI also supported Blizzard workers in winning AI guardrails in their first union contract (2026).

candidates.name: Writers Guild of America (WGA): AI terms in the 2023 and 2026 MBAs
candidates.one_line: US screenwriters' union. Its 2023 agreement established that AI is not a writer, that writers cannot be required to use AI, and that AI-generated material must be disclosed. The 2026 agreement (2 May 2026 – 1 May 2030) adds written notice to the Guild when studios license writers' work to train generative AI, and a right to discuss compensation.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour; creative-industry collective bargaining
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. These are among the most concrete enforceable worker-side constraints on AI anywhere, and the 2026 clause is a first contractual hook into training-data licensing. They show collective bargaining can shape how AI is deployed, not just how much.

candidates.name: SAG-AFTRA: AI framework and 2026 TV/Theatrical Agreement
candidates.one_line: US performers' union (~160,000 members). Members ratified its 2026 TV/Theatrical Agreement on 4 June 2026 by 91.4%; the agreement adds stringent rules to keep 'synthetic performers' the exception, on top of the 2023 consent and compensation rules for digital replicas. It also lobbies on the NO FAKES Act and California's 2026 law requiring disclosure of AI-generated performances.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour; rights of personality and likeness
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It pioneered consent-based controls on digital replicas of people, a template for protecting human identity and presence against AI substitution. It also models how a membership body can turn public concern into binding contract terms.

candidates.name: AFL-CIO Technology Institute and 'Workers First Initiative on AI'
candidates.one_line: The US labour federation's technology arm. In October 2025 it launched the 'Workers First Initiative on AI' and published 'Artificial Intelligence: Principles to Protect Workers', demanding worker voice in how AI is designed, developed and deployed; President Liz Shuler gave a National Press Club speech on AI in April 2026.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour; industrial policy
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It is the largest US labour coalition explicitly arguing that tech firms 'cannot be trusted to self-regulate' AI. It is a potential mass-membership ally for AI-governance coalitions, though it does not engage with frontier risk.

candidates.name: European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC): AI at work
candidates.one_line: EU-level trade union confederation. In October 2025 it called for a dedicated EU Directive on algorithmic management and AI at work, adopted the resolution 'Artificial Intelligence for Workers, Not Just for Profit' (March 2025), and opposes parts of the AI 'Digital Omnibus' that weaken worker protections.
candidates.field_lens: European social dialogue; labour law
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It is the main worker-side voice in EU AI legislation, including the Quality Jobs Act and its response to the European Parliament's December 2025 report on algorithmic management. It shows how AI Act simplification fights intersect with labour.

candidates.name: Alphabet Workers Union-CWA (AI raters organising)
candidates.one_line: Union of ~1,400 Alphabet employees and contractors, a local of the Communications Workers of America. Since May 2025 it has organised the GlobalLogic 'AI raters' who evaluate Gemini and AI Overviews, and it contested the termination of 200+ rater contractors in September 2025.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour; contractor and 'ghost work' organising
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI / ALIGNMENT DATA. Raters' pay and working conditions shape the quality of human feedback used to align models. Organising this workforce is an under-noticed point of influence over how alignment data is produced.

candidates.name: Data Labelers Association (DLA)
candidates.one_line: Nairobi-based association of data labellers and annotators (878+ members across 3+ countries). It runs job placement, community, mental-wellness support (DLA Health), training (DLA Academy) and policy advocacy (DLA Voice).
candidates.field_lens: Labour organising in the Global South AI supply chain
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI / AI SUPPLY CHAIN. It gives voice to the annotation workforce that produces training and safety data for AI. It complements the Data Workers' Inquiry, already in the roster, with a standing membership body.

candidates.name: Tech Workers Coalition (TWC)
candidates.one_line: All-volunteer, worker-led coalition of tech workers with chapters in the US and Europe, including Berlin. It publishes AI-at-work organising resources ('workersdecide.tech', December 2025) and runs the Circuit Breakers conference (NYC, 17–18 October 2026).
candidates.field_lens: Rank-and-file labour organising
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It is a grassroots pipeline of organised tech workers, including at AI firms, whose collective voice could support internal dissent and whistleblowing on unsafe deployment.

candidates.name: AFT National Academy for AI Instruction
candidates.one_line: National AI training hub for educators launched in July 2025 by the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers, with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic as partners. The AFT describes it as 'grounded in safety, and people-first technology'.
candidates.field_lens: Organised labour (teachers); professional development
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It is the most prominent case of frontier labs funding a union's AI capacity. That makes it a test case for whether labour–lab partnerships build worker counter-power or co-opt it, and a model others may copy.

candidates.name: ILO Decent Work in the Platform Economy Convention (C193, 2026)
