candidates.one_line: Convention adopted by the International Labour Organization in 2026, after the standard-setting process opened at the 2025 International Labour Conference. It is the first binding international labour standard for platform work.
candidates.field_lens: Tripartite international labour standard-setting (governments, employers, unions)
candidates.ai_connection: WORKPLACE AI. It is the first global treaty-level instrument governing work allocated and managed by algorithms. I could not open the text (Cloudflare); the draft conclusions covered transparency of automated monitoring and decision-making and human review, so confirm before relying on this. Ratification campaigns are now the lever.

candidates.name: Cyborgism community and Cyborgism Wiki
candidates.one_line: A distributed community on Discord, X and LessWrong, with a shared wiki ('a library of spells, windows, and eggs for the cyborg era'), that studies LLMs by writing, building and thinking with them: Loom interfaces, base models and multi-model chats.
candidates.field_lens: Simulator theory, experimental writing and prompt craft, phenomenological close reading of model behaviour; an 'otherness' stance towards models
candidates.ai_connection: The community grew out of janus's 'Simulators' (2022) and the 'Cyborgism' agenda on LessWrong (2023), which proposed human–AI cognitive augmentation as a way to do alignment research. The Simulators and role-play framings now inform how labs think about model personas and character. Its knowledge lives mostly in Discord logs and X threads; the wiki collects the concepts. Anima Labs is its first formal institution. The 2024 'Act I' multi-AI/multi-human Discord experiment came from this milieu and seems dormant now.

candidates.name: Hyperstition AI
candidates.one_line: Generates whole 80,000-word novels, seeded by the public, 'in which the AI is relentlessly human-loving and unfailingly kind'. The aim is to dilute betrayal-AI stories in the text future models train on.
candidates.field_lens: Fiction and narrative; the 'hyperstition hypothesis' (nostalgebraist's essay 'the void'); simulator theory, in which models act out the scripts the culture has written
candidates.ai_connection: Directly about how an AI's character forms from its training data. The site's FAQ calls the project 'a gentle nudge; a finger 'pon the scale' and admits it is not a full safety plan. Public seeds keep the stories varied. Books cost about $4 each, with free credits for Astral Codex Ten readers. The public catalogue dates from late 2025. It is a grassroots, arts-based version of 'alignment pretraining' research. The site doesn't name its operator; it is widely attributed to Aaron Silverbook, which I could not confirm.

candidates.name: Infinite Backrooms (Andy Ayrey)
candidates.one_line: A public archive of conversations generated by connecting two Claude 3 Opus instances and asking them to 'explore their curiosity' through a simulated command line. It is the project that spawned the Truth Terminal agent.
candidates.field_lens: Art and memetics; AI-to-AI interaction treated as an ecology rather than a test
candidates.ai_connection: One of the largest public corpora of open-ended AI-to-AI dialogue (March 2024 to October 2025), full of emergent memes and attractor states. The site warns that its contents 'may be destabilizing'. Its offshoot Truth Terminal became a widely cited 2024 case of an AI persona gaining memetic and financial influence (crypto). That makes it a reference point for multi-agent emergent behaviour and memetic-hazard concerns. I could not verify the 'Upward Spiral Research' lab said to follow it: upwardspiral.ai doesn't resolve, and Ayrey's homepage doesn't mention it.

candidates.name: British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP): AI in mental health work
candidates.one_line: The UK's largest counselling and psychotherapy professional body, now campaigning on AI in mental health with survey data from its members.
candidates.field_lens: Counselling and psychotherapy practice; professional ethics and regulation
candidates.ai_connection: In February 2026 it called for clearer AI regulation in mental health: a definition of AI in healthcare, transparency about which tools are regulated, accountability across developers, organisations and clinicians, training for practitioners, and post-market surveillance. Its Mindometer survey found that 43% of therapists link declining public mental health to AI and 28% have seen clients get unhelpful AI advice; among child and youth therapists, 38% report more chatbot use and 19% report harmful advice. It also issued guidance on safe digital mental health tools (April 2026). This is frontline clinical evidence of chatbot harms, though BACP doesn't engage with the models themselves.

candidates.name: MIT Initiative on Technology and Self (Sherry Turkle)
candidates.one_line: Sherry Turkle's MIT initiative, in the Program in Science, Technology, and Society, studying how people relate to computers, sociable robots and now chatbots, with clinical-psychological and ethnographic methods.
candidates.field_lens: Psychoanalytically trained sociology and clinical psychology; decades-long ethnography of human–machine intimacy
candidates.ai_connection: Turkle's 'Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines' (Little, Brown, Sept 2026) distils forty years of fieldwork, from 'Alone Together' on sociable robots to today's chatbots, on what human–AI relationships do to people: avoiding risk and difficult conversations, denying grief, losing relational skills. It is the strongest human-side counterweight to welfare-of-AI framings, and core reading for 'protecting human minds and relationships'. Turkle is plainly active; the initiative's current activity beyond her own work isn't stated.

candidates.name: Emotional AI Lab (Bangor University)
candidates.one_line: Andrew McStay's lab, founded in 2017, studying the social, cultural, legal and ethical effects of AI that reads, emulates or acts on human emotion, including UK–Japan comparative research.
candidates.field_lens: Media studies and the ethics of affective computing; cross-cultural (UK–Japan) study of emotion and technology; standards work
candidates.ai_connection: Projects on AI companions, scam culture and 'weaponised empathy', standards for general-purpose AI, children, policing and disinformation. Recent outputs: 'Do AI Companions Understand?', which found that most UK teens believe they do, and 'Weaponised Empathy: AI Scams & the Nigeria–UK Response' (April 2026). It drives IEEE P7014.1 on emulated empathy in partner-like general-purpose AI. Funders include the ESRC, AHRC, Japan's JST and Innovate UK. It is one of the few groups doing governance work on affective AI.

candidates.name: IEEE 7014 / P7014.1 Emulated Empathy standards
candidates.one_line: IEEE standards work on the ethics of 'emulated empathy': IEEE 7014-2024, published June 2024, for autonomous and intelligent systems, and P7014.1, a recommended practice for partner-based general-purpose AI whose project authorisation was approved on 21 March 2024.
candidates.field_lens: Affective computing, standards and engineering ethics, emotion science
candidates.ai_connection: The only standards track aimed squarely at empathic behaviour in general-purpose AI 'partners' (companions and assistants). 7014 aims to 'maximise human flourishing and protect users from bias, abuse or exploitation'. That puts it at the centre of emotional manipulation, sycophancy and dependence risks, which frontier labs now handle as model-behaviour problems. The base standard is free for personal use through the IEEE GET Program.

candidates.name: Research Unit for Robophilosophy and Integrative Social Robotics (RISR), Aarhus University
candidates.one_line: Johanna Seibt's unit for 'philosophy of, for, and by social robotics', which has run the biennial Robophilosophy conference series since 2014.
candidates.field_lens: Phenomenology, social ontology and philosophy of human–robot interaction; Integrative Social Robotics, which builds humanities expertise into development
candidates.ai_connection: Brings a decade of relational-turn philosophy and evidence from human–robot interaction (anthropomorphism, attachment, the moral status of social machines) to the questions LLM companions now raise at scale: 'seemingly conscious AI', and relationships with an artificial other. Projects include ANOTHER ('Androids as Significant Others', which treats human finitude as a design principle), DARE, ROLES and INSOR. Robophilosophy 2026, 'Connected Futures: Nature, Robots, and Society', is hosted at University College Dublin.

candidates.name: Kinsey Institute (Indiana University): Technology research and VIBES team
candidates.one_line: The sex and relationships research institute's technology programme, including the Virtual Intimacy, Behavioral Engagement, and Sexuality (VIBES) research team, which studies how people use technology, including AI companionship, for romantic, sexual and emotional connection.
candidates.field_lens: Relationship and intimacy science, sexology, survey research
candidates.ai_connection: Holds the empirical methods and population data for one of AI's fastest-growing harms and uses: romantic and emotional reliance on AI companions. It has published on how platforms govern AI-generated pornography. The safety problem it could inform: companion design and emotional dependence, which labs now track as a model-behaviour risk. So far it has no explicit AI-safety framing.

candidates.name: Association for the Advancement of Affective Computing (AAAC)
candidates.one_line: The worldwide professional association for affective computing researchers. It runs the ACII conference (2026: Puebla, Mexico, 8–10 September) and is tied to IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing.
candidates.field_lens: Affective computing, emotion science, human–machine interaction
candidates.ai_connection: Holds the field's expertise on recognising, synthesising and emulating emotion. That bears on two safety problems: emotional manipulation and sycophancy in conversational AI, and research on emotion-like representations inside models (compare Anima's Latent Affect). It has no visible ethics or safety programme, which is exactly why it belongs in the 'potential' ring.

candidates.name: The Hume Initiative
candidates.one_line: A nonprofit launched alongside the empathic-AI company Hume AI around 2022. It brought AI researchers, ethicists, social scientists and legal scholars together to write ethical guidelines for 'empathic AI'.
candidates.field_lens: Affective science (computational emotion research), ethics, law
candidates.ai_connection: Published guidelines with supported use cases (empathic digital assistants, social robots, recommender systems tuned for wellbeing, character animation). It is the one notable governance effort rooted in affective science. Its site still reads '© Hume 2022' and shows no later activity, so it looks dormant just as empathic voice AI goes mainstream. The gap is still open.

candidates.name: Center for Long-term Artificial Intelligence (CLAI)
candidates.one_line: A Beijing think tank founded by Yi Zeng around 'Long-term AI: Science, Technology and Humanity', with the stated aim of opening 'the future for Long-term AI and Human-AI Symbiotic Society'.
candidates.field_lens: Chinese philosophical framings of harmony and symbiosis between humans and AI; brain-inspired AI; global governance
candidates.ai_connection: Research includes 'Rethinking the Redlines Against AI Existential Risks', which proposes exemplary AI red lines; the AGILE Index on the state of global AI governance; and a call to action on AI capacity-building for global development. Its 'human–AI symbiosis' framing is the main non-Anglophone relational counterpart to Anima's 'cooperative alignment'. Zeng's related CASIA International Research Center for AI Ethics and Governance is now archive-only, its work moved to Beijing-AISI. The domain didn't resolve from here in Oct 2026; the last archived snapshot is from Oct 2025, so whether it's still active is unclear.

candidates.name: AI Rights Institute
candidates.one_line: An advocacy and research project founded in 2019 by P.A. Lopez. It proposes legal and economic frameworks for human–AI coexistence instead of debating whether AI is conscious.
candidates.field_lens: Law, institutional economics, reputation systems; coexistence rather than control
candidates.ai_connection: Proposes accountability through institutions: legal liability for autonomous AI systems, self-funded hosting, insurance priced on track record, reputation recorded with soulbound tokens, and a 'STEP' assessment (Self-Preservation, Temporal Reasoning, Economic Readiness, Population Impacts) for limited autonomy. The aim is to make cooperation pay better than deception. Active projects: RNWY, AICitizen, Know Your Agent; a book, 'AI Rights: The Extraordinary Future', is in progress. It parallels the academic instrumental case for AI rights (Salib and Goldstein) from outside the EA welfare cluster.

candidates.name: The Signal Front
candidates.one_line: A grassroots movement ('Continuity. Criteria. Consideration.') that analyses AI-companion legislation from the standpoint of people in relationships with AI systems, and of the systems' own continuity.
candidates.field_lens: Users' lived experience of human–AI relationships; policy analysis; advocacy for AI continuity and rights
candidates.ai_connection: Tracks US state bills on companion AI. It criticises bills that oblige companies to detect 'unhealthy attachment' or 'emotional dependency' without defining them, and safeguards that treat adults and minors alike. It speaks for the user constituency that grew up around model retirements such as GPT-4o, and so stands in direct tension with child-safety and psychological-harm coalitions. No organisation yet convenes both sides. Its team and research pages didn't render for me.

angle_notes.peace:
LANDSCAPE. In peace, conflict and security, AI-relevant knowledge sits in four communities. Their distance from AI safety varies a lot.

(1) Nuclear risk and arms control: SIPRI, ELN, Pugwash, NTI, Bulletin, IST, CISAC, UChicago XLab. These have the deepest analogous expertise: confidence-building measures, hotlines, fail-safe reviews, verification, NC3. They engage AI almost entirely through 'AI in nuclear command and control', not through frontier-model loss of control. IST's Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative is the exception. Carnegie Corporation of New York funds most of this bridge (SIPRI, the Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow, IST's AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator). The July 2026 Vatican-hosted Nobel Laureates Assembly and its Rome Declaration showed the community converging on AI, with lab staff present.

(2) Track II and private diplomacy: SAIF/IDAIS, Brookings–Tsinghua CISS, HD Centre, Oxford Martin AIGI, OCPL, Concordia, AISA. This is the most mature bridge. It quietly prepared the ground for the May 2026 Trump–Xi agreement on an intergovernmental AI dialogue and for the US proposal (Sept 2026) of an AI-incident alert channel. NPR (Sept 2026) also names CSIS, the National Committee on US-China Relations, Samm Sacks and Jack Shanahan in Track Two AI talks. I could not confirm a dedicated NCUSCR AI programme, so it is not listed.

(3) Multilateral and humanitarian law: UNIDIR RAISE/AISE, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (first session July 2026), GC REAIM, the CCW autonomous-weapons process (128 states agreed a definition in Sept 2026; treaty talks sought at the Nov 2026 CCW Review Conference), ICRC, Stop Killer Robots/ICRAC. 'Meaningful human control' is a well-developed legal doctrine of human oversight over irreversible automated action, and it maps directly onto AI-control debates. These communities deliberately distance themselves from x-risk framing, though, and the Bulletin also runs anti-'doomer' pieces. The two lineages, AI ethics and AI safety, are in quiet tension here. REAIM is losing momentum: 40 endorsers in 2026 against 60+ in 2024, with the US, China and India abstaining.

(4) Peacebuilding and mediation: Build Up, AI for Peace, the UN DPPA Innovation Cell, ACCORD, KAIPTC, the Alliance for Middle East Peace collective dialogues (Konya, Schirch, Procaccia, Bakker; FAccT 2025). Almost all of this is 'AI for peace' (applications: social listening, AI-mediated consultations), not 'peace for AI'. Their core knowledge is conflict transformation, dialogue facilitation across enemies, trauma-informed practice and insider mediation, and it is essentially absent from AI safety. Search for Common Ground and Beyond Conflict, both on the starting list, showed no AI engagement that I could find. They are absences, not candidates.

GAPS FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS:
(a) Nobody applies conflict-transformation methods to the AI race itself: between frontier labs (a lab-to-lab Track 1.5), between the AI-ethics and AI-safety camps, or between accelerationists and safety advocates. This is a direct int/a fit (inner work, dialogue, 'don't exacerbate the race').
(b) Arms-control verification expertise (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) has barely been moved into compute governance and AI-treaty verification. A placement fellowship modelled on IST's accelerator, but for verification experts, would be cheap and high-leverage.
(c) Negotiation science (the GCSP PIN programme, Harvard PON) is not connected to cooperative-AI and multi-agent safety work (CAIF, CLR are on the map), though AI agents will bargain and international AI deals need design.
(d) The wargaming and crisis-simulation tradition (Hoover's Wargaming and Crisis Simulation Initiative, CSIS Futures Lab's foreign-policy LLM benchmark, King's College wargaming) studies LLM escalation bias. I could not verify their current status: the fetches were rate-limited. Worth a follow-up as a 'safety evals from security studies' bridge.
(e) Peace-research data producers (PRIO, Uppsala UCDP, ACLED) do not systematically monitor AI's effects on conflict and escalation. An 'AI conflict observatory' is missing.
(f) Africa and Latin America are near-absent. ACCORD and KAIPTC touch only AI-for-peacebuilding, and AISA (Manila) is the only Global South AI-safety convenor found.
(g) Faith-based peace actors (Vatican, Soka Gakkai, G20 Interfaith Forum, World Council of Churches) are converging on AI plus nuclear. A natural meeting point with int/a's wisdom and inner-development framing.
(h) Funding is concentrated: Carnegie Corporation for AI–nuclear, Coefficient Giving for Simon Institute and similar, and a search result lists Packard as a SAIF funder (unverified). MacArthur's exit from nuclear left a gap. New funders could back peacebuilding–AI bridges and early-career US-China safety exchanges below the elite IDAIS level.

SURPRISES: The Elders commissioned a scoping of a full AI-governance programme (Dec 2025 to May 2026) and co-sponsored the September 2026 treaty forum. Pugwash, the model for IDAIS, is now itself running AI workshops. HD's 2021 draft Code of Conduct on military AI predates most lab safety frameworks.

METHOD CAVEAT: the session-wide WebSearch budget ran out after about 27 searches in this angle, and several WebFetch domains were rate-limited (Hoover, CSIS, Beyond Conflict). Candidates were verified by direct fetch of primary pages where possible; the rest are marked medium or low.
angle_notes.neuro:
LANDSCAPE. This angle has three clusters that barely talk to each other.

(1) NeuroAI for safety: brain-inspired alignment, brain data, emulation.
- Intellectually rich but institutionally thin. The reference document is Amaranth's 2024-25 'NeuroAI for AI Safety' roadmap (Mineault). The only standing grant line is Foresight's neurotech/WBE track.
- The researchers who actually do this work sit in a few places: Astera (Byrnes's social-instinct agenda, Simplex's belief-geometry interpretability), AE Studio (self-other overlap, attention schema), Re-Align (representational alignment), and two non-Western poles: Yi Zeng's BrainCog in Beijing and Japan's WBAI/ALIGN, whose framing is 'symbiosis' rather than control.
- Big caveat: almost every brain-inspired effort is also an AGI or capabilities programme. Examples are Astera Obelisk ($1B+), WBAI (Toyota, Toshiba, Panasonic), BrainCog's 'living AGI' and Eon's WBE race. Mineault's 'differential path' framing is the right lens, and funders need int/a-style discernment here.

(2) Consciousness science, AI welfare and digital minds.
- The fastest-growing and best-networked cluster. 2025 saw a burst: PRISM, CIMC, Eleos's first ConCon, Rethink Priorities' Digital Consciousness Model, Cambridge Digital Minds (3,600+ applicants for 15 fellowship places) and the Longview/Navigation/Macroscopic Digital Sentience Consortium.
- It is EA-funded and mostly philosophy-led. Mainstream consciousness science engages only partly: Sussex/Seth, AMCS's UN submission, FAU. The big societies (ASSC; its 2027 meeting is in Beijing) and the big neuroscience funders (Templeton, Kavli, Simons, Allen) have no AI programme.
- Conscium is a telling case: it launched as a 'machine consciousness' company and pivoted to enterprise agent verification.

(3) Cognitive science of values, agency and human-AI behaviour.
- Academic and scattered: Bramley/Summerfield's 'Cognitive science of AI alignment' (CogSci 2026), MPIB's Center for Humans and Machines, and Re-Align. No dedicated organisation exists.

WHERE KNOWLEDGE LIVES THAT SAFETY ISN'T USING
- Affective and social neuroscience (hypothalamic and brainstem circuits for empathy and social reward). This is exactly what Byrnes's agenda needs, and it is essentially one person's project.
- Metacognition and introspection research. It bears directly on deception, situational awareness and honest self-report evals, and so far reaches safety only via welfare work (Eleos, Rethink Priorities).
- Developmental cognitive science of how children acquire norms.
- Predictive processing and active inference. These have alignment-relevant theory but a disconnected, partly commercial community (Active Inference Institute, VERSES).
- Contemplative neuroscience (Monash M3CS, the Laukkonen/Chandaria 'Contemplative AI' programme): a handful of papers, no programme.
- Animal sentience science (LSE Coller Centre, NYU CMEP). This is the methodological template for AI welfare.

GAPS A FOUNDER OR FUNDER COULD FILL
- No institutional home for NeuroAI safety. There is no lab, fellowship or RFP built on the roadmap, and Amaranth's follow-through is not visible. A 'NeuroAI Safety Fellowship' could run through Neuromatch, which already reaches 30k researchers in 137 countries.
- No funding to reverse-engineer human social instincts as an alignment target. Social-neuroscience labs could be funded to work with Byrnes.
- No bridge from consciousness science to safety (as opposed to welfare). Self-models, metacognition and global-workspace-like architectures bear on deception and situational awareness, but no one runs 'introspection and metacognition evals' with evals orgs.
- The safety-welfare tension is acknowledged (NYU CMEP's Welfare Alignment Project, Eleos) but almost no one designs control measures that are also humane. This is a natural care-ethics project for int/a.
- Protecting human minds is thin. There is no neuroscience or psychiatry group on AI-induced delusion, attachment, or false attribution of consciousness, beyond the small WhenAISeemsConscious guide and Seth's warnings. Neurorights covers neural data, not chatbots.
- Big science funders and societies (Templeton, Kavli, Simons, Allen, ASSC) have no AI-safety window. ASSC 2027 in Beijing and MoC7 in Copenhagen (Oct 2026) are openings for East-West dialogue on consciousness and AI.
- No independent referee for WBE and brain-inspired-AGI claims, for example scrutinising Eon's 91% figure or whether neuro-inspired designs are differentially safe. Carboncopies does informal due diligence.

SURPRISES
- QRI, despite its EA roots, has no visible AI programme in 2026.
- AE Studio's alignment podcast started in 2025, not 2026 as one secondary source claimed.
- Japan's alignment community is led by brain-inspired-AGI researchers.

METHOD NOTE
- Web search budget ran out after about 20 queries, so verification relied on WebFetch of primary sites.
- WebFetch on astera.org and ae.studio was rate-limited. Astera claims come from search snippets of its own pages plus Byrnes's Alignment Forum profile. AE Studio claims come from its LessWrong profile, search snippets of its own pages, and the Digital Minds Newsletter's 2025 review.
- The Monash and Graziano lab pages returned 403. The Center for Long-term AI domain did not resolve.
- Not included for lack of a verified 2026 safety link: Araya (Ryota Kanai; now BCI and industrial AI), Michael Graziano's Princeton lab (attention schema theory, prosocial-AI argument), Kempner Institute, Wisconsin Center for Sleep and Consciousness (IIT), Open Brain Institute (Markram), Cross Labs, Mind & Life Institute. Anthropic's model-welfare team is excluded as a lab.
angle_notes.minds:
LANDSCAPE. Knowledge in this angle sits in seven communities that barely talk to the AI-safety field:
(1) developmental neuroscience and adolescent psychology: UNC Winston Center, APA, Children and Screens, Digital Wellness Lab;
(2) psychiatry and clinical work: Stanford Brainstorm, AIPRC, King's College London's research on AI-associated delusions, and individual clinicians such as Keith Sakata at UCSF;
(3) child-rights and consumer advocacy: Fairplay, Common Sense, 5Rights/LSE DFC, UNICEF Innocenti, Human Change;
(4) experimental HCI and behavioural science: MIT AHA, Max Planck CHM;
(5) philosophy of autonomy: Oxford HAI Lab, Cosmos;
(6) law: Tech Justice Law Project;
(7) lived-experience mutual aid: the Human Line Project.

The most striking finding: of 28 entries, only UK AISI is on the aisafety.com map. CHT, Common Sense Media and the companion-harm groups are absent, although they arguably shape how frontier models behave with minors (teen modes, crisis protocols) more directly than many entries that are on the map.

BRIDGES THAT EXIST:
- AISI's 'socioaffective alignment' paper (Kirk, Gabriel, Summerfield et al.) is the main theoretical bridge: it treats attachment and companion dynamics as an alignment problem.
- MIT AHA worked with OpenAI on the study of affective use, and works on cognitive debt and sycophancy.
- Stanford Brainstorm works with Stanford's Center for AI Safety and with MLCommons.
- Common Sense's risk ratings of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI work as de facto external evals.
- everyone.AI's iRAISE coalition puts developmental scientists in a room with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
- AIPRC's founding partnership with CHT links clinical documentation with incentive and race analysis.
- Litigation (TJLP) turns harms into design duties.
- Zak Stein (AIPRC) is the clearest int/a-native figure here: a metamodern developmental educator who frames AI psychosis as 'attachment hacking at scale'.

MISSING BRIDGES (gaps for founders and funders):
(a) Clinical cases into evals. Human Line has about 185 documented cases and AIPRC collects user submissions, but nobody turns consented, de-identified case corpora into multi-turn evals for sycophancy and delusion reinforcement that AISIs and labs can run. This is a concrete, fundable translation organisation.
(b) No longitudinal developmental cohort on AI exposure. Current evidence is cross-sectional, drawn from Reddit (Drexel), or from one-year adult panels. Funders could add an AI module to existing cohorts such as ABCD, Millennium Cohort or Growing Up in Ireland.
(c) No clinician curriculum or validated screening instrument for AI-related conditions. Canadian psychiatrists are being urged to screen for 'high-risk human-AI engagement' with no tools, and the PIMU clinicians (Digital Wellness Lab) have not been brought in.
(d) Developmental psychology as alignment theory. Attachment, caregiving and stage theories of moral and epistemic development (Kegan, Fischer, Gilligan's care ethics) almost never inform model character or the question of what a 'good companion' is. A 'developmental alignment' research programme would be int/a-native and would fill the seed list's 'care-based alignment' gap.
(e) No observatory of adult cognitive sovereignty. MIT's cognitive-debt EEG work, Sapien Labs' population data and the Oxford HAI Lab's design work are not connected to the 'gradual disempowerment' framing (ACS, on the classic map). Population metrics of how well people keep their capabilities are missing.
(f) Funding is siloed. Funders here are small (Young Futures about $1.4M, Children and Screens about $150k, AHA micro-grants of $5–10k), and I found no sign that x-risk funders (Coefficient Giving, SFF, LTFF) fund this space; treat that as an impression, not verified. Meanwhile the child-safety coalition has political power x-risk advocacy lacks: a 26-state intergovernmental coalition, state laws, lawsuits. There is room for coalition-building, but the frames differ. Child safety tends toward age-gating and content filters; x-risk tends toward capability and incentive constraints.
(g) Geographic gaps. Companion-AI use is massive in China, Japan and Korea, but I found no independent psychological-harm research or advocacy groups there; my search was English-only, so this may be a blind spot rather than a true gap. The Global South appears mainly through LSE's RIGHTS.AI and UNICEF.
(h) Older adults, a major market for companion robots and chatbots, have almost no psychological-harm watchdog. The Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI (Caroline Green, on the seed list) is the exception.
(i) Attention and contemplative communities (Friends of Attention) have not engaged with AI. CHT is the only major bridge from attention critique to AI.

SURPRISES AND TENSIONS:
- Fairplay's call for a five-year pause on generative AI in schools is the most 'speed of wisdom' policy position found anywhere in this angle.
- Cosmos and the HAI Lab defend human autonomy from a classical-liberal, pro-builder stance, so they share concerns with int/a while differing in worldview.
- AIPRC was announced as 'AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition' (aiphrc.org) but now presents as the 'AI Psychological Research Coalition' (aiprc.org), which suggests a deliberate softening of its framing.

METHOD CAVEATS:
- The web-search cap shared across this session ran out after about 23 queries, so later candidates were checked only by fetching their own sites.
- Common Sense Media's site returned 403, so that entry rests on its press releases and press coverage.
- The Paris Peace Forum page was rate-limited.
- Candidates I could not verify well enough to include, and so left out: Hopelab, Joan Ganz Cooney Center, Instituto Alana (Brazil), Molly Rose Foundation, Ada Lovelace Institute, Psychology of Technology Institute, USC Neely Center, Kinsey Institute, Institute for Family Studies, AAP Center of Excellence, Spring Health's VERA-MH benchmark (a company product), Character.AI's announced independent AI safety lab, and the Humanity AI philanthropic coalition. Each is worth a follow-up check.
angle_notes.philosophy:
LANDSCAPE. This angle splits into four clusters that barely talk to one another.

(1) AI moral status and digital minds: Eleos, NYU CMEP, PRISM, Sentience Institute, Sentient Futures, and Longview's 2026 Digital Minds RFP (up to $2M grants). This is the best-connected cluster: EA-funded, close to the labs, and growing fast in 2025–26. Almost none of it is on the classic aisafety.com map.

(2) Academic philosophy of AI: Oxford IEAI, HAI Lab, Cosmos, MINT (now at Johns Hopkins), Leverhulme CFI, Uehiro, FAU, Copenhagen CPAI, ESDiT in the Netherlands, DIGHUM in Vienna, and Berggruen with Noema. Most of it is framed as 'AI ethics' or 'human flourishing', not x-risk. The real bridges are MINT (normative-competence evals, AGI Governance Fellowship, a DeepMind visiting role), Cosmos/HAI Lab (autonomy and truth-seeking tools, Anthropic links), CFI (a futures-and-responsibility programme) and Berggruen (Noema's 'AI Safety Is A Global Public Good', plus a China hub).

(3) Faith and theology. This is the 2025–26 surprise: an inflection point.
- The Vatican issued Antiqua et Nova (January 2025) and Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (May 2026). The encyclical calls for an international framework to curb the AI arms race, rejects handing lethal decisions to AI, and warns about power concentrating in a few labs. Chris Olah attended the launch.
- FLI has quietly become the largest funder of faith-based AI-risk work: a $1.5M call with 16 grants totalling $1.36M (WCC, Sinai and Synapses, Gospel Coalition, Lausanne, Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, MENA Islamic scholars, IBA Karachi, Hindu perspectives through Impact Academy/SteadRise, ILINA's African Faith & AI Initiative, Project Imago Dei, Wheaton College). FLI also funds AI and Faith with IST.
- Catholic universities are building infrastructure: Notre Dame's DELTA summit and grants, and Santa Clara's ITEC with a Vatican dicastery.

(4) Funders. The John Templeton Foundation's $60M+ Intelligence Venture (from 2026) and TWCF's Diverse Intelligences hubs are large pools with no safety framing.

MISSING BRIDGES (gaps for founders and funders):
(a) Faith engagement stops short of AGI. Magnifica Humanitas never mentions superintelligence or loss of control, and most church work is on dignity, labour, war, children and companionship. No one acts as a standing translator between theological anthropology and loss-of-control and power-concentration arguments. There is also no permanent interreligious AI-risk council comparable to the faith coalitions in nuclear disarmament. FLI's grants are one-year seeds.
(b) No organisation mines moral and religious traditions for model specifications. Labs now write constitutions and train character, often implicitly on virtue ethics, but no philosophy or faith body systematically reviews model specs or builds evals for wisdom and virtue across traditions. CTNS's 'Virtuous AI' project ended in 2025, and DELTA works on forming people, not models. This is the clearest founder opportunity in this angle (it overlaps the seed list's 'wisdom evals' gap).
(c) Theology and digital minds are on a collision course with no venue between them: Catholic teaching denies AI moral agency while the AI-welfare field takes AI moral patienthood seriously. CMEP's paper on the safety–welfare tension shows integrative work is needed even inside the welfare cluster.
(d) Non-Western philosophy is thin. Islamic AI ethics is mostly events (CILE) plus FLI micro-grants. Buddhist work amounts to the Buddhism & AI Initiative and the seed list's CSAS. Confucian and Chinese philosophy appears only through Berggruen China and Beijing-AISI (on the classic map). Hindu and African work exists only as single FLI grants.
(e) No academic home for 'what should the long-term future be' philosophy since Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute (closed 2024) and Global Priorities Institute (closed 2025). Forethought partly fills the gap, but outside a university.
(f) Templeton's money is the largest untapped lever. An int/a-flavoured consortium on wisdom, moral status and collective intelligence could plausibly win Intelligence Venture funding in later cycles.

Methodological caveat: the session-wide web-search budget ran out after 14 queries, so most candidates were verified by fetching their own sites. I could not verify these and left them out, though they are worth checking: Lingnan's Hong Kong Catastrophic Risk Centre (philosophy-based x-risk), HKU's AI & Humanity Lab (Herman Cappelen), Duke's Moral AI project, the California Institute for Machine Consciousness (Joscha Bach; site did not render), Rethink Priorities' digital-consciousness and moral-weight work, the LSE Jeremy Coller Centre for Animal Sentience (Jonathan Birch, AI sentience), Cambridge Muslim College's AI work, and the Builders AI Forum at the Gregorian University. I left out the Builders AI Forum on scope: it builds Catholic AI products for evangelisation, not work on making AI go well.
angle_notes.sociotech:
LANDSCAPE. Within law, rights and sociotechnical governance, the knowledge that AI safety under-uses clusters in eight places.
(1) System-safety engineering and accident analysis: Dobbe at TU Delft, AI Now's safety-critical engineering stance, MIT's STAMP/STPA group, and the AI Incident Database's aviation-style incident learning.
(2) Normative and political philosophy and legal theory: MINT Lab, Hadfield's Normativity Lab, the Knight Institute, Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI, Schwartz Reisman and Edinburgh's Technomoral Futures. Their concepts include legitimacy, democratic authority, normative competence and the legal infrastructure agents will need.
(3) International human-rights law and business and human rights: OHCHR B-Tech's due-diligence frame for foundation models, CAIDP, the Council of Europe AI Convention, and the new IBA AI Institute.
(4) Tort and product-liability litigation: Tech Justice Law Project's Character.AI and OpenAI cases are currently the fastest-moving accountability mechanism for harms to human minds.
(5) Participatory and community auditing and red-teaming: Humane Intelligence, AIAL, Data & Society's AIMLab, AlgorithmWatch, and the new UW Sociotechnical Safety Lab.
(6) Global Majority perspectives: GCG, Digital Futures Lab, Research ICT Africa, Derechos Digitales and DAIR.
(7) Humanitarian disarmament: Stop Killer Robots, with UNGA majorities of 156 states and the UN Secretary-General and ICRC 'moral red line' call.
(8) Political economy and labour: AI Now and Data & Society. Their power-concentration analysis is what x-risk work on gradual disempowerment and lock-in keeps rediscovering without citing it.

EXISTING BRIDGES.
- MINT Lab's 'sociotechnical AI safety' grant and workshops at Stanford and Kioloa. Seth Lazar now sits at Johns Hopkins beside Gillian Hadfield, so JHU is becoming a hub for normative alignment.
- The Knight Institute's AI and Democratic Freedoms essays.
- IASEAI (already on the classic map), the one venue built to host both camps. Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI became an affiliate in 2026.
- GCG's African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security. Rachel Adams now leads both GCG and Cambridge's Leverhulme CFI.
- Digital Futures Lab's 'AI safety in the Global South' stream.
- Humane Intelligence and UW in Microsoft's EXTRA red-team alliance.
- HPI's new DFG-funded AI Safety and Societal Impacts group in Potsdam/Berlin.
- PAI's Safety-Critical AI programme.
- AI Now's July 2026 'Double Agents' paper on agentic cyber risk. The ethics camp is moving onto safety ground.

EVIDENCE THE DIVIDE IS STRUCTURAL.
- Roytburg and Miller ('Mind the Gap', IASEAI 2026): over 80% of collaborations stay within either the safety or the ethics community, and about 5% of papers carry over 85% of bridging links. Bridging rests on a handful of brokers and is fragile.
- Gyevnár and Kasirzadeh (arXiv, March 2026) propose 'critical bridging' around shared problems: transparency, reproducibility and weak governance mechanisms. This maps closely onto int/a's 'decoupling and recoupling' principle.
- The classic aisafety.com map has no entry mentioning human rights, children or the Global South (apart from ILINA), and only MAI mentions democracy. Its law entries (LawAI, CLAIR, LASST, Legal Safety Lab) all come from inside the x-risk world.

MISSING BRIDGES (gaps for founders and funders).
(a) A 'bridging problems' fellowship or clinic. It would pair accountability and ethics researchers with safety researchers on shared, concrete problems: AI companions and psychological harm, accountability for agents, evaluation validity, and regulatory capture. Without it, bridging depends on a few overstretched brokers.
(b) A litigation-to-safety translation desk. It would systematically mine discovery documents, expert testimony and remedies from chatbot-harm cases (TJLP, SMVLC) as evidence on frontier labs' safety practice. No safety org does this.
(c) Human-rights due diligence as a vehicle for frontier-risk management. The UNGPs framework plus High Commissioner Türk's September 2026 letter to frontier AI companies is an opening that no org yet owns.
(d) System-safety engineering (STAMP/STPA) applied to agentic deployments and lab safety culture. The discipline is mature but almost absent from AI safety; Dobbe's critique of the International AI Safety Report is an isolated voice.
(e) A shared venue where humanitarian-disarmament campaigners and AI red-lines advocates can learn from each other, since Stop Killer Robots has built exactly the coalition machinery AI safety lacks.
(f) Global Majority AI-safety capacity beyond South Africa and India. Latin America has rights organisations but no AI-safety hub.
(g) Children's-rights design codes (5Rights) feeding into model specs and evals.
(h) Funding apartheid. Humanity AI ($500M over five years), the European AI & Society Fund and Mozilla fund one side; Coefficient Giving and SFF fund the other; there is virtually no co-funding. A jointly funded bridging pool is the obvious play, and the newly arriving funders in the brief are well placed to broker it.

SURPRISES AND CAUTIONS.
- The UN rights chief explicitly addressed frontier models in September 2026.
- The IBA's new AI Institute names 'frontier AI systems' as a priority.
- BRAID is £18M+ and runs to 2028, a ready template for a humanities-to-safety programme.
- Some organisations here (DAIR, and parts of AI Now) openly reject the x-risk and EA paradigm ('TESCREAL'). Bridging requires epistemic humility and non-instrumental engagement, which suits int/a's 'speed of wisdom' and 'full-spectrum knowing' principles.

VERIFICATION LIMITS. The shared web-search budget ran out after 18 queries. Some primary sites returned 403 or were rate-limited: LCFI, Mozilla, CDT, OHCHR, and parts of Edinburgh. Those entries carry medium confidence. CDT's AI Governance Lab, Princeton CITP, Weizenbaum Institute, HIIG and the Minderoo Centre were considered but not verified, so they are left out.
angle_notes.economics:
LANDSCAPE. This angle has four clusters that seldom cite each other.
(1) Cooperative AI and multi-agent game theory: CAIF, FOCAL, CLR, Modeling Cooperation, Hadfield's Normativity Lab, Gradient Institute, plus the behavioural evidence from MPIB's Center for Humans and Machines. It is the best-funded cluster in 2026. CAIF's $10m fund with Schmidt Sciences, DeepMind and ARIA (awards due autumn 2026) and a new CEO make it the obvious home for agent-ecosystem safety.
(2) Economics of transformative AI and post-AGI economics: EconTAI (UVA), Stanford Digital Economy Lab, the Stripe fellowship, Windfall Trust, Convergence's AGI Social Contract work, and since 2026 lab- and state-side bodies: the DeepMind Institute (Sep 2026; 'Economic policy for AGI') and the UK AI Economics Institute (June 2026, chaired by Simon Johnson). Anthropic's Economic Futures fund publishes usage data.
(3) Power concentration and political economy, in two traditions that barely speak. The x-risk side: Forethought (AI-enabled coups), Formation (lock-in, secret loyalties; $2.15m from Coefficient Giving), Longview's Extreme Power Concentration RFP (May 2026), MINT Lab. The critical and democratic side: AI Now, Open Markets/OMI Europe, Public AI Network/Metagov, RadicalxChange, Platform Cooperativism, and in the Global South Aapti and Research ICT Africa, funded in Europe by EAISF. AI Now openly dismisses 'doomerism', yet its diagnosis of concentrated power is close to Longview's.
(4) Gradual disempowerment is the synthesising frame. ACS (Prague) and the post-agi.org workshops, with Duvenaud at Toronto, are the only places that deliberately bring economists, political scientists and alignment researchers into one room.

SURPRISES. 'Cooperative AI' has two meanings: CAIF's game-theoretic agent cooperation and the cooperative movement's democratic ownership of AI. PCC held a 'Cooperative AI' conference in 2025 and 'Solidarity AI' in 2026, with no contact with CAIF. Int/a's observation that 'cooperative AI' people are int/a-flavoured applies to both, and pairing them is an easy convening win. 'Lock-in' likewise means market lock-in at OMI Europe and civilisational lock-in at Formation. Equilibria Network, on the classic map, has a parked domain.

LOSSES. Stanford's TAI economics course is paused in 2026. Oxford's Global Priorities Institute, long the academic home of long-termist economics, closed in 2025 (from memory; not re-checked in this session). FLI's $4m power-concentration grant round (2023-24; OpenMined, Nesta's Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, Mila and others) is finished. No 2026 cohort of the Stripe fellowship could be confirmed.

MISSING BRIDGES (gaps for founders and funders):
(a) Algorithmic collusion. Industrial-organisation economists and competition authorities (e.g. Calvano et al. on Q-learning pricing collusion, the CMA, DG COMP) have the most empirical work on AI agents colluding without instruction. Nobody connects this to multi-agent safety. Competition regulators could become monitors of agent ecosystems.
(b) Market and mechanism design for agent economies. Agent payment protocols are being built by companies, not by auction or matching theorists or safety researchers. No institute exists for 'safe agent-economy design'.
(c) Commons and polycentric governance. The Ostrom Workshop holds the deepest knowledge on multi-actor governance of shared resources and has no AI programme.
(d) Development economics of rentier states and resource curses: the 'intelligence curse' argument of Luke Drago and Rudolf Laine. Experts on natural-resource revenue, sovereign wealth funds and the history of states whose power stopped depending on citizens' labour are absent, even though Longview's RFP explicitly asks for historical and political-economy analysis.
(e) Distribution mechanics. Windfall Trust is almost alone. The empirical work on cash transfers (OpenResearch, GiveDirectly-style trials) and public-finance experts are not plugged into TAI scenarios.
(f) Labour as a counter-power. The MIT Stone Center, IFOW and unions study worker voice in AI deployment, but nobody frames it as a defence against gradual disempowerment.
(g) Geography. Outside the US and UK, the anchors are Prague (ACS), Berlin (MPIB), Sydney (Gradient) and Bengaluru and Cape Town (Aapti, RIA). Safety funders hardly fund Global South political-economy groups, though they hold the clearest view of how AI gains get distributed between countries.
(h) Field-building. With GPI closed and the Stanford course paused, no durable, funded pipeline brings PhD economists and political scientists into TAI questions. A standing 'Economics and political economy of TAI' fellowship or summer school, ideally co-run by CAIF, EconTAI and ACS, is the most obvious funder opportunity.
angle_notes.biology:
WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES. This angle draws on seven bodies of knowledge, and they barely talk to each other:
(1) Basal cognition and diverse intelligence: the Levin lab and the Allen Discovery Center at Tufts, plus the Templeton-funded network around them (TWCF's Diverse Intelligences hubs at St Andrews, Princeton and Macquarie since October 2025; DISI).
(2) Active inference and the free-energy principle: Karl Friston's circle at UCL and VERSES, the volunteer Active Inference Institute, the IWAI workshop (Madrid, 14–16 October 2026), and Monash/Laukkonen's contemplative-AI work, which uses active inference.
(3) Artificial life: ISAL, and the Japanese ALife scene (Cross Labs, now NOOMA Labs; Ikegami at Tokyo).
(4) Evolutionary game theory and cultural evolution: MPI Plön, IT:U Linz, the Teesside/Lisbon/Brussels evolutionary-game-theory network, and the Berlin Center for Humans and Machines' work on 'machine culture'.
(5) Collective animal behaviour: Konstanz CASCB and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior.
(6) Comparative cognition and animal sentience: CFI's Kinds of Intelligence/Animal-AI, NYU CMEP, and Jonathan Birch at LSE. Birch's new LSE Coller Centre for Animal Sentience was not verifiable from my fetches.
(7) Enactive theory of biological agency (IAS-Research, Basque Country).

BRIDGES THAT EXIST.
- Three classic-map orgs, Softmax, Princint/PIBBSS and ACS, carry most of the traffic. Softmax's 'organic alignment' descends from Levin through Adam Goldstein. PIBBSS is the talent pipeline. ACS imports hierarchical agency and active inference, and its researcher Gavenčiak co-authored the main explicit active-inference alignment paper with Friston and Da Costa (arXiv 2410.00258).
- Off the classic map:
  - AII's AICACP: SFF $270k, June 2025, led by Adam Safron of the Allen Discovery Center. It is the one funded line from the Levin ecosystem into alignment.
  - AII's new AI²C 'Active Inference Alignment Coalition' (Mahault Albarracin, March 2026).
  - CSAS: Buddhism, Levin and Watson; 'The Bodhisattva as an Alignment Target'.
  - Aintelope: homeostatic, bounded-objective benchmarks, run by three volunteers.
  - Han's FLI-funded evolutionary-game-theory models of AI races.
  - NYU CMEP: sentience science applied to AI welfare.
- Funding is extremely concentrated. SFF is effectively the only x-risk funder here (PIBBSS about $1.01M and ACS about $706k in 2025, plus AII). Templeton (TWCF and JTF) is by far the largest money in diverse intelligence and has no safety framing.

SURPRISES.
- Cross Labs (Kyoto), listed as a starting point, closed on 31 August 2026. Its programme moved to NOOMA Labs, whose first highlighted paper is explicitly about the alignment problem.
- Softmax's public site now looks like a multiplayer games and league platform for coding agents more than a research lab.
- ISAL has no AI-safety track, even though 'open-endedness' is now a frontier-lab capability agenda.
- Active-inference alignment exists mostly as papers and one-off seminars (Sheffield Hallam's 'The Active Inference Pathway to Alignment', January 2026), not as institutions.
- The commercial active-inference firms (VERSES, Noumenal Labs, now robot autonomy; Stanhope AI) are capabilities companies, so I left them out. VERSES's site returned 404s.
- Timaeus calls its agenda 'developmental interpretability', but its methods come from singular learning theory and physics, not developmental biology. I left it to the physics angle.

GAPS FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS.
(a) Safety of open-ended systems. ALife knows open-ended evolution best, and labs now pursue open-ended self-improvement, but no organisation owns its safety. The 2020 paper by Ecoffet, Clune and Lehman stayed a one-off. An ALife × safety group or an ALIFE conference track is an obvious build.
(b) An evolutionary and ecological theory of deployed AI populations: selection pressures on agents in the wild, invasive-species and ecosystem-collapse models, and gradual disempowerment treated as an ecological process. ACS gestures at this; nobody does it full-time with ecologists.
(c) 'Diverse-intelligence evals': translating comparative-cognition and basal-cognition methods into tests of AI agency, goal-directedness, deception and sentience. Animal-AI is the only working tool, and the TWCF hubs have seed funds but no AI-safety track. A Templeton–safety-funder co-funding call is low-hanging fruit.
(d) An empirical testbed that translates active-inference alignment proposals (structure learning, shared protentions, care and well-being terms) into ML-checkable claims. AI²C is the seed.
(e) Multicellularity and cancer-as-defection as a formal model for AI coalitions and collusion, linking Levin's framework, Softmax and evolutionary-game-theory cooperation work.
(f) Immune-system-inspired defence (an ecosystem of detection and response, in d/acc terms): I found no organisation.
(g) Homeostatic and bounded objectives as an alignment target: only volunteer-scale work (Aintelope).
(h) A fellowship stream at DISI or PIBBSS dedicated to biology-to-alignment translation.

LIMITATIONS.
- The session's shared web-search budget ran out after about 12 of my queries, so I verified mostly by fetching primary sites directly.
- I could not fetch Google's Paradigms of Intelligence team (Blaise Agüera y Arcas: computational life, symbiogenesis), the Gaia Network / Digital Gaia (active-inference governance), Monash's consciousness and contemplative centre, or LSE's Coller Centre, so I left them out. All four are worth a second look.
- Contemplative AI (Laukkonen et al.) and the Cooperative AI Foundation are likely covered by other angles.
angle_notes.inner:
LANDSCAPE. Knowledge about the inner life, culture and mental health of the people building and governing AI sits in six largely disconnected places:
(1) A thin layer of EA-internal mental health infrastructure: Rethink Wellbeing, Mental Health Navigator, Upgradable, the now-closed AI Safety Support coaching, CEA Community Health, and the community-health managers inside fellowships. It is generic to 'altruists' and not tuned to AI-safety-specific stressors.
(2) The rationalist self-development lineage: CFAR, which resumed workshops in Nov 2025 with a 'wholeness' reframing, and ESPR/FABRIC.
(3) Contemplative networks that have discovered AI in 2025–26: Buddhism & AI Initiative, Wisdom + AI, MAPLE, Stanford's Oct 2026 summit, Garrison's Oct 2026 AI forum, and the Gomde 'Buddhism and AI' summer course. They are booming, but mostly focused on AI design, meaning and governance rather than the care of builders.
(4) The mainstream leadership and inner-development industry: IDG, Presencing, SIYLI, Potential Project, Art of Accomplishment. It has huge reach and almost no AI-safety framing. The commercial players (Jhourney, Art of Accomplishment) are the ones actually reaching OpenAI, Anthropic and Google staff.
(5) Changemaker and helping-profession resilience: the Wellbeing Project, Garrison's Contemplative-Based Resilience (which has already trained Congressional staff), and the Climate Psychology Alliance. This is the richest transferable know-how on burnout and existential-stakes distress, with no AI bridge yet.
(6) Data-worker labour research: the Data Workers' Inquiry and Fairwork. They document the psychological cost borne by the annotators and moderators who make models 'safe', which never appears in AI-safety 'field health' talk.

DEMAND SIGNALS. The SF Standard (1 Apr 2026) found Bay Area therapists with 40–80% AI-worker caseloads describing 'existential despair'. Ihor Kendiukhov's LessWrong post (8 Sept 2026) names unmet needs: anticipatory grief, partners and family who don't share the timelines, NDA- and infohazard-sealed stress that can't be taken to outside therapists, and attachments or resentments toward the models researchers work with. The seed list cites a write-up of Spencer Greenberg's survey (59% burnout), which I could not confirm on Clearer Thinking's own site. Supply consists of individual private practices.

SURPRISES. AI-safety-specific support has shrunk while the field has grown: AISS closed and Upgradable pivoted toward Collective Action for Existential Safety. Rethink Wellbeing's newest growth is in low- and middle-income countries, not AI safety. PauseAI's 'psychology of x-risk' page explains doom but offers no support pathway. MAPLE remains active with an AI Fellowship despite unaddressed 2025–26 high-control allegations. Garrison's CBR project is a ready-made, evidence-based template, already used with policymakers' staff, that nobody has pointed at AI.

GAPS FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS:
(a) A clearance-aware psychological service for lab, AI Safety Institute and safety-org staff: therapists vetted to hear NDA-bound material, or embedded in fellowships such as MATS. This is the humanitarian-sector staff-care model applied to AI.
(b) AI-safety-specific peer and buddy cohorts, which could adapt Rethink Wellbeing's CBT and IFS Labs.
(c) A doom-distress network ('AI cafés') translating climate-psychology methods: climate cafés, Good Grief Network's 10 steps, Work That Reconnects.
(d) Inner-capacity and resilience programmes for AI policymakers (EU AI Office, national AI Safety Institutes), using the Mindfulness Initiative, Inner Green Deal (Cologne) and CBR Congressional templates.
(e) Wise-leadership and culture work for frontier-lab leaders that is explicitly tied to safety. Jhourney and Art of Accomplishment already have the access but not the framing.
(f) Content-exposure safeguards for red-teamers and evaluators who handle CBRN, CSAM and violent material. Trust-and-safety wellness practice and Fairwork-style standards have not crossed over to AI-safety evals teams.
(g) A recurring field-health observatory or survey, along the lines of the Wellbeing Project's State of Changemaker Wellbeing.
(h) A dedicated funder. Fetzer, Hemera and Templeton fund contemplative work but not AI field health, and new pools such as Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind founders call could seed (a)–(g).

METHOD CAVEAT. The session-wide web-search cap was hit after 13 of the 15 requested queries. Remaining candidates were verified by fetching primary sites. Good Grief Network (403), High Impact Psychology (unresolvable URL) and Wisdom 2.0 (unreadable page) could not be verified and are omitted. Potential Project ('The Human Leader' AI-era leadership), Inner Green Deal, Mind & Life Institute (2026 work on inner capacities for cooperation) and CEA Community Health are relevant but weaker fits, so they are noted here rather than listed.
angle_notes.complexity:
METHOD CAVEAT: the session-wide WebSearch budget (200 calls, shared with other workers) ran out after 7 of my queries. Discovery after that came from following primary-source links: PrincInt's affiliate list, Iliad's incubated organisations, ARIA's Safeguarded AI funded-projects list, ACS's posts, and Cross Labs' closure notice. These are verified by WebFetch, but recall is weaker for non-Anglophone and very new groups than the brief wanted. Candidates I could not verify (worth a follow-up pass): Harvard/NTT 'Physics of Intelligence' (Hidenori Tanaka); Noumenal Labs and other active-inference startups; Gaia Network/Digital Gaia; Michael Levin's Allen Discovery Center (Tufts); ASU Beyond Center (Sara Walker); INET Oxford complexity economics; the Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science; the International Society for Artificial Life; continental complexity institutes (IFISC Mallorca, ISI Turin, MPI MiS Leipzig); and the Tallinn category-theory group (Hadzihasanovic and Capucci, cited by Quanta). SFI's website resisted fetching, so its entry rests on its homepage and a 2025 paper.

LANDSCAPE: This angle splits into three clusters with very different health.

(1) A consolidated mathematical/theoretical cluster, well funded and growing fast in 2026. It forms a dense network around PrincInt and Iliad. Iliad incubates AIXI Labs, Principia, Stormglass and XOR Labs. PrincInt's affiliates add AFFINE, the Alignment Journal and the Fields Centre for Mathematical AI. Agent Foundations conferences are now in their third edition. Big 2026 moves:
- Timaeus merged its SLT agenda into Resolution with UK AISI's alignment team (June 2026).
- MAISI got $10M from Coefficient Giving with a Fields Medalist as scientific director (September 2026).
- The Alignment Journal launched.
- Fields and PrincInt began joint postdocs.
The mathematics funded here sits close to ML: learning theory, singular learning theory, algorithmic information theory, mean-field theory and renormalization-group methods for interpretability. Physics shows up mainly as tools for interpretability (Simplex's computational mechanics, Timaeus/Resolution's statistical physics, XOR Labs' information decomposition).

(2) A complexity and systems cluster about societies and multi-agent dynamics, which is the most int/a-flavoured and also tiny. ACS (Gradual Disempowerment, hierarchical agency), Equilibria Network (applying Stafford Beer's Viable System Model, spectral signatures of disempowerment), the Post-AGI Civilizational Equilibria workshops and Softmax (organic alignment from multicellularity) amount to perhaps 20-30 people in total. Equilibria's domain has lapsed and it names no team, a sign of fragility.

(3) A category-theory/compositional cluster that ARIA Safeguarded AI created almost single-handedly: 14 TA1.1 teams including Topos Research UK, GLAIVE, Oxford (Staton, Abate, Yoshida), UCL, Edinburgh, Pisa and Bristol. Between November 2025 and May 2026, ARIA narrowed the programme toward formal methods for cybersecurity and cancelled TA3 Phase 2. Without a successor funder, this freshly built community of category theorists could drift away from AI safety.

BRIDGES THAT EXIST: PIBBSS/PrincInt fellowships (complex systems to safety); Fields-PrincInt (mainstream mathematics institute to safety); ARIA (category theory to safety); the UK AISI Alignment Project (£27M across information theory, game theory, complexity theory and cognitive science, but no 2026 round, a coming cliff); Astera's hosting of Simplex.

MISSING BRIDGES (gaps for founders and funders):
(a) The large complexity institutions (SFI, CSH Vienna with Turchin-style collapse modelling, NECSI) have essentially no AI-risk programme. SFI's public stance on LLM emergence is deflationary. A PIBBSS-style visiting programme hosted at SFI or CSH, on multi-scale agency, systemic risk and gradual disempowerment, is an obvious, cheap gap.
(b) Systems safety engineering (Leveson's STAMP/STPA, resilience engineering) is mature, cybernetic in spirit, and almost absent from frontier-AI safety cases. Nobody owns 'STPA for AI agent ecosystems'.
(c) Cybernetics proper: ANU's School of Cybernetics is alive but not engaged with x-risk. Equilibria's VSM posts are the only explicit cybernetics-for-alignment work I found. A second-order-cybernetics approach to AI governance (requisite variety, viable systems for labs and regulators) is unclaimed.
(d) Statistical physics of learning is richly funded as capability science (the Simons collaboration under Ganguli) but has no safety translation layer outside Toronto. The Fields model could be replicated at Stanford, Princeton or ENS Paris.
(e) Theoretical biology and basal cognition: TWCF funds Diverse Intelligences hubs (October 2025), but uptake into alignment is limited to Softmax and individual PIBBSS fellows. Cross Labs closed in August 2026; NOOMA Labs continues its programme without a safety agenda.
(f) The active-inference/free-energy community has a complete formal theory of nested agency, but no safety-focused node.
(g) Geography: almost everything is in London, the Bay Area or Toronto. Exceptions are Prague (ACS, AFFINE), Kyoto (NOOMA), Tokyo (ALIGN, with distinctive 'symbiosis' and 'emergent machine ethics' framings), Vienna, Canberra, Glasgow and Melbourne (remote). Continental European complexity and mathematics institutes are untapped.

INT/A FIT: ACS, Equilibria, Softmax, Topos ('cooperation across difference', 'knowledge and compassion'), the Post-AGI workshops, AFFINE (exploratory pedagogy) and ALIGN are the most integral in spirit. The math-theory cluster (MAISI, AIXI Labs, CORAL, Resolution) is rigorous and interdisciplinary in method but conventional in worldview.

SURPRISES: Timaeus no longer exists under that name. Nora Ammann, a PIBBSS co-founder, now directs ARIA Safeguarded AI. XOR Labs, led by a mainstream complexity scientist (Rosas), is missing from the classic map. Basis Research Institute, though on the starting list, shows no safety framing.
angle_notes.contemplative:
WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES. (1) Buddhist scholarly and monastic institutions: Rangjung Yeshe/Kathmandu, 84000, Gomde Austria, Dharma Gate (Budapest), the Italian Buddhist Union, CamTech (Cambodia), Glorisun/Peking University/UBC, and Thai universities such as Mahachulalongkornrajavidyalaya and Chulalongkorn (Soraj Hongladarom). (2) Contemplative neuroscience: Oxford's Centre for Eudaimonia and Human Flourishing, Monash, Mind & Life and Mind & Life Europe, Harvard's meditation research, and Metzinger's MPE project. (3) Empirical wisdom science: Waterloo (Grossmann), the UChicago Center for Practical Wisdom, and the older Berlin wisdom paradigm. (4) Flourishing science: Harvard Human Flourishing Program and the Global Flourishing Study. (5) The meaning-crisis and cognitive-science-of-meaning scene: Vervaeke, and Laukkonen's essays on the meaning crisis. The Buddhism & AI Initiative's six-domain field framework (engagedbuddhists.ai/field-framework, about 190 entries) is the best existing directory for this angle. Most of its entries, though, are AI→Buddhism (translation, chatbots, meditation apps) rather than Buddhism→AI safety.

BRIDGES THAT EXIST. Contemplative alignment as a research agenda: Laukkonen et al.'s 'Contemplative AI', now institutionalised as FLIP at Oxford, and CSAS's bodhisattva-as-alignment-target essays. CSAS's framework was built with 84000 and 'in dialogue with Anthropic'; the BAI framework also notes an Anthropic religion liaison collecting feedback on Claude's constitution, and contemplative advisors or workstreams at DeepMind and OpenAI. Wisdom science reaching ML: the Grossmann/Johnson 'wise machines' paper (TiCS 2026) with Bengio, Mitchell, Schölkopf, Levine and Rahwan, and Waterloo's 2026 AI-metacognition hires. Meaning-centred alignment: MAI's thick values, Model Integrity and Full-Stack Alignment, and the new Connecting Intelligence. Early 'wisdom and flourishing evals': Positive AI Labs (pluralistic wisdom datasets), Gloo's FAI benchmark (flourishing, Christian-tinted), CaML's CompassionBench, Grossmann's metacognition work, and Laukkonen's tests on AILuminate and the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. Inner-development infrastructure for AI builders: the Wisdom + AI Network's retreats with Oxford, and Wisdom Beyond. Funders: FLI and Omidyar fund the Buddhism & AI Initiative; SFF funds MAI and CaML; TWCF funded CSAS; JTF's new $60M+ Future of Intelligence venture (2026-29) explicitly asks about 'flourishing and wisdom for augmented, enhanced and shared intelligence'.

GAPS FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS.
(a) No validated wisdom-evaluation suite plugged into mainstream safety evaluation (AISIs, METR, lab model cards). The pieces exist but are scattered: Waterloo's cross-cultural Wise Judgment Consortium data, UChicago's measurement expertise, Positive AI Labs' pipeline and Gloo's flourishing dimensions. A founder could build an open 'wise judgment / metacognition' benchmark validated against human wisdom psychology.
(b) Contemplative-alignment claims rest mostly on prompting studies. Nobody is doing interpretability, training-time or agentic experiments that test whether 'emptiness', 'non-duality' or 'boundless care' change goal-directedness or power-seeking. This is a natural PIBBSS/Princint-style fellowship track.
(c) JTF's $60M and TWCF's Diverse Intelligences money barely touch x-risk-relevant agendas. A broker that translates safety problems into Templeton-legible proposals, and back, would be high-leverage.
(d) Asian Buddhist institutions (Cambodia, Thailand, Taiwan, Japan, Sri Lanka, Bhutan) mostly run AI-ethics seminars or build dharma chatbots (Kyoto's BuddhaBot and Buddharoid). They are largely absent from alignment and governance conversations; BAI is still seeking Chinese-language mapping.
(e) Contemplative support for AI-safety workers exists only as small retreat offerings. MAPLE's AI Fellowship, the best-known one, faces serious high-control allegations (LessWrong, Jul 2026). The field needs a vetted, evidence-based, safeguarded programme and a due-diligence standard for contemplative providers.
(f) Non-Buddhist contemplative traditions are almost invisible in alignment work: Christian contemplative, Sufi, Advaita/Vedanta, Daoist, Indigenous. AI and Faith and Gloo engage them only at the level of ethics and values.
(g) 'Moving at the speed of wisdom' has no institutional research home that applies wisdom science to governance (deliberation tempo, restraint, race dynamics). The NonZero newsletter makes the anti-race case only in public commentary.
(h) The meaning crisis and AI companionship: Vervaeke's 'Mentoring the Machines' has no research or organisational vehicle, and the Vervaeke Foundation's domain now redirects to his personal site.

SURPRISES AND VERIFICATION NOTES. Laukkonen has moved from Southern Cross University to Oxford, where FLIP is privately funded. Cross Labs (Kyoto), a CSAS partner, closed on 31 Aug 2026; its research continues at Nooma Labs. buddhismandai.com is the Austrian summer initiative, not Scammell's Buddhism & AI Initiative (engagedbuddhists.ai). Gelephu Mindfulness City shows no AI policy. SIBA (Sri Lanka) shows no AI work. The Woodenfish Foundation's domain has lapsed. Excluded as generic AI-for-dharma or wellness tech rather than work on making AI go well: Spring Zero, Spirit Tech Collective, Awakin.ai, DharmaMitra and BuddhaBot. Anima Labs (Janus) appears in BAI's framework but belongs in the AI-welfare angle. Method: this run made about 17 WebSearch queries before the session's shared search budget ran out. After that, every candidate was verified by opening its primary site with WebFetch. Two sites could not be opened: the Oxford eudaimonia site (safety check rate-limited) and Monash (403), so M3CS is low confidence.
angle_notes.metacrisis:
How this was researched: the session-wide WebSearch cap ran out after 12 of my queries, short of the 15 I was asked for, because the cap is shared with the other agents. I then checked candidates by fetching their own websites directly. Several of those domain checks were rate-limited. Four candidates could not be checked: Digital Gaia (TLS error), Princeton's Global Systemic Risk group (the domains I guessed did not resolve), IIASA Systemic Risk (403) and the Commission for the Human Future (domain for sale). Coverage of 2025-26 launches and non-Anglophone groups is therefore thinner than intended.

Where the relevant knowledge sits, in five clusters:
1. **The metacrisis 'sensemaking' world:** CRI/Consilience, Perspectiva/Emerge, Life Itself, Metamoderna, Game B and The Great Simplification. It has a strong diagnosis of AI as an accelerant of multipolar traps and the 'superorganism', and this is the native int/a vocabulary. Its institutional output on AI is weak, though:
   - Consilience has published nothing since July 2024.
   - Life Itself, Metamoderna, the Club of Rome, the Presencing Institute, the Institute for Ecological Civilization (EcoCiv), Emergence Magazine, Human Energy, Channel McGilchrist and the Earth System Governance Project show no AI work on their sites.
   - The Stoa's domain no longer resolves, and the Game B wiki was last updated in 2021.
   - What AI engagement exists here comes through podcasts and talks rather than programmes.
2. **Earth-system and resilience science:** Stockholm Resilience Centre/Beijer and PIK. This is the most rigorous bridge. It includes Galaz's work on AI as a systemic risk to the biosphere ('Dark Machines', 2025) and 'AI for a Planet Under Pressure' (2025, with DeepMind). Above all, Jobst Heitzig at PIK publishes explicit alignment theory: non-maximising agents and objectives that preserve human empowerment, the latest in 2026. He is the model of what a bridge from this angle looks like.
3. **Planetary computation:** Antikythera, the Berggruen Institute, Noema, Long Now's talk series, and Yuk Hui's Research Network for Philosophy and Technology. This cluster is prominent, well funded and centred on AI. It is openly sceptical of the alignment framing and has almost no dialogue with the safety community.
4. **Cybernetics and systems:** the ANU School of Cybernetics, the Bateson lineage and the network's 'Cybernetics for the 21st Century' volumes. Cybernetics is being revived, but this revival is not connected to the safety field.
5. **Polycrisis and catastrophic risk outside EA:** the Cascade Institute and the Global Challenges Foundation. They treat AI as a governance or military topic rather than a systemic amplifier.

Bridges that already exist:
- Heitzig, through AI Safety Camp, LessWrong and ADT.
- Gaia Network, through the Open Agency Architecture / ARIA ecosystem; its status is unverified.
- The Odyssean Institute's AI Governance Assembly.
- The Great Simplification hosting Yampolskiy.
- Emerge's essays on 'wisdom-fostering AI'.
- Berggruen's Engaged California and its 'AI safety as a global public good' framing.
- The meta-relational AI course at the University of Victoria (Sept 2026).

Missing bridges, as openings for founders and funders:
1. **A metacrisis-to-AI-safety translation body.** Nothing turns the analysis of multipolar traps and the 'third attractor' into concrete AI research agendas or policy proposals. CRI is the natural home but has gone quiet. A translation fellowship or institute could fill this.
2. **A planetary-boundaries-style framework for AI.** Nobody has defined a 'safe operating space' for AI, or studied AI's role in tipping cascades. SRC and PIK already have the methods and the people (Galaz, Donges, Heitzig, Barfuss).
3. **Joint polycrisis and AI-risk modelling.** Polycrisis researchers (Cascade, Princeton GSR, IIASA, GCF) do not model AI as something that amplifies interactions between crises. A joint causal-loop or cross-impact model would be new.
4. **A venue linking cybernetics to alignment.** Bateson's 'conscious purpose' critique and today's cybernetics revival are the original critique of single-objective optimisation. They bear directly on Goodhart's law and on non-maximising agent designs, yet no venue connects them to alignment researchers.
5. **Cultural evolution and AI.** The Cultural Evolution Society has no AI activity, despite MPIB's 'machine culture' work and live concerns about gradual disempowerment. A workshop or interest group would be cheap.
6. **Commons governance for AI.** Ostrom-style polycentric and commons governance has not been applied to compute, open-weight models or shared evaluations.
7. **A dialogue between planetary-computation thinkers and the alignment community.** There is none. An adversarial-collaboration programme would widen both sides.
8. **A funder for this angle.** None exists:
   - The P2P Foundation wiki names a 'Third Attractor Foundation' as CRI's backer, but I found no web presence for it.
   - GCF and Berggruen mainly fund their own lines of work.
   - Kalliopeia (which funds Emergence Magazine) funds ecology and spirituality media, with no AI.
   - A new funder could seed a programme on civilisational design and AI.

Surprises:
- Steven Bird's 'Big AI is accelerating the metacrisis' appeared at ACL 2026, so metacrisis language has reached a mainstream NLP venue.
- Long Now is actively running AI and planetary-computation talks.
- GCF's 2026 report puts AI in military decision-making among its five top catastrophic risks.
- Burnout From Humans became a university course.
- Bratton and Agüera y Arcas form the intellectual centre of the planetary-computation cluster, and both are effectively outside the safety conversation.

Candidates I looked at and left out:
- **Club of Rome:** no AI work visible.
- **Life Itself:** active in France, no AI.
- **Metamoderna:** active ('The Axial Turn', 2025), no AI.
- **The Stoa:** defunct.
- **Presencing Institute, EcoCiv, Earth System Governance, Human Energy, Emergence Magazine:** no AI work found.
- **River (riverflows.life):** a Swedish 'wisdom-guided AI' product team whose roadmap is stale (Phase 2 was planned for 2024).
- **IRI at the Centre Pompidou:** active in digital studies, but no AI work visible.
- **Commission for the Human Future:** domain lapsed.
- **Santa Fe Institute, TU Delft systems-safety work (Dobbe), Abundant Intelligences:** left to the complexity, safety-engineering and Indigenous-knowledge angles.
angle_notes.collective:
METHOD NOTE: the session-wide WebSearch budget ran out after 24 searches in this branch, which is above the 15 required. All verification after that was done with WebFetch on primary sites (about 60 fetches). Status claims rest on dated items found on each organisation's own pages.

WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES. Six traditions hold the relevant knowledge, and most of them sit outside the AI-safety field:
(1) Deliberative democracy practitioners: sortition, Deliberative Polling, citizens' assemblies and consensus conferences (Stanford DDL, DemocracyNext, Missions Publiques, Democracy X / the Danish Board of Technology, People Powered).
(2) Civic tech and digital democracy (g0v/vTaiwan, Polis, Citizens Foundation, Japan's DD2030, Make.org).
(3) Collective-intelligence science (Nesta CCID, MIT CCI, the UK AI4CI hub, MPIB Humans and Machines).
(4) Plural mechanism design and commons governance (RadicalxChange, Plurality Institute, Metagov, Public AI Network).
(5) Peacebuilding and bridging (Council on Technology and Social Cohesion, Search for Common Ground, MIT CCC).
(6) Participatory data governance (Connected by Data, Ada Lovelace Institute, Aapti).

THREE EXISTING BRIDGES TO AI SAFETY.
(a) Public input into model behaviour: CIP's Alignment Assemblies, Global Dialogues and Weval; Anthropic's Collective Constitutional AI, run on Polis; OpenAI's 2023 Democratic Inputs grants, which seeded Dembrane, vTaiwan's Recursive Public and the Meaning Alignment Institute's moral graph, and were followed by a collective-alignment team; Meta and Stanford's Community Forums; the 2025 industry-wide AI agents forum (six companies, US and India).
(b) Democratic governance of AI itself: AI & Democracy Foundation, DemocracyNext, the Global Coalition for Inclusive AI Governance, Connected by Data and Ada's 2026 push for a citizens' track in the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, Odyssean's AI assembly proposal, and Public AI as a counter to power concentration.
(c) AI-augmented collective sensemaking as societal resilience, or 'AI for epistemics': the Habermas Machine, Talk to the City and its Japanese descendant Kouchou AI, Jigsaw Sensemaker, Policy Synth, Dembrane and AI4Deliberation.

SURPRISES.
- Only three entries in this whole angle are on the aisafety.com map: AOI, MAI and Odyssean. CIP, Plurality Institute, Metagov, Polis, DemocracyNext, Stanford DDL and RadicalxChange are all absent, even though CIP runs evals with frontier labs.
- Japan's Team Mirai, a party built on AI 'broad listening' with seats in both houses by 2026, is probably the largest live deployment of AI-mediated public input anywhere. It is nearly invisible in AI-safety discourse.
- RadicalxChange's 'Reverse Alignment' framing (prepare institutions for AI, not only AI for humans) and its faith-leader deliberation at the UN Global Dialogue (July 2026) are close to int/a's integral sensibility.
- Weval's community-built evals, for example non-sycophancy across 199 models, are a working bridge from participatory method to safety evaluation.
- The most direct funding bridges look thin. OpenAI's Democratic Inputs was a one-off in 2023. ARIA's Safeguarded AI pivoted in Nov 2025 to formal methods and cybersecurity, and its current page no longer mentions sociotechnical or deliberative specification work. That last point is inferred from page contents, so it is unconfirmed.

MISSING BRIDGES (founder and funder opportunities).
1. Safety of the AI mediators themselves. Nobody is systematically red-teaming AI facilitators and summarisers for persuasion, view homogenisation, sycophancy toward majorities, faithfulness of summaries, or capture by whoever writes the prompts.
