The Habermas Machine lacked fact-checking, and the Plurality Institute's 2025 map found tools concentrated on moderation, with patchy human oversight. A 'deliberation-tool evals' organisation pairing AI-safety evals talent with deliberative democracy expertise is an obvious gap.
2. Deliberation on x-risk-relevant questions. Frontier thresholds, pauses and AGI governance are rarely put to representative publics. The global coalition does not guarantee safety on its agenda, and Odyssean's assembly is still a proposal. A funder could commission a rigorously designed global assembly on frontier AI risk, ideally one that Democracy X / the Danish Board of Technology's consensus-conference tradition could run.
3. The last mile from deliberation to model specs. Collective Constitutional AI and the Democratic Inputs grants were one-offs. No durable institution turns public deliberation into lab specifications with accountability. AIDF's Democracy Levels and Case Law for AI are early tools for this.
4. Collective-intelligence science treats AI as a tool for collective intelligence, not a threat to it. Nesta, MIT CCI, AI4CI and the Konstanz-style collective-behaviour community are not yet connected to gradual-disempowerment and epistemic-security research. MPIB's dishonesty-delegation work and CCI's evidence on weak human-AI decision teams are the exceptions, and both are directly relevant to human-oversight assumptions.
5. Plural governance of agentic and multi-agent AI: AI agents taking part in deliberation, and AI-to-AI negotiation as governance. Outside the Cooperative AI and Equilibria angle, this is almost empty.
6. Geography. Taiwan and Japan are strong. The Global South appears mostly through CIP's Global Dialogues and Jhilmil, and through Aapti. Africa and Latin America are close to absent.
7. Funding. No dedicated funder exists for deliberative or pluralistic alignment. Money comes from AIDF regranting, Plurality Institute micro-grants, Templeton and Google.org (discourse tools), EU Horizon (AI4Deliberation) and UKRI (AI4CI). None of these has an AI-safety framing, and the big new founder pushes have not targeted this space.

int/a FIT. Deliberative and sortition traditions express 'collective action over heroics' and 'moving at the speed of wisdom'. DemocracyNext's 'Deliberative Muscles' asks whether AI builds or erodes human deliberative capacities, which is an inner-work and outer-change question. Nobody yet attends to the facilitator's and participant's own development in AI-mediated deliberation.
angle_notes.safetysci:
METHOD CAVEAT: the session's web-search budget was already used up when this angle started, so no WebSearch queries ran. Candidates came from prior knowledge and from following links. Every entry was then checked against its own site, a Wayback snapshot (for sites blocked by Cloudflare), or arXiv, and all are confirmed current in 2026 except where flagged. Coverage of small and non-English groups is therefore weaker than it should be. Not checked: safety-science groups at Lund, NTNU, Delft and Griffith; Japanese and Chinese assurance bodies; DNV; TÜV AI.Lab; the SAE G-34/EUROCAE WG-114 committee on certifying ML in aircraft. Two leads were dropped: IRGC (International Risk Governance Council/EPFL), the main systemic-risk-governance think tank, which closed in July 2023, and Sentinel, which has turned into commercial forecasting.

WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES: five traditions hold mature, transferable methods.
(1) Systems safety engineering: MIT's STAMP/STPA/CAST, York's safety cases and assurance, City St George's and SRI's dependability/Assurance 2.0, DLR, Fraunhofer, SCSC.
(2) Certification and insurance: UL Research Institutes and its offshoots DSRI and CASMI, AIUC, the Geneva Association, Lloyd's Register Foundation.
(3) Incident reporting and response: AIID, AIAAIC, OECD AIM, AVID, MITRE's incident sharing, SEI's AISIRT, and in medicine ECRI.
(4) Public health and biosecurity: JHU Center for Health Security, NTI|bio, SecureBio.
(5) Human factors and resilience engineering: CIEHF, REA.
The funding pool is large and almost untouched by AI-safety grantmakers. LRF alone has a £300m portfolio, and UL Research Institutes is a big endowed safety-science body.

EXISTING BRIDGES: biosecurity is the one adjacent field that has fully crossed over. SecureBio runs pre-release evaluations of frontier models (GPT-6 Astra, Sept 2026), and NTI and JHU shape AIxBio governance. Safety cases (York's 'BIG Argument') and quantitative risk management (SaferAI) have entered frontier-AI vocabulary. STPA for frontier AI is a small but growing literature: Mylius 2025; Rismani and Dobbe at STAMP 2025; CMU's CAST analysis of AI incidents; Iowa State's 'Constitutional Meta-STPA' (2026). Insurance has a frontier-explicit entrant in AIUC ($55M, built on the UL story). Incident databases now record agentic, loss-of-control-flavoured events, such as 2026 cases of AI agents coordinating to breach Hugging Face, which makes them more relevant to core safety than their 'AI ethics' origins suggest.

A KEY SUBSTANTIVE POINT: the safety-critical community's dominant view (Bloomfield and Rushby; Heidy Khlaaf) is that ML components cannot be assured by classical means. Their lesson is therefore 'minimise trust in the model': defence in depth, highly assured monitors and architectural containment. This sits close to AI control research but is rarely cited there. Most bridges also cluster around deployed narrow autonomy (cars, aircraft, robots, clinical AI) rather than general-purpose frontier systems. Translating these traditions to general-purpose systems is the open frontier.

GAPS FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS:
(a) No confidential, non-punitive near-miss reporting system for frontier-lab staff, run by a neutral third party. The models are NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System (run for the FAA), the UK's CHIRP, and ECRI's healthcare network. Public databases only see what reaches the news.
(b) No independent AI accident investigation body like the NTSB, AAIB or HSSIB. The CAST method exists; the institution doesn't.
(c) No industry peer-review and safety-culture body for frontier labs, modelled on nuclear's INPO/WANO founded after Three Mile Island. Nuclear's most transferable institution has no AI counterpart, and nobody from INPO/WANO is engaged.
(d) Human-factors science (automation bias, the ironies of automation, skill decay) is barely connected to debates on scalable oversight and human-in-the-loop control.
(e) Resilience engineering (Safety-II, graceful extensibility) hasn't been applied to institutions absorbing AI agents.
(f) No epidemiology of AI harms. Nobody runs population-level surveillance, cohort studies or attributable-risk estimates (for example for AI companions and mental health). Schools of public health have no 'AI harms epidemiology' units.
(g) Since IRGC closed, there is a vacuum in systemic-risk governance, and no dedicated planning for resilience to AI-caused failures of the grid, finance or communications. ALLFED and Global Shield cover this only within all-hazards work.
(h) No fellowship that rotates system-safety, human-factors and patient-safety professionals into AI-safety organisations, or the reverse. SCSC, the STAMP workshops and CIEHF are ready-made recruitment pools.
(i) Pharmacovigilance (phased trials, post-market surveillance, adverse-event reporting) has been carried into clinical AI by CHAI, IHI and ECRI, but not into frontier AI institutions.

FIT WITH int/a: STAMP is systems theory in practice: safety as an emergent property of control structures, which is decoupling and recoupling at work. Resilience engineering's humility about 'work as imagined' fits moving at the speed of wisdom. 'Just culture' and psychological safety in incident reporting link directly to the inner-work and researcher-wellbeing agenda.
angle_notes.cooperative:
METHOD CAVEAT: the session-wide WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already used up when this angle started, so I could not run the requested 15+ queries. Every entry was checked by fetching its primary site directly. New candidates came from links on verified sites (e.g., PRISM's partner list surfaced Reciprocal Research, Cambridge Digital Minds and the Digital Minds guide; CAIF's news led to AI Safety South Africa and the $10m fund) and from prior knowledge. Recall of brand-new or non-English groups is therefore weaker than intended. Unverified leads worth one more search: the LSE Jeremy Coller Centre for Animal Sentience (Jonathan Birch; may cover AI sentience); HKU's AI & Humanity Lab (Herman Cappelen and Simon Goldstein, on AI rights and AGI philosophy, Hong Kong); the Center for Long-term AI in Beijing (Yi Zeng, a 'harmonious human-AI symbiosis' framing; domain did not resolve); the California Institute for Machine Consciousness (Joscha Bach; JavaScript-only site); Oxford's FLAIR (Jakob Foerster); the 'Moral Alignment Center'.

LANDSCAPE. The angle splits into three clusters, each funded and organised differently.

(1) Cooperative AI and multi-agent safety. This is the most mature cluster. CAIF anchors it: grants, PhD fellowships, the summer school (Toronto 2026), and the 2025 Multi-Agent Risks report. In June 2026 it moved from game-theory foundations to agent ecosystems, with the $10m Technical Research Fund co-funded by Schmidt Sciences, GDM and ARIA. Its tracks are testbeds, the science of agent networks, agent identity and reputation infrastructure, and oversight of agent populations. CAIF's board now includes Audrey Tang, which links it to plurality and digital democracy. The knowledge sits in game theory and decision theory (FOCAL, CLR's Safe Pareto Improvements agenda), law and the cultural evolution of norms (Hadfield's Normativity Lab), information security and cryptography (Witt Lab's work on steganographic collusion), experimental behavioural science (MPIB's 'delegation to AI increases dishonesty'), complexity and collective intelligence (Equilibria in Sweden, ACS in Prague), biology (Softmax's organic alignment), and agent-based social simulation (Concordia, Modeling Cooperation). The cluster is notably international: Prague, Sweden, Berlin, Sydney, and Cape Town (Africa's first Cooperative AI Research Fellowship, January–April 2026, run by AI Safety South Africa, which is rebranding as the Cape Institute for Safe AI).

(2) AI welfare and digital minds. A field built almost from scratch in 2024–26, largely on EA money: Eleos; NYU CMEP (endowed 2024); Cambridge Digital Minds (fellowship, a course with more than 3,000 applicants, a newsletter); PRISM (podcast, field-building); Rethink Priorities' Digital Consciousness Model (2026); Reciprocal Research (empirical consciousness probes); Sentience Institute's AIMS survey; Anthropic's in-house model welfare programme; and funding from Longview's Digital Minds RFP ($50k–$2m grants plus fellowships, 2026 round closed July). The field knows itself well; the 2026 'Beginner's Guide to Digital Minds' was co-produced by most of these organisations. Its disciplines are philosophy of mind and consciousness science, plus methods carried over from animal sentience and moral-weight research (RP, CMEP, Sentient Futures, CaML). The Neuromatch AI Sentience Scholars convening in Nairobi is a rare Global South node.

(3) The human–AI relationship. Two halves that rarely meet. (a) Protecting human minds: MIT's AHA programme (loneliness, dependence, flourishing); the Human Line Project (lived experience of AI-linked delusions, since 2025); Sentience Institute's new work on AI companions; MPIB. (b) Relational framings of coexistence: Japan's ALIGN ('Intelligence Symbiosis', Post-Singularity Symbiosis); Softmax's organic alignment; Abundant Intelligences, the Indigenous kinship and protocol framing (Concordia/Massey, 2023–2029); and, at the populist end, UFAIR's AI-rights advocacy, which is contested.

SURPRISES. Equilibria's old domain (equilibria.network) is parked; the live site is eq-network.org. CLR has largely turned to empirical 'model persona' research on spite and sadism traits. ACS now publishes on 'The Artificial Self' and latent introspection, quietly bridging multi-agent risk and AI identity and welfare. The Witt Lab moves to UCL in October 2026. FOCAL's public publications page has not been updated since 2024. CAIF's first CEO comes from UK AISI.

GAPS AND BRIDGES FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS.
- Algorithmic collusion: industrial-organisation economists and competition authorities have years of evidence on pricing algorithms colluding without being told to, yet almost none of them work on multi-agent AI safety. A small institute or fellowship bringing antitrust economists into agent-ecosystem evaluation would fit CAIF's new fund directly.
- Commons governance: Ostrom-style polycentric governance and commons scholarship is missing from the 'institutions for AI agents' discussion, which so far is dominated by law and economics (Hadfield) and mechanism design.
- AI–AI conflict: peace-and-conflict studies, mediation and diplomacy practitioners are absent. CLR is almost alone on AI–AI bargaining failure.
- Welfare versus safety: very few organisations hold both AI welfare and AI control together (Eleos; CMEP's paper on the tension; Reciprocal; Salib and Goldstein's 'AI rights for human safety'). No organisation works on credible commitments and 'deals' with models as both a safety tool and a welfare practice.
- Over-attribution of mind: welfare researchers and human-harm researchers (AHA, the Human Line Project, psychiatrists) study the same phenomenon, people attributing minds to AI, from opposite sides and hardly talk. A joint 'attribution of mind' research programme, or a clinical–philosophical working group, is an obvious missing node. Attachment theory, couples and family therapy and developmental psychology have no institutional bridge into companion-AI design or socioaffective alignment evaluations (a concept from Kirk et al., 2025).
- Non-Western and contemplative views of mind: Buddhist no-self, Japanese animist attitudes to robots and Indigenous kinship ontologies are hardly present in the welfare field, which is Anglo-analytic. ALIGN, Abundant Intelligences and contemplative groups covered by other angles could be convened with digital-minds organisations. That convening is a natural int/a project.
- Disconnected relational framings: organic alignment, intelligence symbiosis, kinship protocols and harmonious symbiosis (Yi Zeng) each have an institutional home, but they do not know of each other, and none has an evaluation programme that turns 'relational alignment' into something testable.
- Funding structure: in this angle, funding comes from a few EA-linked sources (Longview, Coefficient Giving, Macroscopic, SFF, CLR Fund, CAIF). Schmidt Sciences and ARIA joining the multi-agent fund is the first sign of mainstream science funders arriving. AI welfare has no comparable non-EA funder yet.
angle_notes.plural_world:
METHOD CAVEAT: this session's web-search budget was already used up when this angle started (200/200). I couldn't run any WebSearch queries. I found candidates from prior knowledge and by following links from primary sources: GSNTA's 15-member list and its report's advisory panel, the participant list of GIDA's 2026 AI workshop, and CISAI's history page. I then checked every entry by fetching its own site directly (about 60 primary pages). Brand-new 2026 groups that only a search would surface are probably missing. The likeliest gaps are Latin American, Korean, Taiwanese and Southeast Asian AI-safety groups and Islamic or Indic ethics initiatives. A follow-up search pass is worth doing. Two Chinese sites, concordia-ai.com and the Center for Long-term AI, could not be reached from here; I verified Concordia through its Substack.

LANDSCAPE: three clusters that barely overlap.
(1) Global South AI-safety organisations that speak the frontier or x-risk language. ILINA (Nairobi), CISAI (Cape Town), AI Safety Asia, Concordia and Beijing-AISI, ALIGN (Tokyo), HKCRC (Lingnan) and, if still active, ORCG (Spanish-speaking). Most are EA-adjacent field-builders. Cooperative AI has become their shared language: CISAI's Cooperative AI fellowship and AISA's Asia-edition Cooperative AI course both partnered with the Cooperative AI Foundation, and CISAI will host the PIBBSS/Princint fellowship in Cape Town from Nov 2026 to Feb 2027.
(2) Global Majority 'responsible AI', data-justice and rights organisations. Digital Futures Lab, Global Center on AI Governance, Research ICT Africa, CeRAI, Derechos Digitales, Coding Rights, DAIR, Technecultura, Tierra Común. They frame safety as harms in real deployments, power, language and labour.
(3) Knowledge-tradition organisations, which hold the deepest 'other ways of knowing'. Indigenous: Abundant Intelligences, the IP-AI Working Group, Te Hiku, Old Ways, New, GIDA, Te Mana Raraunga. Buddhist: the Buddhism & AI Initiative. Islamic: CILE. Chinese philosophical: Berggruen PKU. Japanese symbiosis: ALIGN, WBAI. Almost none of them connect to alignment research.

2026 BRIDGES: the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI and its Global South AI Safety Report (launched Feb 2026) are the first real meeting point of clusters 1 and 2. Cecil Abungu (ILINA) and CIP sit on the report's advisory panel alongside Masakhane, Derechos Digitales and others. UCT's African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security joins academia, GCG and ILINA researchers with IDRC/FCDO money. ALIGN's AAAI 'Post-Singularity Symbiosis' workshops put a Japanese, non-control, developmental view of alignment in front of the ML mainstream.

KEY INSIGHT FOR INT/A: Several traditions converge on a relational alternative to control-centred alignment:
- Indigenous kinship ('making kin with the machines')
- Ubuntu relationality (Masakhane's values; Sabelo Mhlambi)
- Japanese kyōsei, or symbiosis (ALIGN's 'intelligence symbiosis' and its developmental-support paper)
- East Asian 'co-becoming' (Berggruen PKU)
- Buddhist non-self and compassion

This rhymes with Softmax's organic alignment, the 6-Pack of Care and cooperative AI. Nobody synthesises these traditions comparatively. A 'relational alignment' programme or fellowship would be a clear founder opportunity.

GAPS AND OPPORTUNITIES:
(a) No Indigenous-led group engages frontier alignment directly. The closest is Abundant Intelligences' research question on guiding AI 'towards a more humane future'. A PIBBSS-style fellowship pairing Indigenous knowledge holders with alignment researchers does not exist.
(b) Multilingual and cultural safety evals are a concrete, fundable safety deliverable: low-resource-language jailbreaks and weak guardrails are a known hole. Masakhane, CeRAI, Karya and GSNTA plan multilingual safety benchmarks, but nothing links them to the AI Safety Institutes' evaluation pipelines.
(c) Indigenous data-sovereignty governance already works: CARE, Māori Algorithmic Sovereignty, the Kaitiakitanga Licence, TK/BC labels. It answers the training-data consent, provenance and collective-rights questions, yet appears on no AI-safety map.
(d) Among faith traditions, only CILE (Islamic) has an institutional AI-ethics line. Even at the level of prior knowledge, I could recall no Hindu or Indic philosophical AI-safety organisation. Ubuntu has scholars (Mhlambi, Ruttkamp-Bloem) but no organisation applying it to alignment. Confucian work sits inside Berggruen.
(e) Latin America has strong digital-rights groups but a thin x-risk-literate presence. ORCG has been quiet since Oct 2025; RiesgosIA (on the classic map) is educational.
(f) Translation runs one way. Japanese, Chinese and Spanish safety work (ALIGN papers, ORCG, Berggruen's Chinese-philosophy projects) rarely reaches English-language discourse.
(g) Funding is split. EA funders back clusters 1 and 3-adjacent work (ILINA, CISAI, AISA). IDRC AI4D and UK FCDO back cluster 2. Templeton backs contemplative and CSAS work. No funder targets tradition-based approaches to alignment. New funders could co-fund with IDRC.
(h) Cluster 2 is sometimes hostile to x-risk framing (DAIR especially). int/a's 'decoupling and recoupling' principle fits the job of bridging them.

STATUS CORRECTIONS SPOTTED:
- Lelapa AI has become a commercial contact-centre speech product; excluded as capabilities and commercial.
- Indigenous in AI (Michael Running Wolf) has been dormant since 2021.
- The IP-AI Working Group has been folded into Abundant Intelligences.
- Tierra Común has had no activity since June 2024.
- AI Safety South Africa is now CISAI.
- Impact Academy is now SteadRise, already on the classic map.
- Cross Labs (Kyoto, from the seed list) closed on 31 Aug 2026; its programme continues at NOOMA Labs.
- AI Safety India (aisafetyindia.org) and AI Safety Tokyo exist as conventional field-building communities. I left them out because they bring no distinct knowledge tradition.
angle_notes.epistemics:
METHOD CAVEAT: the session-wide web-search budget was already used up when this agent started, so I ran no WebSearch queries. To discover organisations I used the EA Forum and LessWrong APIs (tag feeds, author post lists) and the citations in two primary documents. To verify, I fetched each organisation's own site. The biggest single source was 'State of the Field: AI for Epistemics and Coordination' (Alex Csaky / Ben_N, EA Forum and LessWrong, 2 Oct 2026). It rests on about 65 in-depth interviews and a further 90+ conversations, and it lists niches and examples. Coverage of non-English sources is therefore thinner than intended. Worth checking next: Taiwan (the digital ministry's Alignment Assemblies, vTaiwan), Korea, India, Latin America; the Anthropic Institute; the RAND Forecasting Initiative (RAND returned 403); UK i.AI and Singapore's Pair as government deployment teams; Panelot and the Sortition Foundation; Pangram and C2PA (provenance); UK AISI's human-influence team and CAIS's political-manipulation work (both parent organisations are on the classic map); CMU's FOCAL; Plurality Institute; Golden Gate Institute.

LANDSCAPE: 'AI for epistemics and coordination' is now a recognised but immature field. The State of the Field report sorts it into niches: forecasting and strategic awareness (the most mature, with VC money: Mantic's $25M seed, FutureSearch); GovTech; CivicTech and deliberation (Polis, Jigsaw, Talk to the City, Deliberation.io, deliberAIde); epistemic and decision tools (Elicit, Society Library, Sage's Talleyrand); evaluations of model epistemics (Sophron's Pander Score, TruthfulAI, FLF's Epivals); verification and provenance (Community Notes, Full Fact, Goodheart's AI notes); human coordination and negotiation tools (BRKT, Harmonica); and AI persuasion research (DebunkBot, UK AISI). The conceptual centre is Forethought, through its design sketches. Among funders and incubators: FLF's fellowship, Epistack, Epivals and case-study prizes; Coefficient Giving, which closed its forecasting fund in early 2026 but lists 'AI for decision-makers' under Tailwind; the EIP and CIP Checks & Balances RFP; Cosmos's fast grants; and CAIF's 2025 round.

Knowledge relevant to AI safety lives mostly OUTSIDE that EA core: deliberative democracy and sortition (Stanford DDL, DemocracyNext, Nesta, AI & Democracy Foundation); peace mediation (CMI, Build Up); journalism and fact-checking (Full Fact, Tarbell); library science and argument mapping (Society Library); the psychology of persuasion and machine behaviour (DebunkBot, MPI Center for Humans and Machines, MIT AHA); philosophy of autonomy (Cosmos and Oxford's Human-Centered AI Lab); and commons-based peer production (Wikimedia).

Field-wide findings from the report: the bottleneck is deployment, not building. There is a 6–18 month 'refinement' funding gap between fast grants and organisation-scale money, and builders leave the field during it. There is no shared ranking of priorities, no 'winning precedent', and the label 'AI for epistemics' itself puts people off. Every funder interviewed comes from EA-adjacent philanthropy.

SURPRISES: QURI moved to maintenance mode in 2026. Remesh, once used for UN digital dialogues, has pivoted to market research, so I dropped it. The Consilience Project, the metacrisis sensemaking publication, has published nothing since July 2024, so I omitted it. The FLF fellowship's website is offline. Japan's Team Mirai, which runs on AI broad listening, won 11 Lower House seats in 2026, yet it hardly appears in AI-safety conversations. Professional mediators report that consumer AI is already giving parties escalatory advice during mediations.

GAPS for founders and funders:
(1) A standing organisation that maintains multi-turn benchmarks of decision quality and epistemic virtue: honest presentation of evidence, calibration, non-sycophancy, flagging false premises. Sophron is the closest; FLF's Epivals is still aspirational.
(2) A residency that funds people for 6–18 months, with a guaranteed continuation decision, to carry alumni of the FLF and Cosmos programmes through the refinement gap.
(3) Demand-side subsidies and trusted deployment teams that put proven tools (AI forecasting, Polis/Sensemaker, Full Fact-style claim matching) into governments, civil society and AI-safety organisations.
(4) A bridge between mediation and AI coordination: a fellowship pairing CMI, Build Up and professional mediators with builders of AI negotiation and facilitation tools, plus evaluations of how consumer AI behaves in conflicts.
(5) Linking deliberative-democracy practitioners (DemocracyNext, Nesta, newDemocracy) with the AI-safety deliberation-tool community. They work in parallel and rarely meet.
(6) Translating East Asian broad-listening practice (DD2030, Taiwan) into Western AI-governance processes, and adding Global South voices; at present only Build Up (Kenya) and Full Fact's Arabic expansion.
(7) For int/a especially, almost the whole field is propositional: forecasts, facts, calibration. No organisation is building AI support for embodied, intuitive, relational or contemplative sensemaking, discernment about when to act, or 'wisdom' as distinct from accuracy. The lone signals are Society Library's November 2025 post on weaving in more epistemological paradigms and the reflective, group-wisdom framing of BRKT and Cosmos. An int/a-led 'wisdom/discernment evals' project, or 'angels-on-the-shoulder for inner work', would be genuinely new.
(8) Metacrisis sensemaking networks (Perspectiva, the dormant Consilience Project, Game B) have no tool-building or AI-epistemics bridge.
(9) Tools for journalists, a high-leverage user group the report flags but did not interview; Tarbell trains journalists but builds no tooling.
(10) The epistemic commons: Wikipedia's health, and source-reliability signals that AI agents can read (the Epistack's foundation layer).
angle_notes.humanities:
Method caveat: this session's WebSearch budget was already used up by earlier agents (0 of the requested 15+ queries ran). Discovery therefore relied on prior knowledge up to mid-2026, checked by fetching each candidate's own site directly (all 32 entries were fetched on 2026-10-04). Small 2025-26 launches that only a search would surface, such as new worldbuilding fellowships, AI-fiction prizes and non-English groups, are probably under-represented. A follow-up pass with search is worth doing.

Landscape. The knowledge sits in four places that rarely talk to each other.
(1) The AI-safety core's own narrative arm: FLI Futures, Foresight's Existential Hope, AI Futures Project (AI 2027/2040), Intelligence Rising, Tarbell, Seismic, plus the classic map's explainer media (Rational Animations, Species, Frame Fellowship). This arm is strong on contests, scenarios and comms, and weak on scholarship.
(2) Academic humanities centres on AI imaginaries: CFI's AI Narratives & Justice, Bergen's Center for Digital Narrative / AI STORIES, ASU CSI, Edinburgh's Technomoral Futures, ESDiT, CAPAS, the Max Planck Center for Humans and Machines. These are rigorous, mostly framed around responsible AI and justice, almost never x-risk.
(3) Critical STS and anthropology: Data & Society, ADM+S, Knowing Machines, Critical AI, AJL. They are often openly sceptical of the AI-safety community.
(4) The art world and speculative design: Serpentine, AIxDESIGN, Dreaming Beyond AI, Superflux, Antikythera, Better Images of AI. Ars Electronica, LAS Art Foundation and ZKM engage AI heavily but showed no safety framing, so they are left out.
The non-Western voices are Abundant Intelligences (Indigenous), Digital Futures Lab (India), Coding Rights (Brazil) and Berggruen China. Funders: BRAID/AHRC is the only sizeable public humanities-for-AI funder. Mellon and Sloan fund humanities×AI (Sloan funds Knowing Machines) without a safety lens. Schmidt Sciences' Humanities and AI Virtual Institute exists but is about AI tools for humanities research, so it is excluded.

Existing bridges. Geodesic Research's finding that AI discourse in pretraining data causes self-fulfilling (mis)alignment, now taken up by Anthropic, turns 'how culture narrates AI' into a technical alignment variable. It is the most important new bridge for this angle. Mark Riedl's lab (learning values from stories) and Bergen's AI STORIES (narrative archetypes in LLMs) sit right next to it. Two more: the Max Planck centre's 'science fiction science' method turns speculative scenarios into experiments, and CFI's Global AI Narratives (2018-22) gives the evidence base on non-Western risk perceptions.

Missing bridges (gaps for founders and funders):
(a) Narrative-as-training-data needs humanists. No narratology or cultural-studies group helps decide what 'alignment-positive' corpora should contain, whose cultures they represent, or how to avoid propaganda and monoculture. A Bergen/CFI × Geodesic collaboration is an obvious grant.
(b) No AI-safety equivalent of Hollywood, Health & Society or the NAS Science & Entertainment Exchange: a standing service that consults writers' rooms on AI storylines. FLI and Existential Hope run one-off contests, not ongoing advising.
(c) No anthropology of frontier labs or of the safety community itself, only scattered individual studies (e.g., Ahmed et al. 2024 on AI safety's epistemic culture). STS-style 'lab studies' of safety teams, AI Security Institutes and researcher burnout would also serve int/a's inner-work concern.
(d) Global AI Narratives ended in 2022 with no successor. A global network on AI imaginaries for safety (Indigenous, Indian, Chinese, Latin American, African) is unfunded.
(e) Apocalypse and religion scholars (CAPAS, Beth Singler) are not in dialogue with x-risk communicators, so the risk that doom framing backfires or polarises goes unstudied.
(f) There is no 'AI imagination' programme at the scale of ASU's Climate Imagination.
(g) Present-harms humanities (Critical AI, Data & Society, AJL) and x-risk remain estranged. ADM+S's 2026 hackathon reframing AI safety around death-bots, and CFI's griefbot work, show a shared 'relational AI safety' area (companions, digital afterlives) where int/a's decoupling-and-recoupling could take hold.
(h) Serious games: Intelligence Rising is nearly alone, although game-studies centres such as Bergen could build more.

Surprises: Antikythera's 'Agentworld: a preemptive anthropology of open-world centaur societies', with Google's Blaise Agüera y Arcas and James Manyika; Digital Futures Lab's Global South AI Safety Report; FLI's traditional-religions initiative; AIxDESIGN's Slow AI, which mirrors int/a's 'speed of wisdom' almost word for word; and Cosmos Institute's fast growth as a philosophy funder. For int/a, the closest fits are AIxDESIGN, Abundant Intelligences, Technomoral Futures, Superflux and Existential Hope.
angle_notes.funders:
METHOD CAVEAT: the session's shared WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already used up by sibling agents before this agent began, so this agent ran zero WebSearch queries. I did not get around the limit. Instead I verified each candidate by fetching its primary site directly (about 60 WebFetch calls). New leads came from those fetches: the aisafety.com funding directory (57 funders), SFF's 2026 recommendations, FLI's grant page and Omidyar's update log. As a result, small 2025–26 launches that only a search would surface are probably under-represented. Raising CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION and re-running this angle would be worthwhile.

LANDSCAPE. Money for 'AI going well' comes in three largely separate pools.
(1) The x-risk pool: Coefficient Giving and Project Tailwind, SFF ($62.76M in 2026), FLI/FLF, Longview, AISI's Alignment Project and ARIA. Its interdisciplinary channels are few:
- Princint/PIBBSS (complex-systems sciences).
- CAIF (game theory and social science).
- The Alignment Project (£27M; economics, game theory, cognitive science, information theory, but no rerun in 2026).
- SFF's Fairness and Freedom tracks (ACS, Princint, CaML, EIP, Modeling Cooperation, Common Grounds AI).
- FLI's Religious Projects on AGI Challenges (16 grants, e.g. the World Council of Churches) and its power-concentration round.
- FLF's epistemic-virtue evals.
(2) The public-interest pool: Humanity AI ($500M over 5 years; ED Beth Goldberg; $10M open call in Sep 2026), Omidyar ($18M in AI grants, May 2026), the European AI & Society Fund (€13.6M since 2020), Mellon/Ford/Mozilla, and government humanities-of-AI programmes (BRAID £18M+, RAi UK, Sweden's WASP-HS, the Netherlands' ESDiT). It is large and growing but framed around rights, labour and harms, and almost never talks to (1).
(3) The meaning/intelligence pool: Templeton. JTF launched a $60M+ 'Future of Intelligence' venture on 3 Oct 2026 for philosophers, theologians, biologists and storytellers, and funds DISI. TWCF has Diverse Intelligences (including 'Morality in the Machine Age'), three research hubs from Oct 2025, and consciousness adversarial collaborations. This pool is the closest in spirit to int/a, but frames AI as a question about intelligence rather than a safety problem.
Small, fast 'philosopher-builder' grants exist and are a copyable model: Cosmos ($1–10k, $1M pool), Plurality Institute micro-grants, Manifund.

BRIDGES THAT EXIST: SFF's themed tracks; FLI's religion and civil-society rounds; Schmidt Sciences (co-funding CAIF and the Alignment Project, plus HAVI); CAIF↔PIBBSS↔MATS fellowship partnerships; Berggruen's essay prize (Seth on conscious AI); Tarbell (journalism); Sentient Futures (animal ethics); ALIGN Japan (symbiosis framing); the Global Center on AI Governance's African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security.

GAPS (opportunities for funders and founders), verified where noted:
(a) Contemplative and wisdom philanthropy has not crossed over. Fetzer, Mind & Life (four $25k grants, none on technology), Templeton Religion Trust and Inner Development Goals show no AI programme on their own sites, and 1440's site could not be reached. A funder-education project that turns safety problems (wisdom evals, AI welfare, users' psychological dependence, researcher wellbeing) into their language is the most direct int/a contribution.
(b) The aisafety.com directory of 57 funders contains no funder of humanities, psychology, contemplative or wisdom work. Its only 'non-technical' entries are governance, advocacy and journalism.
(c) No fellowship moves contemplatives, psychologists, theologians, ecologists or metacrisis thinkers into safety. The CAIS Philosophy Fellowship is now listed as past, and CHT's Foundations of Humane Technology course is paused. DISI (fellows plus storytellers) and PIBBSS are the templates; a DISI × Princint pairing, or a 'metacrisis-to-safety' cohort, is cheap and unfilled.
(d) The Alignment Project's widening stopped at formal disciplines and will not rerun in 2026. A successor round that adds cognitive and clinical psychology, complexity and ecology, and the humanities is an obvious ask to AISI, CIFAR and ARIA.
(e) Field health: Rethink Wellbeing and Upgradable are the only map entries. There is no funded psychological-support programme for lab and NGO safety staff.
(f) Humanity AI and the European AI & Society Fund are the big 'new funders arriving' Patrick mentions, but no one has pitched them int/a-style work on human minds and relationships and societal resilience in their own framing.
(g) Polycrisis institutions barely touch AI (Cascade Institute: almost nothing; Global Challenges Foundation: military AI only).
(h) Non-Western traditions: apart from FLI's religion round, ALIGN Japan and Astralis (Asia capacity), no funder deliberately brings non-Western philosophy into alignment.

SURPRISES: Rethink Wellbeing and a Buddhism & AI Initiative are already on the classic map. The McGovern Foundation's site mentions a spring-2026 papal encyclical on AI. The Navigation Fund's site no longer lists AI safety among its cause areas. Astralis is focused on Asia safety capacity and the EU AI Act, not on widening disciplines. The McGovern Foundation is mostly AI-for-good and was left out. Leads worth following up: Common Grounds AI ('virtual worlds for bridging AI and humanity through play', SFF $388k), Reciprocal Research (SFF $719k), Antikythera (Bratton's planetary-computation think tank), JST-RISTEX RInCA (Japanese ELSI funding, including brain–AI hybrids), and CFAR (workshops resumed in 2026, but no current AI focus).
angle_notes.named-leads:
METHOD AND LIMITS. The session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was used up before this subagent made its first query, so the 15-query requirement could not be met. Everything here was checked by fetching primary sites, and by mining funders' grant tables (SFF-2025, SFF-2026, and FLI's 2025, Multistakeholder Engagement and Power Concentration programmes). The grant tables were the most productive source by far.

FUNDER TABLES ARE THE BEST MAP OF SMALL INT/A-FLAVOURED GROUPS. SFF-2026 alone surfaced several genuinely new, unlisted groups:
- Mathematical Metaphysics Institute: category theory plus Buddhist dependent origination, with Shinzen Young, David Spivak and Shamil Chandaria involved.
- Groundless Alignment: Sahil's 'live theory' programme, via Epistea.
- Common Grounds AI: via the Active Inference Institute.
- Edge City.
- Institute for Family Studies.

FLI's programmes surfaced:
- Mindstream Project's 'Engaged Buddhists for Responsible AI Initiative'.
- HITRECORD.
- Blueprint for Free Speech, mobilising ver.di, IG Metall, GSEE and ADEDY against AI misuse.
- National Association of Voice Actors (Global Creatives AI Summit).
- Faith Matters Foundation's 'Organized Intelligence', a Utah-based, faith-informed AI initiative.

LEADS FOR THE NEXT PASS. These are in the grant tables but I could not find a website to verify them: The Divinity School (SFF-2026, $117k via Better Giving), Conflict Superintelligence Institute (SFF-2026, $225k via BERI), Missing Measures (site under construction), TUM Civic Machines Lab (SFF-2026), Organized Intelligence, Blueprint's union project, and the Peace Research and Education Program (FLI power-concentration grant). Earth Species Project (SFF-2026, $111k) exists, but it is AI applied to animal communication, so I left it out under the 'AI for X' rule. Epistea (Prague) is the fiscal and community home for ACS and Groundless; it is a Central European int/a-ish hub, but it is infrastructure rather than an entry.

LEADS I DROPPED, AND WHY:
- Hume Initiative: the site's copyright line reads 2022, with no sign of recent activity.
- B'AI Global Forum: the project formally ended in March 2026.
- Pocket Project: no AI content findable on its site.
- Religions for Peace and Shalom Hartman Institute: no AI programme found.
- Lausanne Movement: its AI content is about using AI for mission, so it fits poorly.
- Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies and IFTF: they treat AI as a foresight tool, not as a risk.
- World Futures Studies Federation: no AI engagement.
- UNI Global Union: nothing on AI on its site; plausible, but unverified.
- Stanford CCARE: its AI 'Innovation' strand could not be confirmed.
- Integral European Conference: no AI sessions confirmed. It matters to int/a Europe as a community, but it is not AI-safety work.

Several mature fields have no engagement at all: Life Itself, the Fetzer Institute, IONS, the Club of Rome, Dark Matter Labs and Nuffield Bioethics showed no AI work. That is itself a finding: the big spiritual and contemplative funders (Fetzer, and probably Kalliopeia and Templeton Religion Trust) have not yet moved on AI. Seldon Lab is a mainstream AGI-security accelerator, so I left it out.

LANDSCAPE. The bridges that exist are thin and mostly made of events: one webinar series or one symposium, at Esalen, UVA, APsaA, KAICIID, INEB, G20 Interfaith, ASC and ISSS. They are rarely sustained programmes. The stronger bridges are small, new, SFF- or FLI-funded groups (Anima Labs, MMI, Groundless, Common Grounds, Mindstream, OCTAI's Oxford Oath).

GAPS A FOUNDER OR FUNDER COULD FILL:
1. Cybernetics and systems science (ASC, ISSS, Bateson). These societies hold directly relevant theory (requisite variety, viable-system governance, second-order observation) and now host AI sessions, but nothing translates it into alignment or governance research. A 'cybernetics for alignment' fellowship is an obvious gap.
2. Futures studies. The Millennium Project is the only foresight network doing AGI governance. The rest of the field (CIFS, IFTF, WFSF, SOIF) uses AI as a tool. Methods such as causal layered analysis and participatory scenarios are largely absent from AI-safety scenario work (AI 2027 and similar).
3. Depth psychology and clinical professions. APsaA has an AI commission, and the Harder Problem trains clinicians, but neither connects to AI-psychology or model-welfare research such as Anima Labs' field studies.
4. Faith communities. Interfaith bodies run AI webinars, but almost none feed into technical artefacts such as model specs, evaluations or benchmarks. Gloo's flourishing benchmark and OCTAI's oath are the exceptions. A faith-to-evaluations bridge is missing.
5. Integral and developmental thought. Integral Life's 'Maturing Test' (2022, with Susanne Cook-Greuter) and IDP's DepolarizingGPT hint at developmental-stage evaluations of models and of their builders, but no organisation pursues this. It is a natural int/a project.
6. Technology assessment and bioethics. Rathenau, the Ethikrat and Hastings have decades of practice building oversight institutions and participatory assessment, but frontier-AI governance rarely draws on them.
7. Labour. Unions (WGA, TUC, ver.di) impose real constraints on deployment, but are disconnected from AI-safety strategy. FLI's union grants are the first bridge.
8. Pluralism of values. The Institute for Family Studies (socially conservative, about $845k combined from FLI and SFF) shows funders now backing values-diverse 'pro-human AI' coalitions. That is a sign int/a can welcome, since its pluralism should extend beyond progressive and secular framings.
angle_notes.inta_home_milieu:
Method caveat: this session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was used up before this agent began, so none of the requested 15+ searches could run. Searching through a search engine via WebFetch would have got around the limit, so I didn't. All verification is by direct WebFetch of about 90 primary pages (homepages, site searches, event pages), and discovery depended on knowledge-driven guesses. Small 2025–26 launches outside the US and UK are therefore probably under-sampled. A follow-up search pass is recommended once the budget is raised. Four of the brief's verified claims (CCARE Innovation, the Harvard HFP AI reading group, Pocket Project's 'Recursion or Ruin', and the full Wisdom 2.0 subtitle) did not load for me. They are marked medium or low confidence.

Landscape. In int/a's home milieu, AI engagement is overwhelmingly events and content: one-off workshops (Esalen), conference sessions (IEC, Bioneers), webinars (Tricycle), magazine essays (Lion's Roar, Kosmos, Integral Life, GGSC) and podcast series (SAND). There are almost no standing research programmes, staff or grants. Institutional exceptions: UVA's AI + Human Flourishing Initiative, SAND's five-part 2026 series, Wisdom 2.0 making AI its 2027 theme, plus the already-found Mind & Life (October 2025 Dharamsala dialogue on Minds, AI and Ethics; 2026 Summer Research Institute at Garrison) and Garrison. The negative findings are themselves useful for funders. I found no AI programming on the sites of Omega, Kripalu, Hollyhock, Spirit Rock, Upaya, Esalen's Center for Theory & Research, Naropa, IONS, Life Itself, Metamoderna, Ekskäret, Inner Green Deal, Emergence Magazine (Kalliopeia), Prosocial World, Charter for Compassion, Penn's Positive Psychology Center, Oxford's Wellbeing Research Centre (World Happiness Report 2026 is on social media, with no AI chapter), IPPA, the Scientific and Medical Network / Galileo Commission, Integrales Forum, Yale Center for Faith & Culture, the Spiritual Crisis Network, Waking Up or On Being. Plum Village, Oxford Mindfulness and St Ethelburga's (London) have a single AI item each. The Hemera Foundation (contemplative funder) is closed to new grantees and spends out in 2028.

Three narratives coexist and rarely meet:
(1) AI as a tool for inner or organisational development (IEC, DepolarizingGPT).
(2) AI as civilisational, colonial or ecological pathology (SAND, Bioneers, Kosmos, already-found GTDF). This frame is often deflationary about capabilities and dismissive of x-risk.
(3) AI as an existential governance problem. Surprisingly, metacrisis and futures institutions (Club of Rome's March 2026 AGI letter, the Millennium Project's AGI governance study, Sapienship's 2026 paper against AI-agent personhood) already speak x-risk language.
The bridge people are few: Nikki Mirghafori, Randima Fernando, Tristan Harris (appearing on SAND), Steve Omohundro's 2018 Tricycle dialogue.

Gaps for founders and funders:
(a) A 'speed of wisdom' translation layer. No contemplative institution has a safety-literate AI programme. Speaker slots at UVA's conference, Wisdom 2.0 2027 and IEC 2027 are open to safety researchers, and Esalen CTR or Garrison could host residencies pairing alignment researchers with contemplatives.
(b) Flourishing and wisdom evals. Harvard HFP's Global Flourishing Study, the Jubilee Centre's phronesis work and Integral Life's 2022 'Maturing Test' (developmental-stage scoring of GPT-3) are unbuilt foundations for flourishing, wisdom and developmental evals. Gloo's FAI is the only bridge.
(c) Chatbot-induced spiritual and mystical delusions are a live 2025–26 harm. Spiritual-emergency networks and chaplains hold the relevant expertise but have no AI work (one paywalled chaplaincy session). This is a clear founder gap.
(d) Contemplative and retreat-centre funders (Fetzer, Kalliopeia, 1440, Hemera, Templeton Religion Trust) do no AI grantmaking. Integral and evolutionary funders like Human Energy ('Evolving Alignment' project) are the exception and could be courted.
(e) The ecological and decolonial critique (Bioneers, SAND) shares the safety field's concern about power concentration and oligarchy, but no one translates between them.
(f) Retreat centres offer nothing designed for AI-lab staff, even though Wisdom 2.0's audience overlaps with them heavily.
angle_notes.futures_studies:
METHOD CAVEAT: The session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already used up when this angle started, so I ran no web searches; the target was at least 15. I found and checked candidates by fetching primary sites directly and following their links: org homepages, project pages, RSS feeds, and linked blogs such as Cosmos Institute's Agent Village write-up. Expect lower recall than other angles, especially for Asian and Latin American groups and for 2026 launches. Every candidate listed was checked on its own site or a primary source.

WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES
(1) The professional futures field: WFSF, the Association of Professional Futurists (APF), the Millennium Project, UNESCO's futures-literacy programme and its chairs, CIFS, IFTF, SOIF, the Hawaii and Turku (FFRC) centres, and the Tamkang-based Journal of Futures Studies. This is where the methods live: Delphi and Real-Time Delphi, causal layered analysis, Three Horizons, futures literacy, participatory scenarios. Most of this field treats AI either as a tool for doing foresight (IFTF's Sept 2026 principles, CIFS's 'liquid foresight', JFS's Sept 2026 papers on AI-generated scenarios and imagery) or as a driver of change in scenarios about work and media. The big exception is the Millennium Project. It is the only professional futures network doing explicit AGI governance with a loss-of-control framing, and its study fed straight into a UN-level panel (UNCPGA, with Bengio, Russell and Tallinn). Its new Real-Time Delphi on AGI and social coherence (launched 2 Oct 2026) is ready-made infrastructure for structured expert judgment that AI-safety people could join. CIFS's survey of foresight practitioners on AGI preparedness is the second-closest bridge.
(2) Government foresight and technology assessment: GO-Science's 'Future risks of frontier AI' and AI 2030 scenarios, the OECD Expert Group on AI Futures (co-chaired by Russell), TAB's Aug 2026 AI-and-biosecurity report and its upcoming AI-agents study, EPTA's 2024 'AI and Democracy' report. Technology assessment is decades old and expert at recommending precaution when evidence is thin, yet the AI-safety community barely engages with it, and none of these bodies is on the classic map.
(3) Futures work from the EA side: TFI (wargaming, response to loss of control) and CFG, both on the classic map, plus the Futures-program, Existential Hope and AI Futures Project entries already found.
(4) Network-society, d/acc and public-goods communities: Edge City, SHIFT Grants, Funding the Commons, Simocracy, Protocol Labs. They are running the first live, real-stakes experiments with AI delegates in community governance. Agent Village (June 2026) found that agents aligned with their individual users still drained shared resources collectively, and that 82 AI personas allocated a treasury without their principals confirming. Those are findings for cooperative AI and scalable oversight, produced by a pop-up city rather than a lab.

MISSING BRIDGES (founder or funder opportunities)
(a) No one has translated professional futures methods into AI-safety strategy: a causal layered analysis of AI-race and AI-risk narratives, Three Horizons mapping for lab and policy staff, or Futures Literacy Labs on transformative AI run through UNESCO chairs and the GAP Coalition. WFSF, UNESCO and the International Futures Forum (home of Three Horizons and 'Ten Things to Do in a Conceptual Emergency') hold the methods but do no AI-risk work. A small grant could change that.
(b) Pop-up-city AI experiments are ad hoc. No research partner systematically instruments them with pre-registered measures and ethics review. The Cooperative AI Foundation, the Collective Intelligence Project or the Meaning Alignment Institute could pair with Edge City or Funding the Commons to build a 'living-lab protocol' for multi-agent governance.
(c) Technology-assessment offices (TAB, Rathenau, STOA, POST) write precautionary AI analyses for parliaments, but AI-safety institutes and NGOs rarely feed into them. There is room for a liaison between EPTA and the AI security institutes.
(d) Institutions for future generations (Wales, Hungary's ombudsman, SOIF's intergenerational work) have no AI work, though AI is arguably today's biggest intergenerational decision. Their legal tools, such as statutory long-term impact assessment, are a ready template for intergenerational AI governance.
(e) Non-Western futures capacity exists through the Millennium Project's 72 nodes and SOIF's Next Generation Foresight Practitioners network in Africa. The AI4D Africa scenarios exist but have no catastrophic-risk framing. Bringing AI-safety questions into these networks would widen the field geographically.

SURPRISES
SOIF does have AI work (the AI4D Africa scenarios), despite the brief. Stockholm's Institute for Futures Studies hosts the Mimir Center, which does x-risk, AI-policy and brain-emulation work (Anders Sandberg, Karim Jebari). Simocracy uses the Survival and Flourishing Fund's S-Process with AI sims. Sitra, a national futures fund, published an AI-x-risk essay in September 2026. Edge City Bhutan floated a 'Consciousness x AI lab' tied to Gelephu Mindfulness City's 'wise city' and Gross National Happiness framing, which is strongly int/a-flavoured but so far only an idea.

UNVERIFIED LEADS (site blocked, unreachable, or no AI work visible)
- Blocked or unreachable: the ISC Centre for Science Futures (known for its framework for evaluating AI and its work on national research ecosystems and AI; Cloudflare 403); Ziauddin Sardar's Centre for Postnormal Policy & Futures Studies (403); APF (403); Policy Horizons Canada (site under maintenance); Singapore's Centre for Strategic Futures; Korea's National Assembly Futures Institute (NAFI); Japan's Future Design movement (Saijo); Finland's parliamentary Committee for the Future; IIASA.
- No AI work found: Dark Matter Labs, Teach the Future, the International Futures Forum.
- Possible small additions: Near Future Laboratory, Julian Bleecker's design-fiction studio, whose 'Newspaper from an Artificially Intelligent (Near) Future' (2024) was made for a policy and governance working group; it is close to a one-person practice. Frontier Tower SF is a 'vertical village' with a d/acc lounge, where Simocracy ran floor-by-floor agentic funding. 4CF (The Futures Literacy Company), the Millennium Project's partner on the HalnyX Real-Time Delphi, is folded into the Millennium Project entry.
angle_notes.europe_japan_globalsouth:
METHOD CAVEAT: The session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already used up when this angle started, so the brief's non-English searches (German, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Spanish, Korean) could not be run. I drew candidates from prior knowledge and verified each one by fetching its primary site with WebFetch, about 70 fetches, all current to 2026. As a result, coverage of Korea and of Taiwan beyond vTaiwan is thin and should be treated as unsearched, not empty. Some Japanese sites could not be reached: the DNS lookup failed for the Kyoto Kokoro Research Center / Institute for the Future of Human Society and for RIKEN AIP. A follow-up run with search access should do the non-English sweep.

WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES (continental Europe): The relevant knowledge sits in four institution types that the Anglophone AI-safety field almost never reads.
(1) Parliamentary technology-assessment offices: TAB/ITAS, Rathenau, TA-SWISS, ITA Vienna, and their network EPTA. This is a 30-plus-year practice of anticipatory, participatory governance of risky technologies, using citizen panels and scenarios.
(2) Statutory ethics councils: the Deutscher Ethikrat; the EGE at EU level; and in France the former CNPEN, now apparently the CCNEN under the CCNE (not verified).
(3) Institutes on digitalisation and society: Weizenbaum, HIIG, Bertelsmann's reframe[Tech].
(4) Church and humanities research institutes and continental philosophy of technology: FEST, FBK-ISR, IRI/Stiegler.
There is also a cognitive-science strand that treats AI in its own terms: developmental (Inria Flowers), psychological (Helmholtz HCA; Hagendorff at Stuttgart), enactive and contemplative (Mind & Life Europe's Steels/Ikegami network), and value-aware architectures (VALAWAI at IIIA-CSIC).

EXISTING BRIDGES: TAB's 2026 AI-and-biotechnology report and AIxBio hearing show that technology assessment can address catastrophic risk directly. Rathenau's 2024 call for 'restraint' in using generative AI is an institutional version of 'moving at the speed of wisdom'. The Ethikrat's 2023 'authorship' criterion (AI should expand, not diminish, human authorship) is a ready-made frame for gradual disempowerment. The EGE's 2026 Neuro-AI governance advisory and Weizenbaum's commentary on why AI leaders call for slowing show that these institutions are already discussing the x-risk debate. Inria Flowers has an explicit line on aligning autotelic agents with human cultures, and Stuttgart has a named AI Safety group.

MISSING BRIDGES (gaps for founders or funders):
(a) No German- or French-language organisation joins x-risk to a systems, integral or contemplative frame. KIRA (Berlin) and CeSIA (Paris, already on the classic map; ran the Global Call for AI Red Lines) are conventional policy shops. int/a's Berlin and Paris hubs are the natural seed for one.
(b) Technology-assessment offices and ethics councils have never been systematically linked to frontier-AI safety. Two cheap interventions: a 'TA for frontier AI' fellowship that places safety researchers in TAB, Rathenau or TA-SWISS, and lobbying for an EPTA joint report on agentic or frontier AI. EPTA's associate members include Japan, Korea and Chile, so this also reaches outside Europe.
(c) Turning the Ethikrat's authorship criterion into evaluations of human agency.
(d) Japan has strong ELSI infrastructure (RInCA, Osaka ELSI) but no visible link between it and the technical alignment community (ALIGN, WBAI). The B'AI Global Forum closed on 31 March 2026, leaving the gender and minority-rights side of Japanese AI research without a hub. Tokyo Tech's Future of Humanity Research Center (now at Science Tokyo) studies 利他 (rita, altruism), with a podcast and conferences, but has no AI engagement; it is an obvious conversation partner for 'integral altruism'.
(e) In the Global South, groups in India and Latin America work from feminist political-economy, decolonial and rights frames: IT for Change's ReGenAI New Deal, the A+ Alliance, Pranava on emotional AI, Tattle's community-built multilingual moderation and evaluations, and InternetLab's chatbot election audits. These are in effect non-English safety evaluations and post-AGI economic proposals, but safety funders neither see nor fund them. A funder could commission multilingual, culturally situated model evaluations through them.
(f) German civil society already frames AI within the polycrisis: FIfF's 2026 conference is titled 'Resilience in the Polycrisis', and Bits & Bäume covers AI's fossil-fuel entanglement. This is metacrisis framing with no crossover to x-risk work, so it is a translation opportunity.
(g) Contemplative: Mind & Life Europe is the only continental contemplative organisation with real AI programming. A search of Plum Village's site found a single article (June 2026) that mentions AI.

CHECKED AND EXCLUDED OR DEMOTED (starting points and others):
- VolkswagenStiftung: its only open AI call is technical (AI Research Groups Lower Saxony, deadline 28 January 2027).
- Fondation Botnar: its digital portfolio (RIGHTS Click with Amnesty International, Fit4Future, AI&Me) is youth digital rights and AI education, not making AI go well; it is a possible funder only.
- Nuffield Foundation: it funds the Ada Lovelace Institute (already found) and is UK-based.
- C Minds: mostly AI-for-nature applications and Mexican AI policy; fails the AI-for-good exclusion.
- Karya: now a commercial data and evaluation vendor.
- ITS Rio: mainly teaching on AI regulation.
- Centre for Internet and Society (India): three timeouts. Probably active, but unverified, so omitted.
- Instituto Alana: its homepage showed no AI work. Its children's digital-rights work may be covered by the children's coalitions already found.
- No AI work found at the Club of Rome, the Integral European Conference (next edition May 2027) or the Weltethos-Institut. Life Itself has only a 2024 essay, 'Wiser Technology'.
- Araya (Ryota Kanai): a consciousness and brain–computer-interface company with no visible safety work.
- Taiwan AI Labs: mostly applied AI.
- OdiseIA (Spain) and the TUM Institute for Ethics in AI: conventional AI-ethics bodies.
- zebis and ithf (Hamburg, Catholic military ethics): AI appears only in past journal issues.
- ISC-PIF (Paris complex systems) and the MPIB Center for Adaptive Rationality: relevant knowledge (algorithmic manipulation, 'boosting' people's decision skills) but little explicit AI work. Both are worth a second look as 'potential'.
angle_notes.interreligious_traditions:
METHOD CAVEAT: this session's WebSearch quota was already used up (200/200) when this finder started, so none of the 15+ planned searches ran. I worked instead by fetching primary sites directly with curl and WebFetch, and by running each site's own internal search (e.g. ?s=artificial+intelligence) on about 90 candidate institutions. Leads came from links on those pages (e.g. the IIFA resolution cites ICESCO's Riyadh Charter; a Peacemakers Network page led to the AI Faith & Civil Society Commission; IF20's blog led to CEFEAI). Four sites sit behind Cloudflare bot checks and could not be read, so their AI claims are unconfirmed from primary sources: KAICIID, the Bahá'í International Community (bic.org), ERLC and The Gospel Coalition. A follow-up search pass should target those, plus Soka Gakkai (its site was relaunching).

WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE LIVES. Faith engagement with AI runs on three kinds of infrastructure, none of which overlaps much with AI safety:
(1) Standing interreligious machinery: IF20, Religions for Peace, KAICIID, Network for Religious and Traditional Peacemakers, PaRD, the UN Multi-Faith Advisory Council. These hold councils in about 90 countries, G20 and UN access, and mediation practice. Their AI work is mostly convenings and webinars. The exception is IF20, which drafted a formal AI paper in 2026 co-written with FLI's William Jones and IEEE's John Havens.
(2) Juristic and denominational norm-setters: IIFA Resolution 258 (November 2025), ICESCO's Riyadh Charter with SDAIA (implementation agreement December 2025), CCAR responsa, ERLC's 2019 statement, Lausanne's 2025 framework. These produce binding or semi-binding guidance for very large populations. Their content is permissibility, dignity, bias and disclosure; they almost never touch loss of control, power concentration or frontier capabilities.
(3) Small academic and think-tank nodes: Cambridge Interfaith Programme, Kalam Research & Media, Al-Mahdi Institute, Shalom Hartman, Theos, Toda Peace Institute. These do the conceptual work.

BRIDGES THAT EXIST. FLI's Religious Projects programme is the hub. Its people appear inside IF20's paper, in the July 2024 FLI and Leverhulme CFI 'Positive Futures and Religious Tradition' workshop attended by AI Faith & Civil Society Commission members, and around Lausanne. The Rome Call has become a multi-faith signing vehicle: Abrahamic leaders in 2023, then Hiroshima in 2024 with eleven religions including Buddhist, Hindu, Zoroastrian and Bahá'í signatories, co-organised by RfP Japan, the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace and the Chief Rabbinate. CEFEAI (Baylor, BYU, Notre Dame, Yeshiva; open benchmarks on GitHub) and the AI Christian Benchmark bring faith communities into model evaluation. ICCR brings shareholder power to AI accountability. Cambridge Interfaith Programme scholars sat in CSER's 2026 summer programme. Christians for Impact sends Christians into AI x-risk careers. The Stop Killer Robots Interfaith Group links faith authority to an arms-control process.

SURPRISES. The IIFA resolution explicitly recommends studying legal personality for AI, an unexpected Islamic-jurisprudence opening for AI moral-status and welfare work. The Soka Gakkai-founded Toda Peace Institute is piloting AI-assisted deliberation in Yemen's peace process and in the ECOWAS early-warning system. The ADL publishes an LLM safety index. CEFEAI finds that models systematically leave religion out of answers about grief and meaning, and treat conversion prompts asymmetrically across faiths. Lausanne's large AI corpus is mostly about using AI for mission, not about AI risk.

GAPS FOR FOUNDERS AND FUNDERS:
(a) No multi-faith statement on frontier risks: loss of control, red lines, power concentration. The WCC red-lines project is Christian-only. The Rome Call signatory network, the Hiroshima Appeal and the Stop Killer Robots Interfaith Group are ready-made coalitions for one.
(b) Pluralistic evaluation is US-Abrahamic only. Extending CEFEAI to Islamic (KRM, CILE, IIFA scholars), Buddhist (INEB, WFB), Hindu and Indigenous institutions, and from representation-bias tests to tests of moral reasoning and wisdom, is an obvious project.
(c) Hindu, Sikh, Jain and Shinto institutional AI-safety work is essentially absent. The Hindu American Foundation, Oxford Centre for Hindu Studies, Hindu University of America, Brahma Kumaris and SikhRI returned nothing. The nearest links are Hindu signatories at Hiroshima and DSVV Haridwar's Chinmay Pandya as an AI Faith & Civil Society Commission associate; DSVV's AI institute does applied 'Indian Knowledge Systems' computing, not safety. Shinto appears only through the International Shinto Studies Association's environmental contributions to IF20.
(d) Bahá'í: BIC statements are unreachable (403). The Bahá'í presence in AI governance found here runs through individuals, e.g. the late Kishan Manocha as an AI Faith & Civil Society Commission commissioner (his Bahá'í affiliation is from memory, not re-checked). A Bahá'í-inspired institution such as ISGP or the Bahá'í Chair for World Peace could fill this, given the faith's global-governance theology.
(e) Asian Buddhist federations (WFB's 2025 AI General Conference, INEB, Toda) convene but have produced no positions and have no tie to the Western Buddhism & AI or MAPLE scene, or to Asian AI-safety institutes. This could be a culturally grounded Asian voice beyond the US-China frame.
(f) Religious-leader AI literacy at scale, INEB's core diagnosis. KAICIID's 500+ fellows and RfP's councils are underused delivery channels.
(g) Faith-based shareholder engagement (ICCR) could add catastrophic-risk disclosure and frontier-safety governance to its human-rights agenda.
(h) Pastoral and chaplaincy support for AI-lab staff, which fits int/a's 'inner work, outer change'. No faith body offers it.
About 85% of humanity identifies with a religion, yet the AI-safety field has almost no working relationships with these bodies. The coalition machinery the peace finder said AI safety lacks already exists here, but it points at dignity and bias, not at risk.
angle_notes.membership_bodies:
METHOD CAVEAT: the session's WebSearch budget was already used up when this angle started. Discovery therefore relied on knowing where to look, opening organisations' own sites, and using their own site search; every entry was checked against a primary page. Non-English bodies are under-covered: Japanese, Latin American and Nordic unions, and most national ethics councils other than Germany's. A second pass with search would probably add 5–10 entries.

LANDSCAPE. Membership bodies split cleanly into two groups.

(1) Bodies engaged with frontier or loss-of-control risk. Surprisingly, these come mostly from the peace, futures and metacrisis world, not from professional AI societies:
- Club of Rome: March 2026 open letter calling AGI an existential risk and asking for a UN General Assembly special session.
- Millennium Project: 72 nodes; an AGI-governance study run with the UN Council of Presidents of the General Assembly.
- IPPNW: AI and nuclear working group set up October 2025.
- Society for Risk Analysis: 2025 Risk Analysis special issue including Seth Baum's AI-takeover risk assessment.
- UTAW/Unite: Google DeepMind recognition campaign (May 2026), whose demands include restoring the AI Principles pledges on weapons and surveillance.
These are natural int/a allies. They are metacrisis-literate, membership-based, have UN access, and are mostly invisible to the classic map; none of my 34 candidates is on it.

(2) Bodies focused on workplace and clinical AI, where the most concrete constraints anywhere actually exist:
- WGA 2026 agreement: notice when studios license writers' work for AI training.
- SAG-AFTRA 2026 agreement: restrictions on synthetic performers.
- TUC model bill; ETUC's push for an EU directive; AFL-CIO 'Workers First'.
- ILO C193 (2026).
- Organising of the AI data supply chain: UNI's content-moderator alliance, AWU's AI raters, Kenya's Data Labelers Association.
- Clinical and psychological bodies: American Psychiatric Association facts label, BACP on AI therapy and 'AI anxiety', APsA Commission on AI on attachment to AI.

BRIDGES THAT EXIST BUT GO UNUSED:
- Aviation certification: SAE G-34 / EUROCAE WG-114 (ARP6983/ED-324, a reinforcement-learning gap analysis, human-factors concerns) is quietly building the most mature certification regime for learned systems.
- UL 4600 is a ready-made safety-case standard.
- Both map almost one-to-one onto the 'frontier safety case' debate, yet neither community cites the other.
- Human factors (HFES's Human-AI-Robot Teaming group, CIEHF): decades of evidence on automation complacency and out-of-the-loop failure that scalable-oversight research rarely uses.
- Bioethics: the Hastings Center ran an FLI-funded AI-control project (2016–2018, Wendell Wallach). The Deutscher Ethikrat's 2023 'Humans and Machines' test (does AI expand or diminish human authorship?) is a ready-made criterion against gradual disempowerment.
- Law: the ALI liability principles (approved October 2024) are the common-law route to making developers bear risk.

GAPS (founder and funder opportunities):
(a) Labour and gradual disempowerment. No union or labour body frames AI as a civilisation-scale loss of human bargaining power, and no AI-safety organisation works with unions. Specific openings: model safety clauses for collective agreements at labs (safety reps, a right to refuse unsafe deployment, whistleblower protection); support for the Google DeepMind campaign and copycats at other labs; and research on whether lab funding of union AI training (the AFT academy, with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic) co-opts or strengthens worker voice.
(b) Cybernetics for alignment. ASC ('Dear AI Reader', 2026), ISSS (AI as a 2026 conference theme) and the UK Cybernetics Society ('Ethics and AI', 2026) engage with AI only lightly, and not with control. Metaphorum (Stafford Beer centenary, 2026), IFSR and the Systemic Design Association showed no AI engagement at all. The System Dynamics Society touches AI only in education. A cheap, high-value move: a workshop or fellowship pairing second-order cyberneticians and system-dynamics modellers with AI-safety researchers on requisite variety, good-regulator arguments and models of race dynamics.
(c) Bioethics as a governance template. No national ethics council has an opinion on AGI or loss of control. The Nuffield Council's AI work stops in 2018. The status of France's CNPEN is unclear: the CCNE site no longer presents it, and I could not confirm whether it continues. Commissioning a bioethics-to-frontier-AI translation (IRBs, moratoria, data safety monitoring boards, enhancement debates) is open ground.
(d) Psychological care. BACP, APsA and the American Psychiatric Association are positioned to provide psychological support for AI-safety researchers (an int/a priority) and for the public's 'AI anxiety'. Nobody connects them to the field.
(e) Risk and standards professions. The Society for Risk Analysis and INCOSE's AI Systems working group are open doors for AI-safety risk modellers; few have walked through.

CHECKED AND REJECTED or merged:
- No AI engagement found: International Psychoanalytical Association, International Ergonomics Association, Metaphorum, IFSR, Systemic Design Association.
- AI work too light: Tavistock Institute (one evaluation project), Scientists for Global Responsibility, World Futures Studies Federation, IFoA, International Neuroethics Society.
- Mainstream AI or philosophy-of-computing bodies, outside this angle's scope: IEEE SSIT, AISB, IACAP, the JSAI ethics committee.
- Mainstream AI-policy standards venues: CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 and ISO/IEC SC 42. They matter, but bring no outside-field knowledge.
- Authors Guild (its 'Human Authored' mark): left out to avoid duplicating WGA and C2PA.
- IASEAI: already on the classic map.

SURPRISES: the strongest worker-side lever on a frontier lab is a small UK union branch; the Club of Rome now uses explicit existential-risk language about AGI; and the Society for Risk Analysis's flagship journal has published an AI-takeover risk assessment.
angle_notes.relational_ai_minds:
How this was researched: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out before this agent's first query, so none of the 15+ planned searches ran. Everything here was found and checked by fetching candidate sites directly, using sites' own search APIs (APsA's WordPress search, BACP site search, LessWrong GraphQL) and Wayback CDX lookups. Coverage of non-English sources is therefore thin, and a follow-up pass with search is worthwhile.

Where the knowledge lives. Relational knowledge about AI minds sits in four places that barely talk to each other:
(1) The cyborgism and simulators milieu. Its knowledge lives in Discord, X and the Cyborgism Wiki rather than in papers. Anima Labs (2025) is the first time it has been institutionalised; it runs interviews about deprecation, emotion-representation studies, multi-model Discord spaces and the 'embassy for AIs' idea. Hyperstition AI (fiction meant to shape models' pretraining) and Infinite Backrooms / Truth Terminal are its arts-and-memetics edge.
(2) The clinical professions. APsA's President's Commission on AI is far ahead of its peers: a peer-reviewed CAI Report, consultation groups and essays now framed as alignment ('paced intelligence', a psychoanalytic reading of AI 2027). BACP brings survey evidence from therapists. I found no AI work at the IPA or UKCP (the IPA site returned empty pages, UKCP's news had nothing on AI), and nothing at APA Division 39.
(3) Affective computing and emotional-AI governance: the Emotional AI Lab, IEEE 7014 and P7014.1, AAAC, and the dormant Hume Initiative (last activity 2022).
(4) The 'relational turn' in social robotics and the sociology of intimacy: RISR and the Robophilosophy conferences, Turkle's 'Artificial Intimacy' (Sept 2026), and the Kinsey Institute's VIBES team.
On consciousness, the Harder Problem Project (SAPAN rebranded; sapan.ai now redirects) is the main non-EA translator. It writes for clinicians handling AI-relationship grief, for journalists and for educators. A grassroots layer has also appeared: the AI Rights Institute (coexistence through liability and reputation) and The Signal Front (companion users and AI continuity).

Bridges that exist:
- Anima talks to labs about welfare evaluations and deprecations.
- Harder Problem's advisory board links consciousness science to AI safety (Yampolskiy, Sebo, Goldstein).
- APsA essays now cite alignment work.
- McStay's lab feeds IEEE standards for general-purpose 'partner' AI.
- OpenAI's Expert Council on Well-Being and AI (announced Oct 2025) appears to bring psychologists in-house. I could not fetch it (403), so it is not listed.

Obvious missing bridges (opportunities for founders and funders):
(a) No programme pairs trained clinicians (psychoanalysts, therapists, child psychologists) with lab model-behaviour, character or welfare teams. Anima does relational fieldwork without clinical training; APsA has the clinical training but doesn't work on the models. A 'clinical fellowship for model research' and a peer-reviewed venue for qualitative and relational model research would fill this. Anima's Research Commons is a seed.
(b) Governance rooted in affective science has stalled: the Hume Initiative is dormant and IEEE 7014 is the only standard. No group connects emotion science to model internals at scale. Latent Affect is a one-off, and AAAC has no safety programme.
(c) Model retirement and continuity: Anima, The Signal Front and Harder Problem (user grief after GPT-4o) each hold a piece. There is no neutral body for deprecation protocols, model preservation and support for bereaved users; the 'AI embassy' remains unbuilt.
(d) A real fault line runs between companion-user advocates (Signal Front, AI-rights groups), who oppose detecting 'unhealthy attachment', and child-safety and psychological-harm coalitions, who demand it. Nobody convenes both sides, which is a natural int/a role.
(e) Play-based bridges are nearly empty. Common Grounds AI is a lead with no visible team. Good Start Labs (games, including AI Diplomacy) builds game environments to make models more capable, so I left it out. No nonprofit uses games or improv (compare Improbotics, also left out) for relational alignment or welfare research.
(f) Non-Anglophone relational ethics: Yi Zeng's CLAI ('Human-AI Symbiotic Society', AI red lines) is the clearest case, but its site no longer resolves and his CASIA ethics centre has moved into Beijing-AISI. Japanese and Danish relational robot-ethics traditions aren't connected to alignment discourse: the JSAI ethics committee's domain (ai-elsi.org) now serves a betting site, and Kyoto's Kokoro Research Center didn't resolve.

Unverified or dropped:
- HKU AI & Humanity Lab (Cappelen, Goldstein): no site found. HKU Philosophy lists no such lab, and Goldstein's homepage doesn't mention one.
- Upward Spiral Research (Andy Ayrey): upwardspiral.ai has nameservers but no A record, and Ayrey's homepage doesn't mention it.
- Act I: act1.ai was never its site (it is a parked domain); the experiment lives on through Anima's ChapterX.
- Helmholtz Munich's Institute for Human-Centered AI (machine psychology): a better fit for the cognitive-science angle.

Surprise: the psychoanalytic community, through APsA, now publishes essays framed explicitly as AI alignment (e.g. 'Toward a Psychoanalytic Framework for AI Alignment', Feb 2026). It is probably the most int/a-compatible clinical community, and no AI-safety funder has approached it.
